So, should parents worry that moving to Mexico will limit their children’s academic or athletic opportunities? Golden’s answer is both yes and no. Certain resources and facilities are undeniably easier to access in the United States, he says, particularly in sports. But access and opportunity aren’t necessarily the same thing.

“If you’re motivated, you can find the people or the place to practice that sport,” Golden said.

But when I asked if he wished our family had stayed in New York, he didn’t hesitate.

“No, I don’t,” Golden said. He credits Mexico, and particularly the people he grew up around, with making him who he is today. “I wouldn’t be myself if I didn’t grow up in this place.”

Zella Golden grew up in San Miguel de Allende and is a senior in high school in Marin, California. Golden is completing an internship with MND.

World.title: MND Local: Murals, an eclipse and aura farming in San Miguel de Allende
World.content:
The arroyo mural project is finally dedicated, a botanical sculptor reveals his latest project, a partial lunar eclipse is on its way, a spreading social phenomenon is coming to town and registration is open for the 2027 writers’ conference. Read on about some of the many community activities happening in and around San Miguel de Allende this month.

Mural project dedicated along the Las Cachinches Arroyo

A dozen new large-scale murals were dedicated Aug. 1 along 90 meters of the Las Cachinches Arroyo just west of Calzada de la Aurora and across from Fábrica La Aurora.

The mural corridor project, coordinated by Audubon de México, was designed to transform the previously neglected area into an open-air gallery celebrating the arroyo’s history, ecology and enduring presence.

“A lot of people don’t even know it’s there,” said Audubon de México President April Gaydos. “It will be a lovely green place for people to walk.”

Gaydos emphasized that the area is often “tagged” with graffiti, and that “murals are a deterrent for tagging.” She added, “There have been studies done on this. It’s educational as much as creating a place people want to visit.”

See the Audubon de México website for additional details about the project and the artists and sponsors who participated.

Regular cleanup efforts are also taking place along the Las Cachinches Arroyo. Volunteers have spent their Saturdays hauling out a large amount of garbage from between Calzada de la Aurora and Canción de India.

This work is being organized by Colectiva Ecología en la Montaña with coordination by Gabriel González and Juanita Nolasco. For more information or to donate to the arroyo cleanup project, email arroyocachinches@gmail.com.

Botanical sculptures combine wood, plants and metal

“Rooted in Rust” is former landscape designer Matt Wilson’s latest artistic project. The work combines reclaimed iron relics, wood and succulent plants in permanent botanical sculptures.

“For 1,000 years, you’ve seen a single plant in a pot,” Wilson told Mexico News Daily. “Mine is a single composition with color, with a filler plant, and everything that hangs out of the pot is called the spiller. Those make up the criteria, and they’re very attractive, and nobody else is doing that in San Miguel.”

Wilson hails from San Diego and lived in the San Francisco Bay Area for 40 years. He then moved to Costa Rica for four years and relocated to the Los López area south of San Miguel about 3.5 years ago. He started creating the Rooted in Rust sculptures last year.

“My girlfriend asked me, ‘Can you do something with this metal suitcase?’ and I laughed, and I said, ‘Of course, what do you want?’ So I came up with this succulent, which were unfamiliar to me, and there are thousands of succulents,” he said.

Wilson said the plants grew quickly, and in six months, the result was a “very nice” sculpture.

“I saw there was something there, and it really engaged my creative side,” he said. “I went out and bought an old rusted inner spring mattress, an old rusted tricycle with no rubber on the tires and an old Coca-Cola cooler. I put on an exhibition, and people said, ‘Oh, that’s great,’ and it just went from there.”

More images of Wilson’s work can be seen here.

Partial lunar eclipse coming later this week

The partial lunar eclipse starting Thursday night and ending early Friday morning is expected to be visible from San Miguel. The penumbral eclipse will begin about 7:23 p.m. Thursday in the east-southeast and reach maximum eclipse about 10:12 p.m., creating a reddish-orange effect known as an “almost blood moon.”

A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth moves directly between the sun and the moon, casting the Earth’s shadow onto the moon’s surface. They only occur during a full moon when the sun, the Earth and the moon all line up.

Close to 1 billion people in South and North America will be able to fully see the eclipse, while more than 3 billion should be able to view part of the five-hour event. According to NASA, a similar eclipse last occurred on Aug. 16, 2008, and the next one will be on Sept. 7, 2044.

Ready for an ‘Aura Farming Battle’ this Sunday?

It’s possible to observe the social phenomenon of “aura farming” on Sunday at 3 p.m. at Parque Juarez on the small basketball courts. The prize is 500 pesos.

Aura farming is a trend that started on TikTok and Instagram and consists of young participants silently making moves designed to appear confident and cool without seeming deliberate. The audience’s response decides who wins.

Aura farming battles have been spreading throughout Mexico, with recent ones occurring in Mexico City, Veracruz and Coahuila. Additional gatherings have been reported in Argentina, Brazil, Peru and Bolivia.

Writers’ Conference registration discount ending soon

The San Miguel Writers’ Conference and Literary Festival is offering $95 off its registration packages until Aug. 31. The regular prices go into effect Sept. 1.

Scheduled for Feb. 10-14, 2027, at the Hotel Real de Minas, the conference will feature keynotes by U.S. authors Amor Towles and Jennifer Finney Boylan, Canadian author Michelle Good and Mexican author Martha Bátiz, along with literary presentations, workshops and many other events.

More information, along with the 2027 conference schedule, bilingual programming and free community events, is available here.

Cathy Siegner is an independent journalist based in San Miguel and Montana. She has journalism degrees from the University of Oregon and Northwestern University.

World.title: México Canta and Spotify partner up to amplify young talent across Mexico-US border
World.content:
México Canta is turning up the volume for its second season, tapping the music streaming service Spotify to give the cross-border contest’s top singers even more exposure.

The partnership will give the 14 semifinalists from Mexico and the United States an official Spotify playlist and offer them a career-development master class, and the three winners will be invited to a Spotify flagship event for emerging artists, the Mexican government said in a press release.

México Canta (Mexico Sings) is a federal initiative led by the Culture Ministry in collaboration with the Mexican Music Council.

Open to Mexican and Mexican American artists ages 18 to 29, it is akin to “American Idol” with one overriding rule: It seeks songs promoting themes such as love, tradition and culture rather than glorifying violence, drugs, discrimination or misogyny.

Unlike last year’s inaugural contest — which staged semifinals in Chicago, Houston, Los Angeles, Tijuana, Oaxaca and Mexico City that blossomed into must-see TV — this year’s whittling-down process was left in the hands of the Mexican Music Council. It reviewed online auditions to determine the best of more than 16,000 entries (about 1,200 more than last year).

Of the 5,760 U.S.-based registrants, seven were chosen for the first semifinal, which was Sunday at the Orpheum Theatre in Los Angeles. It produced three finalists.

The second semifinal is scheduled for Sunday at the Ángela Peralta Theater in Mazatlán, where three more finalists will be selected, plus a wild card from either semifinal. The contest drew 10,528 registrants from Mexico.

The finals are set for Sept. 13 at the Auditorio Nacional in Mexico City, where winners will be selected in three as-yet-unnamed categories. Last year’s titles were for best performer and best song, alongside a wild-card pick.

The agreement with Spotify comes during a boom in regional Mexican music.

Global listening to the genre on Spotify has risen 450% over the last five years, while consumption in Mexico increased 560%, the Ministry of Culture noted. Moreover, more than 70% of Spotify Mexico’s daily Top 50 is made up of Mexican artists compared to 10% a decade ago, the ministry added.

Also, for the first time, Mexico has entered the world’s 10 largest recorded-music markets, noted Spotify representative Karen Duque.

“A decade ago, it was quite difficult to imagine that Mexico would become one of the most important powers in the world of the music industry,” she said.

Following the finals in Mexico City, the three winners will be scheduled to perform during Mexican Independence Day celebrations on Sept. 15.

With reports from La Jornada and Informador

World.title: Mexico’s first solar panel recycling plant coming to Jalisco
World.content:
The western state of Jalisco will soon boast Mexico’s very first solar panel recycling plant, an installation with the capacity to recover up to 95% of the materials from equipment that reaches the end of its useful life.

The project evolved in response to the growth of photovoltaic generation in Jalisco, which has approximately 1.6 million installed solar panels, equivalent to about 50,000 tonnes of equipment.

Rafiqui — a non-profit civil organization dedicated to recycling and repurposing — is building the plant in Ciudad Guzmán, about 125 kilometers south of the state capital, Guadalajara.

In its initial phase, the recycling plant is expected to process up to 1,000 tonnes of “retired” solar panels annually, recovering core materials like silicon, aluminum and silver to be used in other production chains.

Rafiqui director Ximena Cantú said her company’s model “goes beyond recycling because we believe in the circular economy.”

Before sending any materials to the recycling plant, the decommissioned equipment will be evaluated to determine if it is still functional. Those that remain in suitable condition may be reused or donated to communities and non-profit organizations.

Manuel Gómez-Herrera Lasso, executive director of the Mexican Photovoltaic Industry Association, praised Jalisco as a pioneer in the adoption of solar energy. The first photovoltaic system interconnected to the national energy grid was installed in Jalisco in 2007.

The growth of the technology, however, presents a challenge for managing the waste generated by the replaced equipment.

The International Renewable Energy Agency estimates that 30,000 tonnes of solar panels in Mexico will be retired due to premature failure by 2030, while at the same time 6,500 tonnes will reach the end of their life cycle naturally.

As part of the strategy to address this, Rafiqui has established a collection center in a southern Guadalajara neighborhood to receive small volumes. It has also developed a collection scheme for larger quantities in different regions of the country.

Additionally, Rafiqui is holding discussions with municipalities and industrial associations to expand the alternatives for collecting solar panels in Jalisco.

With reports from Mexico Industry, Jalisco TV and El Financiero

World.title: Schneider Electric plans major Querétaro expansion to meet growing power demand
World.content:
Schneider Electric, a France-based multinational, plans to expand its manufacturing capacity in Querétaro state with 115,000 square meters of new industrial facilities that will support the creation of 4,000 direct jobs by the end of 2027, the company has announced.

The expansion includes two completed facilities and a third planned for a later growth phase, where the firm will manufacture solutions for electrical distribution, equipment for critical energy infrastructure, and specialized projects under custom “engineer-to-order” (ETO) models.

Schneider Senior Vice President of Power Systems and ETO Guillaume Le Gouic said that Querétaro, in Mexico’s Bajío region, provides the talent, industrial capacity, and strategic location required to advance the region’s electrification and digitalization processes.

“We are very pleased to continue growing in Querétaro, and very grateful for the support of the state government,” Schneider Mexico and Central America President Luis D’Acosta Anezin said. “The truth is, we feel right at home here, and this is the first of many investments to come, and we’re very happy and excited.”

According to the announcement, Schneider is now hiring between 200 and 250 workers a month and training engineers, technicians, and specialists in advanced manufacturing and energy infrastructure to support its operations.

Querétaro Governor Mauricio Kuri González met with Schneider Electric executives last Wednesday to discuss the project. While the company did not share an investment figure, Kuri González said he expects the total job creation from new facilities to reach 7,000 or 8,000 by 2028.

Schneider currently has production plants in Querétaro, Nuevo León, and Tlaxcala, supporting industrial demand in North America and Central America.

The firm aims to strengthen production for sectors with a higher demand for electrical infrastructure, such as data centers, industry and the digital economy.

In a 2025 interview with MND, the president and managing director of Schneider Electric Mexico & Central America, Jesús Carmona Colina, said that President Claudia Sheinbaum had “correctly recognized that more energy is needed in Mexico” to meet demand, including from the country’s growing industrial sector.

He noted an energy imbalance in Mexico, with sufficient electricity in some regions and a shortfall in others.

As part of its overarching economic strategy, Plan México, the government aims to increase electricity generation by 22,000 megawatts by 2030, investing US $12.3 billion over the next six years to build new power plants, $7.5 billion to strengthen transmission networks and $3.6 billion to improve distribution networks.

With reports from Mexico Industry, Mexico Now and TYT

World.title: Despite a Q2 dip, first-semester Foreign Direct Investment was Mexico’s highest ever
World.content:
Listen to this article

Mexico attracted US $34.968 billion in Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) between January and June 2026, marking the highest amount ever recorded for a first semester, the Economy Ministry (SE) reported.

The figure represents a 2.1% year-on-year increase compared to the same period last year and confirms Mexico’s continued appeal as a destination for established international companies.

Going back further, foreign investment practically doubled, with an accumulated growth of 89.7%, compared to the first half of 2021, when Mexico attracted US$18.433 billion,

The 2026 advance lost momentum, however, during the second quarter, when revenues reached $10.464 billion, 3.5% less than the $10.848 billion originally recorded during the same period in 2025.

The SE attributed the contraction to last year’s high base of comparison and indicated that it does not represent a change in trend. Despite the year-on-year decline, the result for the second quarter of 2026 was the second highest in the last 16 years.

Who received the foreign investment?

The manufacturing industry was the primary recipient of the arriving resources, receiving $13.482 billion, equivalent to 38.6% of total FDI. The figure represents a 9.3% year-over-year increase for manufacturing.

Financial and insurance services ranked second, with $10.15 billion, followed by the transportation, postal, and warehousing sectors, which registered the strongest growth, attracting $2.65 billion.

Mexico City came in as the top destination for foreign investment, receiving $16.862 billion, or 48.2% of the national total. It was followed by Nuevo León, with $3.712 billion; México state, with $2.114 billion; Baja California, with $1.743 billion; and Jalisco, with $1.406 billion.

Together, these five states accounted for 73.9% of all FDI received during the first half of the year.

Where did the first semester FDI come from?

In the first half of 2026, the United States remained the leading source of FDI in Mexico, with a flow of $16.871 billion, equivalent to 48.2% of the total.

Spain ranked second with $4.954 billion, followed by Canada ($1.741 billion), Australia ($1.698 billion) and Germany ($1.647 billion).

According to the SE, the positive FDI numbers are attributed to the country’s macroeconomic and institutional fundamentals and the guidelines of Plan México, the government’s flagship economic and policy strategy.

World.title: MND Local: Is the tourism outlook in Los Cabos improving?
World.content:
Spring was a poor season for tourism in Mexico. International air arrivals — the driver of 80% of all tourism revenue in the country, with two out of every three passengers hailing from the U.S. — were down nationwide in March, April and May.

That trend continued in June, as spring turned to summer, despite Mexico’s role as a host for the 2026 FIFA World Cup. But outside of the host cities, which received a boost from the event — albeit not to the extent expected — high-value tourism to traditional beach tourism destinations in Mexico like Los Cabos continued to plummet. International air arrivals fell 7.1% in Los Cabos in March, 9.7% in April, 10.5% in May and 14.2% in June, relative to the same months in 2025.

July was even worse, with international air arrivals falling by 16.6%. That means that in the first seven months of the year, international tourism fell by 7.2% in Los Cabos, with overall tourism declining by 5.4%. Unfortunately, things don’t look much better for the second half of the year, with U.S. air bookings for the next six months down 13% from 2025.

That said, there are some signs of a brightening outlook for Los Cabos.

Domestic tourism is beginning to improve

After seeing falling numbers for 10 straight months — from July 2025 to April 2026 — the domestic travel market has recently shown signs of life in Los Cabos. Domestic arrivals nosed into positive numbers in May and were up 7% in July, with nearly 20,000 more Mexican nationals visiting the destination relative to the same month in 2025.

Low season rates are part of the appeal. High season prices typically peak in April (US $470 per night for hotels in 2026), with summer seeing lower average hotel room rates in Cabo San Lucas (US $336 as of the most recent numbers from May) and San José del Cabo (US $339), as well as for the destination as a whole (US $414).

But since airline bookings for the next six months are up 5.4% domestically, with a better than 9% increase in passengers from Mexico City expected through the end of the year, it appears that this isn’t just a seasonal spike, but rather a welcome return to form for what has traditionally been an important market, accounting for over one-third of overall tourists to Los Cabos.

Tourism from Canada is on the uptick

The Canadian tourism market is not as robust as the U.S., at least not in Los Cabos. Last year, for example, over two million tourists from the U.S. visited Los Cabos, versus 215,000 from Canada. So even though tourism from Canada is up 8.8% in 2026, that doesn’t make up for U.S. tourism being down by more than 7%.

Still, it’s significant that numbers are up this year for visitors from Canada, as well as for visitors from Europe, the Caribbean, and Central and South America. This diversification is important to the local economy, especially if U.S. tourism to Mexico continues to slump.

Cruise tourism continues to boom

The reason international arrivals are considered “high-value” is because these tourists, on average, spend more than US $1,300 each. Cruise ship tourists, by contrast, traditionally spend less than US $100 per person. Every little bit helps, however, especially when it comes to keeping businesses alive in downtown Cabo San Lucas.

Last year, the Land’s End city set a record, surpassing one million cruise ship tourists for the first time. This year, that record will almost certainly be broken, as through June, cruise ship arrivals were up by 64.5% through June; 789,919 through the first six months of 2026, compared to 480,198 during the same timeframe in 2025.

If this pace continues, Cabo San Lucas will top 1.5 million cruise ship passengers for the year, cementing its position as the nation’s fourth largest cruise ship destination, behind only Cozumel, Mahahual and Ensenada.

New air routes added to replace those that have been lost

Airline capacity cuts due to rising jet fuel costs, combined with a declining demand for seats to Mexican beach destinations, have led to the cancelation of several Los Cabos-bound routes this year, including the loss of Southwest flights from Baltimore, Chicago and Indianapolis, and a Delta flight from Seattle.

Fortunately, though, new flights have been added this summer to make up for, or at least mitigate, previous tourist losses. Southwest added its first nonstop flight from Las Vegas to Los Cabos during the first week of June, the same week a new domestic route was added by Volaris connecting Puebla to Los Cabos.

Once high season returns this fall, expanded service to Los Cabos will also be offered by several airlines, including Volaris in Mexico; American, Southwest and United in the U.S.; and Air Transat, Porter and WestJet in Canada.

Chris Sands is a writer and editor for Mexico News Daily, and the former Cabo San Lucas local expert for the USA Today travel website 10 Best and writer of Fodor’s Los Cabos travel guidebook. He has also contributed to numerous other websites and publications, including The San Diego Union-Tribune, Marriott Bonvoy Traveler, Forbes Travel Guide, Porthole Cruise and Travel, and Cabo Living.

World.title: Honduras CNBS Warns Public as Investment Fraud Schemes Proliferate
World.content:

Central America · ECONOMY

Key Facts — The alert the Honduras CNBS warned on 25 August 2026 of proliferating fraudulent investment and money-collection schemes

— The advice verify that any person or entity is authorized before handing over money or investing

— The risk resources given to unauthorized entities have no legal protection or supervision, the regulator said

— The names in a March statement, the regulator flagged the platforms UNIFIN, Monavex and Cryptaespon as unregulated

— The precedent the Koriun Inversiones scheme promised five percent weekly interest and left around 30,000 victims

Honduras’s financial regulator warned of proliferating fraudulent investment schemes and reminded the public that money given to unauthorized entities has no legal protection.

Honduras’s banking and insurance regulator issued a public alert on 25 August 2026 over what it called the proliferation of fraudulent investment and money-collection schemes. The Honduras CNBS urged citizens to verify that any person or company taking their money is duly authorized, warning that funds handed to unauthorized entities have no legal protection.

The Central Bank of Honduras building in Tegucigalpa. The Honduras CNBS, the country’s financial supervisor, warned on 25 August 2026 of proliferating fraud schemes.

What the Regulator Announced

In a statement reported by Hondudiario, Tiempo and Proceso on 25 August 2026, the National Banking and Insurance Commission said it was acting under its constitutional and legal mandate to safeguard financial stability and protect Hondurans’ assets. The Honduras CNBS said possible fraudulent schemes are proliferating and putting the savings and resources of families across the country at risk.

According to the regulator, these schemes promote supposed investment, savings and equipment subleasing services while promising quick, risk-free income. They typically request membership fees, guarantee deposits or advance payments in exchange for the supposed benefits.

The commission reminded the public that no individual or company may collect resources from the public without proper authorization. It recommended avoiding platforms that promise quick profits or excessive returns, that operate through social networks, applications or unverifiable links, or that provide no clear information about who runs them or where they are located.

No Legal Protection for Victims

Resources delivered by any means to unauthorized entities or persons do not have legal protection or supervision from the commission or other entities, the statement said, a line local outlets highlighted as the core of the warning.

The alert coincided with a new case reaching prosecutors. Prosecutor’s office spokesman Yuri Mora confirmed that a citizen from western Honduras filed a complaint on Monday 24 August against a company he accused of running a pyramid-style fraud. The citizen handed over supporting documentation, and the complaint was accepted by the reception module for analysis to determine whether there are signs of a crime.

UNIFIN, Monavex and Cryptaespon

The August alert is the second this year. In a 30 March 2026 statement, the Honduras CNBS named three platforms it said operate outside the regulated financial system: UNIFIN, Monavex and Cryptaespon, according to reporting by Criterio.

That statement said the regulator had identified the promotion of irregular financial schemes through social media and websites offering attractive returns without legal backing, similar to the collapsed Koriun Inversiones operation. It added that simulated legal structures do not exempt anyone from responsibility when they collect resources from the public without authorization, and that investigations would continue in coordination with other institutions.

The Koriun Precedent

Koriun Inversiones remains the emblematic case. Based in Choloma, in the Cortés department near San Pedro Sula, the company promised five percent weekly interest, equivalent to 20 percent monthly, and drew in tens of thousands of savers before prosecutors raided its offices nationwide on 23 April 2025, finding more than 358 million lempiras in cash.

Investigators described a Ponzi scheme in which money from new depositors paid the returns of older investors. Around 30,000 Hondurans were left affected, according to Criterio, and the company’s administrator, Iván Velásquez, faces money-laundering charges along with several associates.

Despite that collapse, new structures kept capturing money without permits, Criterio reported, which is why the Honduras CNBS returned to public warnings in March and again this week.

Fraud by the Numbers

Official statistics show how widespread the problem has become. Between 2019 and 15 June 2026, the prosecutor’s office registered 39,104 fraud complaints, by far the most reported crime of its type under the penal code, El Heraldo reported in July.

Marco Cerrato, an intendant at the Honduras CNBS, advised the public to be cautious with electronic offers that seem too good to be true. He warned that promises of exorbitant benefits are schemes that can tragically wipe out savers’ resources, and urged victims to turn to financial authorities and criminal prosecutors.

How to Check an Entity Before Investing

The regulator’s practical advice can be reduced to a short checklist. Confirm that the entity appears in the commission’s registry of authorized institutions before depositing anything. Treat any promise of fixed weekly or monthly returns as a warning sign, since no supervised institution can guarantee such yields.

Be especially wary of operations that recruit through social networks, messaging applications or investment events, that ask for membership fees or guarantee deposits up front, or that cannot provide a verifiable address and the names of those responsible. Suspected schemes can be reported to the prosecutor’s office, which received the latest complaint this week.

What This Means for Savers

Honduras’s regulated financial system, the banks, cooperatives and insurers supervised in Tegucigalpa, offers deposit protection frameworks that informal schemes lack entirely. Once money leaves that perimeter, recovery depends on criminal proceedings that can take years.

The regulator’s message is essentially preventive: check the authorization registry before investing, treat social-media investment advertising as a red flag, and report suspected schemes to the prosecutor’s office.

For international readers, the episode shows how quickly unregulated digital finance is spreading in Central America, and how thin the institutional tools remain for stopping it before savers are hurt.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did the Honduras CNBS warn about? The Honduras CNBS warned on 25 August 2026 about proliferating fraudulent investment and money-collection schemes that promise quick, risk-free returns through social media and unverifiable platforms. It urged the public to verify that any entity is authorized before handing over money. Which platforms has the regulator named? In a 30 March 2026 statement, the Honduras CNBS identified UNIFIN, Monavex and Cryptaespon as platforms operating outside the supervised financial system, offering attractive returns without legal backing, according to Criterio. What was the Koriun Inversiones fraud? Koriun Inversiones promised five percent weekly interest and collected savings from around 30,000 Hondurans before prosecutors raided it on 23 April 2025, seizing more than 358 million lempiras. Its administrator, Iván Velásquez, faces money-laundering charges.

World.title: Petropar Fuel Price Hike Adds 300 Guaraníes per Liter Across All Fuels
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Paraguay · ECONOMY

Key Facts — Increase a uniform 300 guaraníes per liter on every Petropar fuel from Monday, 17 August 2026

— New prices Diesel Porã 8,290, Diesel Mbarete 10,300 and Kape88 gasoline 6,990 guaraníes per liter

— In dollars Kape88 costs about US$1.17 per liter at roughly 6,000 guaraníes per dollar

— Price gap Petropar says it stays below private brands, by at least 400 guaraníes per liter on diesel

— Outlook the company estimates prices can hold at least until the first half of September

The first increase since May leaves Petropar’s prices below the private brands, the company insists, as a stronger guaraní softens the blow of imported fuel that still costs more than US$1,000 per cubic meter.

The Petropar fuel price hike took effect across Paraguay on Monday, 17 August 2026, adding 300 guaraníes per liter, about five US cents, to every product sold by the state oil company. Diesel Porã now costs 8,290 guaraníes per liter, Diesel Mbarete 10,300 and the Kape88 gasoline 6,990, about US$1.17 at roughly 6,000 guaraníes per dollar. Petropar president William Wilka said the Petropar fuel price hike was kept as small as possible after the company stretched its inventories as far as it could.

A fuel station price board in South America; in Paraguay, the Petropar fuel price hike added 300 guaraníes per liter to all products from 17 August 2026.

Why the state company moved prices now

Wilka explained the Petropar fuel price hike in a radio interview on La Tribu 650 AM, La Tribuna reported. ‘The adjustment comes after receiving the latest shipments, the latest replenishments. We stretched everything we could, we held on,’ he said, pointing to international fuel prices that remain elevated. Between 83 and 84 percent of Petropar’s import cost depends on the international quotation, plus about three percent in freight, he said: ‘There you already have 86 percent of the weight in the cost structure.’

Diesel remains above US$1,000 per cubic meter and gasoline near US$850, according to the company. Since February and the start of the war, diesel has risen the equivalent of about 1,700 guaraníes per liter and gasoline around 1,600, while the dollar’s slide of roughly eight percent against the guaraní was not enough to compensate. Wilka rejected the idea that biodiesel blending drove the increase, estimating its impact at about 85 guaraníes within the cost structure.

The president defended gradual adjustments over waiting. ‘If you hold on until the last round, then the adjustment, instead of 300 guaraníes, will have to be double or triple,’ he warned, adding that if external prices fall, Petropar ‘will be one of the first to lower immediately.’ The company is also watching tensions in the Strait of Hormuz, La Tribuna reported.

The new price board and the gap to private brands

After the Petropar fuel price hike, the company’s board reads as follows, according to Oviedo Press and La Nación: Diesel Porã at 8,290 guaraníes per liter, Diesel Mbarete at 10,300, Nafta Kape88 at 6,990, Nafta Oikoite 93 at 7,490 and Nafta Aratirí 97 at 8,840.

Wilka insists the state company remains the cheaper option. Before the adjustment, Petropar was 700 guaraníes below private brands on diesel and 500 on gasoline; the new board leaves a gap of at least 400 guaraníes on diesel and 200 to 400 on gasolines, he said. Regionally, he told La Nación, Paraguay is now slightly more expensive than Brazil across the border in Foz do Iguaçu for one diesel grade, but cheaper than the Argentine border zone. ‘With this we estimate we can hold prices easily until the first half of September, even longer,’ he said, crediting well-timed spot purchases.

A pivotal year in Paraguay’s fuel market

The Petropar fuel price hike lands in a year of unusual volatility. President Santiago Peña announced a 250-guaraní cut in late January, the thirteenth reduction of his administration, La Nación reported at the time. Then came the war-driven surge: increases of 450 guaraníes on 23 March, 750 on 10 April and a further 750 on diesel and 300 on gasoline on 4 May, before a rare 210-guaraní cut to Diesel Porã on 1 July.

Petropar operates 302 service stations, about 10 percent of the country’s outlets, and holds 23 percent of the fuel market, making it the top seller, Wilka told La Nación, projecting profitability for the year. Paraguayans bought 3,671 million liters of fuel in 2025, up 8.8 percent, with diesel accounting for 55 percent of sales and Shell, Petropar and Petrobras together holding 46.8 percent of the market, according to industry data reported by Mentu.

Because Paraguay imports all of its liquid fuels, the company’s pricing decisions ripple through agriculture, trucking and bus fares, and its board has become an instrument of government price policy as much as a commercial signal.

Beyond the pump: Petropar enters aviation fuel

One week after the price adjustment, the state company opened a new front: on 24 August 2026 it formally entered Paraguay’s aviation-fuel market, launching sales of Jet A-1 for jet aircraft and AVGAS for piston-engine planes, La Nación reported.

The plan calls for five fuel plants serving Asunción, Ciudad del Este, Mariscal Estigarribia and Concepción, the country’s main air gateways and strategic points in the Chaco. Notably, the expansion uses a public-private partnership in which a private operator finances all of the investment, so Petropar puts no state money at risk, the company confirmed; financial terms were not disclosed. The entry breaks a market long served only by private importers and gives airlines and airports a state-backed supplier for the first time.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much is the Petropar fuel price hike? The Petropar fuel price hike is 300 guaraníes per liter, about five US cents, applied uniformly to all diesel and gasoline grades at Petropar stations nationwide from 17 August 2026. What are the new prices after the Petropar fuel price hike? After the Petropar fuel price hike, Diesel Porã costs 8,290 guaraníes per liter, Diesel Mbarete 10,300, Kape88 gasoline 6,990, Oikoite 93 at 7,490 and Aratirí 97 at 8,840 guaraníes per liter. Will Petropar’s new fuel prices hold? President William Wilka says the new prices can hold at least until the first half of September, helped by competitive spot purchases, and that Petropar will be among the first to cut if international costs fall.

World.title: Marriott Isla Verde Beach Resort Opens After US$38 Million Transformation
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Caribbean · BUSINESS

Key Facts — Investment US$38 million transformation of the former Courtyard by Marriott on the Isla Verde beachfront

— Rooms all 260 rooms and suites renovated, each with a private balcony, plus new lobby and dining spaces

— Timeline work ran in phases over nearly three years with the hotel open; new flag inaugurated 18 August 2026

— Market Puerto Rico posted record tourism in 2025, with 6.8 million airport arrivals and 7.9 million room nights booked

— Rates March 2026 hotel occupancy hit 87 percent, a record for the month, with first-quarter RevPAR near US$309

The former Courtyard on the Isla Verde strip now flies the full-service Marriott flag after a US$38 million overhaul. The 260-room resort arrives as Puerto Rico posts record arrivals, record room rates and a fresh wave of hotel investment.

The Marriott Isla Verde Beach Resort officially opened its new flag in San Juan, Puerto Rico, on 18 August 2026, completing a US$38 million transformation of the former Courtyard by Marriott, El Nuevo Día reported on 19 August. The Marriott Isla Verde project renovated all 260 rooms and suites, each with a private balcony, along with the lobby, public areas and the dining offer, carried out in phases over nearly three years while the hotel stayed open.

The Isla Verde beachfront hotel strip in San Juan, Puerto Rico, where the Marriott Isla Verde Beach Resort opened after a US$38 million transformation.

From Courtyard to full-service Marriott on the Isla Verde strip

The transformation covered every corner of the property. All 260 rooms and suites were renovated, each keeping a private balcony, and the project extended to the lobby, the public areas, the gastronomic offer and part of the hotel’s operational infrastructure, El Nuevo Día reported. The work was executed in phases over nearly three years, allowing the hotel to remain open and keep receiving guests throughout the construction.

The reflagging moves the property a step up in Marriott International’s brand ladder, from the select-service Courtyard by Marriott to a full-service Marriott resort. The Marriott Isla Verde keeps its direct access to Isla Verde beach, one of San Juan’s best-known stretches of sand, and sits minutes from the Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport, a location that has long made the corridor the island’s densest hotel district.

For Marriott International, the upgrade converts a reliable airport-adjacent property into a beach resort capable of competing for higher daily rates and longer leisure stays, the segment where Puerto Rico’s tourism numbers have been growing fastest.

A record tourism market behind the reflagging

The resort opens into the strongest tourism market Puerto Rico has ever recorded. According to Discover Puerto Rico, the island’s destination marketing organization, Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport received more than 6.8 million passenger arrivals in 2025, three percent more than in 2024, while some 1.6 million cruise passengers came through the Port of San Juan, up 12 percent year on year.

Lodging demand reached nearly 7.9 million room nights booked in 2025, an annual increase of eight percent according to STR and AirDNA data cited by the organization, and leisure and hospitality employment hit a historic 102,600 jobs in November 2025. The meetings and events sector added a record 262,779 room nights in group bookings.

The momentum carried into 2026. Hotel occupancy in March 2026 reached 87 percent, up five percentage points from a year earlier and a new high for the month, while first-quarter RevPAR climbed to an estimated US$309, from US$288 in the same quarter of 2025. March lodging revenue reached an estimated US$259 million, a monthly record. Air arrivals have softened slightly, with first-quarter traffic at the San Juan airport down about 2.6 percent, but rate strength has more than offset the slower volume.

Demand is being fed from several directions at once: expanded airlift from Florida, New York and Madrid, a cruise calendar above pre-pandemic levels, and an events engine that ranges from concerts and festivals to sports, with group and incentive bookings picking up through the second quarter. For a full-service beach resort minutes from the airport, that mix of leisure, group and events traffic is exactly the demand base the reflagging is designed to monetize.

Part of a wider hotel investment wave

The Marriott Isla Verde is one piece of a broader investment cycle. Discover Puerto Rico counts nearly 1,000 hotel rooms under construction across the island, with significant projects scheduled through 2028. The openings pipeline includes the Hyatt Centric San Juan Isla Verde, a direct neighbor on the same beachfront strip, as well as the Spark by Hilton Ponce and boutique properties such as Magdalena 1163 and El Oasis Hotel.

At the luxury end, Invest Puerto Rico highlights the Four Seasons project set to replace the St. Regis Bahia Beach Resort in Río Grande, and Mandarin Oriental’s first property on the island, planned for Cabo Rojo as part of the US$2 billion Esencia resort development. Act 60 investment incentives continue to attract extended-stay travelers and investors, industry analysts note.

Developers are not blind to the risks. CoStar and Tourism Economics have trimmed the 2027 United States RevPAR forecast to 1.4 percent growth, with average daily rate expected to remain the main driver, and builders flag construction costs, permitting, power continuity and hurricane-season exposure as planning constraints. Even so, a full-service flag on Isla Verde beach positions the resort to capture weddings, conventions and longer leisure stays that smaller or select-service properties cannot serve.

Frequently Asked Questions

What changed at the Marriott Isla Verde Beach Resort? The former Courtyard by Marriott in Isla Verde, San Juan, reopened as the full-service Marriott Isla Verde Beach Resort on 18 August 2026, after a US$38 million renovation of its 260 balcony rooms, lobby, public areas and dining offer. How long did the Marriott Isla Verde transformation take? The US$38 million project ran in phases over nearly three years while the hotel stayed open, according to El Nuevo Día. The renovation covered rooms, common areas, restaurants and part of the operational infrastructure. How is Puerto Rico’s hotel market performing in 2026? The market that receives the Marriott Isla Verde is at record levels: March 2026 hotel occupancy hit 87 percent, first-quarter RevPAR reached an estimated US$309, and nearly 1,000 new hotel rooms are under construction across the island through 2028.

World.title: Maria da Penha Law Now Covers All Gender Violence, Brazil’s STF Rules
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · JUSTICE

Key Facts — Maria da Penha urgent protective measures now cover all gender-based violence, not only domestic or family settings

— The ruling unanimous, in Tema 1.412 of general repercussion, with rapporteur and court president Edson Fachin

— Also decided judges without jurisdiction must still rule urgent requests, and police delegates may grant measures

— First application a Conceição das Alagoas municipal employee won protection against the chamber’s president

— The law in force since 2006, it requires judges to decide urgent protective measures within 48 hours

In Tema 1.412, rapporteur and court president Edson Fachin anchored the ruling in the Belém do Pará Convention; within days, a Minas Gerais judge had already applied the new thesis to protect a municipal employee from a councillor.

Brazil’s Supreme Court ruled unanimously on 19 August 2026 that the urgent protective measures created by the Maria da Penha Law apply to every form of gender-based violence against women, regardless of whether there is any domestic, family or intimate relationship between victim and aggressor, in a landmark decision reported by the legal outlet Migalhas.

Maria da Penha, the activist whose name Brazil’s landmark 2006 law bears; the Supreme Court extended its urgent protections beyond the home.

What the Supreme Court decided

Ruling in Tema 1.412 of the general repercussion docket, the plenary established that the urgent protective measures of Law 11.340, the Maria da Penha Law, reach any violence against a woman motivated by her gender, whether it occurs in the home, at work, in the community, in institutions or in politics. The decision is binding on the entire Brazilian judiciary.

The court fixed three further theses. Even a judge who lacks jurisdiction over a case must decide an urgent protective request when there is immediate risk to the victim’s physical or psychological integrity, forwarding the file afterward to the competent judge or, where one exists, to the specialized violence-against-women court. Protection expressly covers political gender violence, a crime under article 326-B of the Electoral Code that falls to the Electoral Justice. And police delegates and agents may grant urgent measures in emergency situations, under the terms the court set in ADI 6.138, limited to removing the aggressor from the home or shared residence, with judicial review within 24 hours.

Justice Flávio Dino concurred in full with the rapporteur and asked that the thesis mention political gender violence explicitly, a suggestion incorporated into the final text.

The case behind the ruling

The appeal, ARE 1.537.713, began in Formiga, Minas Gerais, where a woman reported being stalked and threatened with death for months by a neighbor who believed, or wished, that he had a romantic relationship with her, following her whenever she left or returned home. A lower court denied her protective measures and sent the case to a misdemeanor court; the Minas Gerais state court upheld the denial, reasoning that the Maria da Penha Law was restricted to domestic, family or intimate relationships.

The Minas Gerais prosecutor’s office appealed to the Supreme Court, arguing that the restrictive reading violated international commitments Brazil assumed under the Inter-American Convention to Prevent, Punish and Eradicate Violence Against Women, the Belém do Pará Convention, which obliges the state to protect women from gender violence in any context, public or private. The court recognized the general repercussion of the question in August 2025, and groups such as the Brazilian Bar Association argued for the broad reading in oral arguments in May 2026.

In his vote, Fachin, who is also the court’s president, said gender violence is structural and is not confined to the domestic sphere, and that the central element is that the aggression is motivated by the victim’s female condition. He also stressed that protective measures are autonomous: they do not depend on a criminal charge, a police inquiry or even a police report, so the victim’s later retraction did not extinguish the case.

First application, within days

The new thesis reached a courtroom within a week. Migalhas reported on 26 August that an employee of the municipal chamber of Conceição das Alagoas, in Minas Gerais, won protective measures under the Maria da Penha Law against the chamber’s president, a city councillor, in what the outlet described as an application of the just-issued ruling.

According to the Minas Gerais prosecutor’s office, the employee reported episodes of psychological violence, moral and sexual harassment, threats and embarrassment. Prosecutors argued the facts went beyond an ordinary workplace conflict and indicated, in a preliminary analysis, gender-based violence. The judge ordered the councillor to keep his distance from the employee and to make no contact with her.

The case illustrates precisely the gap the Supreme Court set out to close: before the ruling, a woman harassed by a superior, a colleague, a neighbor or a political figure could be denied urgent protection simply because the aggressor was not a partner or relative.

Why the law matters

The Maria da Penha Law, in force since 2006, is Brazil’s landmark statute against violence toward women. Named for the activist Maria da Penha Maia Fernandes, whose fight to see her attacker punished took decades, it created the system of urgent protective measures, such as restraining, no-contact and removal-from-home orders, that judges must decide within 48 hours.

Until this month’s ruling, those measures were anchored in the law’s article 5, which ties protection to domestic, family or intimate settings. The Supreme Court did not rewrite the statute: it extended the reach of one instrument, the urgent protective measure, to the broader universe of gender violence, while leaving the specialized courts’ jurisdiction otherwise intact.

Brazil records some of the highest femicide and domestic-violence numbers in Latin America, and women’s advocates have long argued that the protective apparatus should follow victims into every space where violence finds them. The unanimous ruling, anchored in an international treaty Brazil ratified three decades ago, is the most significant expansion of the Maria da Penha framework since its creation.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Brazil’s Supreme Court change about the Maria da Penha Law? On 19 August 2026 the court ruled unanimously, in Tema 1.412, that the Maria da Penha Law’s urgent protective measures apply to all gender-based violence against women, even when victim and aggressor have no domestic, family or intimate relationship. It also ruled that judges without jurisdiction must still decide urgent requests and that police delegates may grant emergency measures. What was the case behind the Maria da Penha ruling? A woman from Formiga, Minas Gerais, was stalked and threatened with death by a neighbor who claimed a romantic interest in her. State courts denied her protection because no intimate relationship existed. Prosecutors appealed citing the Belém do Pará Convention, and rapporteur Edson Fachin, the court’s president, won a unanimous vote for the broad reading. Has the expanded Maria da Penha protection already been applied? Yes. According to Migalhas, a municipal chamber employee in Conceição das Alagoas, Minas Gerais, won protective measures against the chamber’s president, a councillor she accused of psychological violence, moral and sexual harassment and threats. The judge ordered no approach and no contact, applying the new thesis within days of the ruling.

World.title: Ambipar’s US$2 Billion Debt Vote Fails on Quorum, Reset for September 1
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · MARKETS

Key Facts — Ambipar the 25 August creditors’ meeting failed for lack of quorum; the second call is 1 September at 2 p.m.

— Attendance 95% of the unsecured class was present, but labor, secured and supplier classes fell short

— Debt Ambipar listed R$10.5 billion (about US$2.04 billion) when it filed for judicial recovery on 20 October 2025

— The deal a support agreement with 53.8% of bondholders swaps old bonds for US$925 million in new seven-year notes

— Management chief executive Tércio Borlenghi Jr. and CFO Thiago da Costa Silva remain in their posts under the plan

Brazilian law requires more than half of each creditor class to attend a first-call meeting, and only the foreign bondholders showed up in force. In the second call, any quorum suffices to vote the R$10.5 billion plan.

The general creditors’ meeting called to vote on the judicial recovery plan of Ambipar, the Brazilian environmental services group, was not installed on 25 August 2026 for lack of quorum, Estadão’s Broadcast service reported, pushing the decision on R$10.5 billion in debt, about US$2.04 billion, to a second call scheduled for 1 September at 2 p.m.

An Ambipar emergency response unit; the group’s creditors will vote its judicial recovery plan on 1 September after the first meeting failed for lack of quorum.

What happened at the meeting

Creditors representing 95% of the unsecured class, mostly foreign holders of the group’s overseas bonds, were present at the hybrid meeting, held in person at the Square Design Hotel in Barra da Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro, and online through the Assemblex Pillar platform. But Brazilian law requires a first-call creditors’ assembly to be installed with more than half of each class, including labor, secured and supplier creditors, and those classes did not reach the threshold.

The meeting was called by notice published on 10 August by the court-appointed judicial administrators in the case before Rio de Janeiro’s 3rd Business Court. In the second call, set for 1 September at 2 p.m., the assembly can be installed with any number of creditors, which makes approval or rejection of the plan effectively possible on that date.

Notably, the plan itself had not been formally presented in advance. Broadcast reported that the company is still negotiating the document with a broader group of creditors than the bondholders who backed a restructuring proposal in early June, aiming to maximize support and reduce the risk of future litigation and delays in executing the plan.

A US$2 billion collapse built on derivatives

Ambipar filed for judicial recovery on 20 October 2025, and judge Caroline Fonseca of the 3rd Business Court granted the request ten days later, suspending lawsuits and executions against the group. The filing listed R$10.481 billion in debt, of which R$10.439 billion was unsecured; supplier claims totaled R$35.9 million and labor claims R$6.3 million. About R$2 billion is owed to banks, with Santander the largest at R$663 million, followed by Banco do Brasil at R$352 million.

The crisis erupted in September 2025, when the company revealed that an amendment to a derivatives contract with Deutsche Bank had begun draining its cash, with an outflow of more than R$200 million, and obtained an injunction protecting it from accelerated debt maturities. The company blamed its former chief financial officer, João Arruda, for signing the amendment without the knowledge of other executives; Arruda’s defense denies the accusations and points to other directors’ signatures on the documents.

The group’s foreign-listed subsidiary, Ambipar Emergency Response, filed for Chapter 11 protection in Houston, Texas, and the company later sought U.S. Chapter 15 recognition of the Brazilian proceeding covering its roughly US$1.05 billion in outstanding green notes. Brazilian banks and foreign bondholders have fought over the case in U.S. court.

The plan on the table

In early July, the group announced a restructuring support agreement with holders of 53.8% of its green notes due 2031 and 2033, which total about US$1.043 billion. The deal swaps those bonds for US$925 million in new secured notes with a seven-year term and full principal payment at maturity. Interest runs at 10% a year in payment-in-kind form for the first 18 months, meaning no cash outlay, and then shifts to 2% payment-in-kind plus 8% in cash.

The package also includes US$50 million in fixed payments to bondholders tied to the sale of court-ordered receivables known as precatórios, split into two US$25 million installments, and a separate restructuring of a US$90 million debt with Itaú BBA. Under the agreement, filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission on 8 July, Tércio Borlenghi Jr. remains chief executive and Thiago da Costa Silva chief financial officer, leading operations after the restructuring is implemented.

Domestic creditors sit outside the bondholder deal: about R$3 billion in debentures and R$2 billion in bank debt owed to Sumitomo Mitsui, Santander, Banco do Brasil, Deutsche Bank and Bradesco were expected to negotiate separately or challenge the plan, which is one reason the company has been widening the negotiation before putting the document to a vote.

The missing balance sheets

The days before the meeting were contentious. Oliveira Trust, the fiduciary agent for the group’s debentures, and the bank Sumitomo asked the 3rd Business Court to postpone or suspend the assembly, arguing the company has not published financial statements for the third quarter of 2025, the full year 2025 or the first and second quarters of 2026, and that the convocation deadline was irregular.

The judge declined to stop the meeting but ordered the company to hand the figures to creditors that request them, with the balance sheets remaining under seal. The company has attributed the reporting delays to the judicial recovery process and to changes in its financial leadership, which forced adjustments to internal accounting validation routines.

If the plan is approved on 1 September, Ambipar still needs judicial confirmation and must meet the conditions of the support agreement, including definitive documentation and regulatory approvals. If it fails, a group that grew from waste management into a global environmental services brand, and whose shares once soared on São Paulo’s B3 exchange, could face the liquidation route that its creditors have so far avoided.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Ambipar’s creditors’ meeting fail? The 25 August 2026 meeting was not installed because Brazilian law requires more than half of each creditor class to attend a first-call assembly. Creditors representing 95% of Ambipar’s unsecured class, mostly foreign bondholders, were present, but Ambipar’s labor, secured and supplier classes did not reach quorum. A second call is set for 1 September at 2 p.m., when any quorum suffices. How much does Ambipar owe? Ambipar listed R$10.5 billion in debt, about US$2.04 billion, when it filed for judicial recovery in Rio de Janeiro on 20 October 2025. Almost all of it is unsecured, including about US$1.043 billion in green notes held abroad and roughly R$2 billion in bank debt, with Santander the largest bank creditor at R$663 million. What does Ambipar’s restructuring deal with bondholders include? The support agreement signed in July with 53.8% of green note holders swaps the existing bonds for US$925 million in new secured notes with a seven-year term, adds US$50 million in fixed payments tied to receivable sales, and keeps chief executive Tércio Borlenghi Jr. and CFO Thiago da Costa Silva in charge of the company.

World.title: Fitch Raises Brava Energia to BB After Ecopetrol’s US$1.2 Billion Takeover
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · MARKETS

Key Facts — Brava Energia Fitch raised the long-term ratings to BB from BB-, outlook stable, off positive watch

— National scale the rating went to AA+(bra) from AA-(bra), Fitch said

— The trigger Ecopetrol completed its US$1.2 billion acquisition of 51% of Brava on 17 and 18 August

— Scale Brava Energia should average about 85,000 boepd in 2026 and 93,000 in 2028, keeping it at the low end of BB

— Cash R$4.7 billion in June covers all debt and acquisition obligations through 2028

Analysts Lucas Rios, Erick Pastrana and Natalia O’Bryrne said the Colombian state oil company’s control brings clear strategic incentives, though production scale keeps the Brazilian producer at the lower end of the BB category.

Fitch Ratings has upgraded Brava Energia to BB from BB-, with a stable outlook, and raised the Brazilian oil producer’s national-scale rating to AA+(bra) from AA-(bra), Valor reported on 26 August 2026, one week after Colombia’s Ecopetrol completed its acquisition of a controlling 51% stake in the company.

An offshore oil platform of the type operated by Brava Energia; Fitch raised the company to BB after Ecopetrol’s takeover.

What Fitch said and why

Fitch analysts Lucas Rios, Erick Pastrana and Natalia O’Bryrne wrote that the upgrade of Brava Energia reflects the effects of Ecopetrol’s takeover, which brings clear strategic incentives for the Colombian state oil company: the deal expands its proved reserves by 12% and lifts consolidated production and EBITDA by 11% and 10%, respectively. The ratings had been on Rating Watch Positive since May, when the bid was announced; the watch was removed and the outlook set at stable.

The agency kept Brava Energia at the lower end of the BB category because of its production scale, estimated at an average of 85,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2026 and 93,000 in 2028. The stable outlook reflects an expectation that the company will replace produced reserves and hold at least 400 million barrels of proved reserves over the projection horizon.

Liquidity was another support. Brava held R$4.7 billion in readily available cash in June, an amount Fitch considers sufficient to amortize all debt and merger obligations maturing through 2028. The ratings also assume the arbitration filed by Westlawn over the Atlanta field, which began in June, will have no relevant impact on the company’s credit profile.

The US$1.2 billion takeover behind the upgrade

Ecopetrol completed the acquisition on 17 and 18 August through its subsidiary Ecopetrol Investimentos do Brasil, ending up with 236,924,207 common shares, about 51% of the voting capital of Brava. The aggregate consideration was roughly US$1.2 billion, funded through an intercompany loan from Ecopetrol Capital AG.

The position was assembled in two legs. In a tender offer auction on the B3 exchange on 5 August, the Colombian company bought 116,110,717 shares, about 25% of the capital, at R$23 each, a total of about R$2.67 billion, roughly US$520 million at 5.14 reais to the dollar. A separate block of 120,813,490 shares, about 26%, had been agreed privately on 23 April with the funds Somah Printemps Quantum Group, Jive Group and Yellowstone at R$24 per share.

The price gap between the two legs drew scrutiny from Brazil’s securities regulator, the CVM, which suspended the offer in June while questioning why tender-offer holders were being offered less than the private sellers. The regulator’s board accepted Ecopetrol’s appeal on 14 July, the suspension was lifted the next day, and the amended notice set the auction for 5 August, with financial settlement on 17 August.

A long road of regulatory clearances

The deal, first announced on 23 April at a premium of about 27.8% over the 90-day average price of Brava’s shares, needed several consents before closing. Debenture holders of the company’s third 3R and third Enauta issuances granted waivers on 8 June, removing the risk of accelerated repayment because of the change of control. Antitrust regulator Cade approved the transaction on 13 May, a decision that became final on 16 June.

For Ecopetrol, the acquisition strengthens its growth platform in Brazil, where it already partners with Shell in the Gato do Mato pre-salt blocks, and fits its 2040 strategy of geographic diversification. On a 51% basis, the stake adds about 42,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day of production and a proportional share of the 459 million barrels of oil equivalent in proved reserves that Brava reported for 2025.

Brava Energia, formed by the merger of 3R Petroleum and Enauta, averaged about 81,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2025 and reached about 84,400 in June 2026. For the twelve months ended in June, the company reported revenue of about US$2.34 billion, EBITDA of about US$1.05 billion and net income of about US$122.2 million, according to unaudited figures cited by Ecopetrol.

What the upgrade means from here

The BB level still sits two notches below investment grade, but the upgrade lowers funding costs for Brava just as it starts life under state-controlled ownership from Colombia. It also closes a ratings cycle that began in May, when Fitch placed the company on positive watch hours after the bid was disclosed.

Attention now shifts to integration: how Ecopetrol will manage a company that produces most of its oil and gas in Rio Grande do Norte’s Potiguar cluster and offshore at Atlanta, and whether the promised reserve replacement, at least 400 million barrels proved, materializes under the new controller. Fitch’s stable outlook signals the agency expects it will.

Frequently Asked Questions

Why did Fitch upgrade Brava Energia? Fitch raised Brava Energia to BB from BB-, with a stable outlook, because Ecopetrol completed its acquisition of 51% of the company on 17 and 18 August 2026. The agency cited clear strategic incentives for the Colombian state oil company, whose proved reserves grow 12% with the deal, plus Brava’s robust liquidity of R$4.7 billion in cash. How much did Ecopetrol pay for control of Brava Energia? About US$1.2 billion in total. Ecopetrol bought 116,110,717 shares at R$23 each in a 5 August tender auction, worth about R$2.67 billion, roughly US$520 million, and a separate 26% block from the funds Somah, Jive and Yellowstone at R$24 per share under an April agreement. How big is Brava Energia in production and reserves? The company produced an average of about 81,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day in 2025 and reported 459 million barrels of oil equivalent in proved reserves. Fitch projects around 85,000 boepd in 2026 and 93,000 in 2028, and expects the company to hold at least 400 million barrels proved.

World.title: Dark Horse: Dino Lets Federal Police Mine São Paulo Fraud Probe Files
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Brazil · JUSTICE

Key Facts — Dark Horse Federal Police gain access to evidence from a June São Paulo police operation against producer Go Up Entertainment

— The operation eight search warrants hit the producer, the Instituto Conhecer Brasil NGO and a city hall secretariat

— At stake suspected fraud and diversion of public resources in a R$108 million wi-fi contract with São Paulo’s city hall

— Parallel front in July, Justice André Mendonça authorized a Federal Police probe into the film’s financing

— Context Bolsonaro, the film’s subject, was convicted by the Supreme Court in September 2025 and sentenced to 27 years

The decision, issued under seal and first reported by O Globo, merges a state fraud investigation into the film’s producer with a Supreme Court inquiry into whether congressional budget amendments helped finance the Bolsonaro cinebiopic.

Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino has authorized Brazil’s Federal Police to access evidence seized by the São Paulo Civil Police in a June 2026 fraud operation against the producer of Dark Horse, the cinebiopic of former president Jair Bolsonaro, a confidential decision first revealed by O Globo and confirmed by CNN Brasil on Monday, 24 August 2026.

Justice Flávio Dino, of Brazil’s Supreme Court in Brasília, authorized the Federal Police to access evidence from a São Paulo probe targeting the producer of Dark Horse.

What Dino’s decision changes

Dino’s decision responds to a request from the Federal Police itself, which wants to mine the material seized in São Paulo for its own investigation into whether parliamentary budget amendments, the transfers known in Brazil as emendas parlamentares, were diverted to finance Dark Horse. The case runs under seal at the Supreme Court, and Dino is the rapporteur of a series of proceedings examining irregularities in the use of congressional amendments.

The authorization was first reported by columnist Bela Megale at O Globo and quickly confirmed by CNN Brasil, UOL, Metrópoles and Gazeta do Povo. Because the proceedings are confidential, the court released no formal statement. The move does not create a new investigation: it allows federal agents to incorporate phones, documents and financial records gathered by the state police into the inquiry already under way in Brasília.

It is the second time in two months that a Supreme Court justice has widened federal access to material concerning the film. In July, Justice André Mendonça authorized the Federal Police to investigate the financing of the film on a separate front, after revelations that the production received tens of millions of reais from Daniel Vorcaro, the owner of Banco Master, who has been jailed since November 2025 on billion-real fraud charges.

The June operation against Karina Ferreira da Gama

The São Paulo operation that produced the evidence was launched in the first hours of June by the 2nd Police Station for Crimes Against Public Administration, Corruption and Money Laundering, known as DICCA. Its target was Karina Ferreira da Gama, owner of Go Up Entertainment, the company behind Dark Horse, and of the Instituto Conhecer Brasil, or ICB, a non-profit she controls.

Investigators suspect fraud and diversion of public resources in a R$108 million contract between the ICB and São Paulo’s city hall to provide free wi-fi coverage in public spaces, the WiFi Livre SP program. Eight search-and-seizure warrants issued by the 1st Regional Warrant Court were served on the headquarters of the ICB and of Go Up Entertainment, two residential addresses of Karina, and the headquarters of the Municipal Secretariat of Innovation and Technology.

The civil police also asked the courts for access to analyses by Coaf, Brazil’s financial intelligence unit, of transactions made by the ICB, Go Up and Karina. In filings, investigators described consistent suspicions of asset commingling between the institute and the production company, and raised the hypothesis that funds from the wi-fi program may have supported activities linked to the film while it was being produced. Karina has denied that the film received public money and says the city contract has no connection to the film; the administration of Mayor Ricardo Nunes said it is cooperating and has found no irregularities so far, noting the contract predates the production.

Amendments, Vorcaro and two judicial fronts

The federal inquiry that will now absorb the São Paulo material examines whether amendments destined by lawmakers to entities linked to the production were used to pay for the film. Five parliamentarians appear in the investigation, among them federal deputy Mário Frias, the former culture secretary under Bolsonaro who wrote the screenplay of Dark Horse and who, in 2024, directed R$2 million in amendments to Karina’s ICB. In May, Frias answered Dino’s questions and denied any triangulation of funds, calling the allegation speculative and legally irrelevant.

The Mendonça front is separate. It grew out of the collapse of Banco Master and the revelation, first by The Intercept Brasil, that Vorcaro financed more than 90 percent of the film’s budget, with at least R$61 million traced to the production, and that audio messages showed Senator Flávio Bolsonaro, the former president’s eldest son and a presidential pre-candidate, pressing the banker for payments. Mendonça also authorized investigators to examine whether Master funds paid for the U.S. stay of former deputy Eduardo Bolsonaro. UOL reported that the evidence-sharing case handled by Dino has no relation to the Vorcaro payments.

Flávio Bolsonaro, who denies any irregularity and says no public money was used, asked that the amendments case be redistributed to Mendonça so both fronts would sit with the same justice. The production company has also denied receiving money from Banco Master. No charges have been announced in either federal inquiry.

A film at the center of Brazil’s political storm

Dark Horse dramatizes the political rise of Bolsonaro, with American actor Jim Caviezel in the lead role. The film was first shown at an event in Las Vegas and its Brazilian release was scheduled for August 2026, weeks before an election in which the Bolsonaro family is a central actor even with the former president imprisoned.

Bolsonaro, who governed from 2019 to 2022, was convicted by the Supreme Court in September 2025 of attempting to overturn the 2022 election and sentenced to 27 years in prison. The overlapping investigations into how his cinebiopic was financed now touch the Supreme Court, the Federal Police, the São Paulo state police and the city’s comptroller agencies, ensuring the film will remain in the headlines through the campaign.

For now, the Dino decision is procedural: it widens what investigators can read, not who they can accuse. But it gives federal agents a far richer evidence base, including seized devices and financial records, at a moment when both judicial fronts around Dark Horse are accelerating.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Flávio Dino decide about the Dark Horse case? He authorized the Federal Police to access all evidence seized in a June 2026 São Paulo Civil Police operation against Karina Ferreira da Gama, owner of Go Up Entertainment, the producer of the Bolsonaro film. The material will feed the Supreme Court inquiry into whether parliamentary amendments helped finance the film. The decision runs under seal. What is the São Paulo operation about? State investigators suspect fraud and diversion of public resources in a R$108 million wi-fi contract between the Instituto Conhecer Brasil, an NGO controlled by the owner of the Dark Horse production company, and São Paulo’s city hall. Eight search warrants were served in June, and police suspect funds may have been commingled with the film producer. Who financed Dark Horse, the Bolsonaro film? Reporting by The Intercept Brasil and federal investigators indicates banker Daniel Vorcaro, owner of the collapsed Banco Master, financed more than 90 percent of the budget, with at least R$61 million traced to the production. Separately, the Supreme Court is examining whether congressional budget amendments were diverted to the production. The producer denies receiving Master or public money.
