World.title: Croatian Railway Ambitions Tie in With European Defence Efforts
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatian railway ambitions are closely linked with European defence efforts, as the country’s “decade of the railway” is still not really being felt on the ground by most.

Any reason for the renewal and development of the railway system in Croatia is very useful, including the security and defence one. But its civilian role remains primary. Index/Deutsche Welle/Igor Lasic reports that following two serious railway traffic incidents at the beginning of this month in Croatia, this mode of passenger and freight transport is once again a topic for the Croatian public.

Moreover, the general public has been reminded of the fact that Croatia is apparently currently in the middle of its “decade of the railway”. This is a state project for the development of this long-neglected mode of transport, with an investment of six billion euros for new tracks and vehicles. Yet despite years of reconstruction, the results are still not really visible on the ground, even though some concrete works have long been planned. The announced “railway renaissance” will therefore clearly still have to wait, and the recent traffic accidents have uncomfortably highlighted this uncertainty.

On top of everything, a new element has been included in the reasoning for the renewal of the Croatian railway sector, and that’s the wider European defence system. Europe is rapidly arming itself, and Croatia has also bought, among other things, more than 40 German Leopard 2 tanks. These, however, because of their exceptional weight, require equally exceptional railway transport capacities. All of this ultimately enters into the final calculation of the development project of the public company Croatian Railways. On the other hand, its relative urgency and the need for centralisation of the system somewhat remove the possibility of imminent privatisation of the sector, which until recently was quite realistic.

so long, privatisation

“Only through the security sphere and social cohesion around the issue of defence have we come to the conclusion that the railway must be managed by the state if we want an efficient system,” Ante Klečina, a railway expert and lecturer at the Department of Sustainable Mobility and Logistics of the University Sjever (North) in Koprivnica and Varaždin, told DW. He referred to the experience of some more developed European countries, such as Great Britain, whose experiments with railway privatisation ended rather ignominiously. Services became of poor quality and too expensive, the system failed in various aspects, and over time it was abandoned.

“First and foremost should be their functionality for civilian needs and, in fact, the organisation of civilisation,” Klečina continues, “which is relevant at every moment if we do not put that priority out of our minds. Whoever swears by the advantages of market mechanisms forgets that they are not developmentally suitable for large public systems, those that enable basic requirements.” In his opinion, the same applies to other elementary systems, e.g. healthcare, education and the judiciary, etc. The private sector, says Klečina, can be a supplement in certain segments, but the backbone must remain public.

“The reason is the necessity of central planning of such systems, as well as their primarily non-profit task, but also the need for enormous investments for which private individuals usually have neither the capacity nor the interest. Having seen this in practice, Europe has recently abandoned the idea of privatising railways, and the defence topic came afterwards as an additional reason,” considers Ante Klečina, formerly president of the Railway Alliance in the Republic of Croatia. He further notes that this mode of transport has no equal with regard to a series of key factors: above all overall cost-effectiveness, economic multiplier effects and environmental suitability.

central planning will always be needed

Socioeconomist Toni Prug, for his part, believes that behind the question of Croatian railways lies the general problem of political and scientific rejection of planning and public production as a relic of the past. That past concerns the period of socialism and Yugoslavia, and everything connected with it remained at the very least stigmatised after the war in Croatia. “In reality, however, all successful states are huge public production systems,” says Prug, “in which planning decides on the largest budgets within economies, on interventions whose importance for the population surpasses the importance of decisions that market actors make.”

This assistant professor at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences of the University of Rijeka highlights the rule in business that when a market actor makes a mistake, i.e. when things go badly, competition replaces him. “And railways, like all other production systems of a public character that are physically fixed and have monopoly status, need to be carefully planned. Mistakes are much harder to correct. They are also managed differently, different parameters are optimised, a focus on profit does not help. It often cannot even be the goal; the goals are determined by the plan.” At the same time the question arises of whether the Republic of Croatia has the professional staff for designing and implementing this.

“private goals have prevailed over practicality”

“Our profession and managerial staff are educated through faculty and professional curricula that say almost nothing about why and how to produce systems and services of a public character, and why they are superior for certain needs,” Prug is convinced, adding that this knowledge still exists in some Croatian public systems, while in others it has collapsed and been left to spontaneity. In his assessment, the City of Zagreb represents a recent example in Croatia that planning can return and capacities be rebuilt. And on higher-quality, data- and analysis-based foundations, which does not concern the railway but can be a general model.

Toni Prug, who in his scientific work has dealt quite a bit with the topic of public sector management, finally conveyed to us the impression that Croatian Railways have so far been a kind of victim of the oil and automobile lobby. “Their private and profit goals have prevailed over the practicality, efficiency, safety and ecological superiority of modern railway systems,” he told DW. Such a hierarchy could change soon thanks to military priorities. But the future of the railway and of social development in general will certainly not be bright if its primarily civilian advantages remain somewhere beside the tracks.

World.title: Croatia Among European Record Holders for Firefighter Numbers
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatia is among the European record holders when it comes to firefighter numbers as the overall number within Europe has fallen.

Poslovni reports that the total number of firefighters across the EU fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a year that was the worst in EU history in terms of burned area.

Croatia is among the European record holders for firefighter numbers, holding one of the highest shares of professional firefighters in employment in the entire EU. Back in 2025, they accounted for 0.43 percent of total employment, making Croatia second among the 22 EU Member States for which data has been made available. This places Croatia right behind Greece (0.47 percent), according to Euronews. The EU average was 0.18 percent. Portugal follows with 0.33 percent, while the lowest shares are recorded by the Netherlands (0.05), Austria (0.07) and Sweden (0.10 percent).

Across the entire EU there were around 372,400 professional firefighters. Germany had the most, 57,700, followed by France with 47,700 and Italy with 43,500. Next come Poland with 40,000 and Spain with 38,500; the four largest EU economies together account for 187,400 firefighters, or 50.3 percent of the total number. The overall figure in the Union fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a single year that was the worst in EU history for burned areas. The European Trade Union Confederation and EPSU call this drop “reckless cuts” and note that Poland lost 9,000 and France lodt 4,100 firefighters.

Croatia doesn’t rank among the leaders in total numbers, but its share of total employment is among the highest. Eurostat data refers to professional firefighters, including forest firefighters, but not volunteer firefighters. The data also doesn’t show precisely how many professional firefighters are specialised specifically in fighting open-air fires.

The data comes at a time when Europe is facing an ever-growing fire risk. According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) by the 13th of August, the figure had risen to 568,415 hectares from 1,647 fires. For comparison, 2025 was the most destructive season ever recorded in the EU, with 1,079,538 hectares burned in 25 of the 27 EU Member States.

For 2026 the EU has secured a fleet of 22 firefighting aircraft and five helicopters, and in the event of major fires member states can request additional firefighters and equipment through the European Civil Protection Mechanism. In addition, a record 777 firefighters from 14 European countries have been pre-positioned in Cyprus, Greece, Italy, France, Spain and Portugal. Croatia contributes two medium amphibious aircraft to the European fleet, and in 2026 the Commission is also opening a new regional firefighting base in Cyprus with capacity for six aircraft.

World.title: Basketball star Henri Drell to be 'man in the mask' in Hungary qualifier
World.content:
National team basketball forward Henri Drell is having to don a mask during this week's FIBA World Cup qualifier away to Hungary, following an injury.

Estonia's basketball team arrived in Miskolc, Hungary, on Tuesday ahead of tomorrow's game.

Drell (Neptūnas Klaipėda) had an excellent game in a recent friendly against Lithuania, but then took a blow to the nose against Italy. He will be able to play, but will have to wear a mask. "Nothing else directly restricts him, his breathing is unobstructed and he can play. After the window, the relevant specialists can deal with it further," team doctor Kaido Stroom said. "It will certainly cause some discomfort, but Henri is very professional in that regard. It doesn't directly limit his playing minutes; that's up to [team coach] Heiko [Rannula] to decide."

Guard Martin Paasoja will however miss the game, as he is recovering from an upper respiratory tract infection, Stroom said.

Kasper Suurorg, another guard, fell awkwardly during training and knocked his elbow on his non-shooting hand, so will miss the Hungary game.

Beyond that, the team will take the traveling to and fro between Estonia and Hungary in their stride, Stroom added.

The national team reached the second phase of the qualifying campaign with a record of 3:3, the same as other group L teams Slovenia, Hungary and Sweden. After playing Hungary, Estonia faces Finland at the Unibet Arena on Sunday.

Both the Hungary and Finland games can be watched live via ERR's Sport portal.

World.title: Difficult to believe Putin would meet CIA chief, says Ex-ISS director
World.content:
Former Internal Security Service Director General Arnold Sinisalu said the head of the U.S.' Central Intelligence Agency's visit to Russia this week does not necessarily mean a secret agreement is being made and it is worth remaining calm.

On Tuesday, it was reported that CIA Director John Ratcliffe had unexpectedly flown to Moscow via Latvia. U.S. media wrote that he held talks with Russian officials, but the subject of the discussions is unknown.

The last time the head of the U.S. intelligence agency visited Moscow was a few months before Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. The Americans wanted to make it clear to the Russians that their plans were known and to advise them to stop.

Sinisalu, now a visiting professor at the University of Tartu's Johan Skytte Institute, told Vikerraadio's "Uudis+" program on Wednesday that communication between the services of two major powers is normal and could cover many topics, not only Ukraine.

"We should not think that the only issue between Russia and America is the war in Ukraine," he said. Sinisalu said the military conflict between Iran and America may be the top priority, as it also affects U.S. domestic politics.

Sinisalu said if the U.S. had wanted to keep the visit completely secret, it could have done so. "They could have changed planes several times," he explained.

Additionally, the ex-general director said there is no reason to fear that the two countries are making secret agreements with each other, because the level of trust between them is low.

However, the large aircraft on which Ratcliffe flew to Russia should be looked at separately. He explained that both the FBI and CIA chiefs generally use smaller aircraft to travel. Sinisalu concluded that there must be something on board the aircraft or that it is a matter of security.

Prisoner exchange?

"There has been speculation about many different things here, including whether this is a prisoner exchange," he said. Sinisalu noted that this would seem the most logical explanation. At the same time, prisoner exchanges have been carried out much more quickly and have sometimes even been shown live. "We should take this calmly and proceed from the assumption that it is probably something with much simpler content," he said.

Sinisalu added that the CIA director has generally not traveled to Russia in person for prisoner exchanges, but said there could be something accompanying it. "For example, last-minute bargaining over someone that can only be decided at the very highest level, excluding the presidents," he explained.

The former director general said the question is rather how broad a spectrum of issues the major powers discussed. "U.S. intelligence certainly has various pieces of information that are being used in attempts to start Ukraine-Russia negotiations or resolve the situation with Iran," he said.

Sinisalu noted that there has recently been a great deal of speculation about whether Russia is planning some kind of operation against the Baltics or NATO. He said that Russia currently does not have the strength to carry out a frontal attack in the sense of conventional warfare. "That would also be foolish, because it would give the Ukrainians an excellent opportunity to launch a counterattack, since Russia simply does not have the manpower or weaponry," Sinisalu said.

Developments in space should not be forgotten either. "There has been talk of certain satellites monitoring European and American satellites," Sinisalu noted.

Remain calm

The U.S. newspaper The Wall Street Journal reported that Ratcliffe may also have met with President Vladimir Putin to deliver some kind of warning to him. The U.S. has gathered intelligence indicating that Russia is making preparations for a possible mobilization and also plans to test NATO's resolve.

Sinisalu said that Putin generally does not meet with officials of this kind. "Some kind of message may be relayed there, but I find it difficult to believe that he would physically meet with him," he noted.

Sinisalu said talk of testing NATO is psychological pressure aimed at keeping people in Europe anxious and creating domestic political turbulence.

"Some small special forces provocation is possible, but a large-scale war would be seen coming, and NATO's land, sea and airspace along the borders is monitored very closely," he said, adding it is worth remaining calm.

Sinisalu noted that since the meeting did not take place covertly, it cannot be called a secret meeting.

World.title: Expert: Center Party leader can't stop his MPs voting in presidential election
World.content:
Kõlvart, who is not a Riigikogu member, said earlier in the week that his party would not be voting in the Riigikogu ballots next Wednesday and Thursday, as there is no alternative candidate to Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise.

"A party chairman cannot forbid any member of the Riigikogu from taking part in a presidential election. At this point, I would recommend that Mihhail Kõlvart read the Constitution," political expert Annika Arras told ERR's "Otse uudistemajast" on Wednesday.

The fact that there is only one candidate registered to run – Madise, who was signed off on by 75 MPs where only 21 are needed – along with the process generally over the summer, has raised questions again about the way in which Estonia elects its president.

The head of state is not directly elected by the people, but by the Riigikogu in the first instance, passing to a regional electoral college if this draws a blank. This system was put in place to avoid undue outside interference in the election of the head of state.

Arras said direct presidential elections would certainly be much more exciting than the current vote at the Riigikogu. "In that case, candidates would have a reason to travel around Estonia, present themselves and talk to the people. There would be considerably more opinion polls than there are today," she said.

Also, the issue of outside interference applies to Riigikogu and local elections too, Arras noted, though these enfranchise all Estonian citizens – plus all EU citizens in the case of local elections. "In reality, there is no really watertight argument as to why [the president] could not be directly elected, but it is a matter for discussion and a question of choices. I would be fine with either option," she went on.

The transparency or culture of the presidential elections is ultimately up to the politicians and their actions, she noted; amending the electoral system would not change that on its own. At the same time, Arras noted, another criticism of the process this time around and at past presidential elections is how last-minute the formal nomination of candidates is, or even their public presentation.

"If we altered it so that candidates got nominated earlier, we asked them questions, held debates right here at the public broadcaster and at other media outlets, then politicians would make their choice and people would have a much better idea of whom parliament is electing," she went on.

As for why Isamaa swung the balance further by getting behind Madise last week, Arras said most likely Madise impressed at her meeting with the party's Riigikogu faction – potential candidate Tiit Land had also met with the party before that – and this convinced Isamaa she would be a good head of state.

Also, it might have been difficult to stem a flood of support for Madise from individual Isamaa MPs and others – as Kõlvart has been trying to do with his party.

"This in turn demonstrates that presidential elections in Estonia are so important to every member of the Riigikogu personally that the classic party discipline often used with different parliamentary votes is not easy to maintain," Arras added.

Annika Arras appearing on 'Otse uudistemajast'. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

The Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE) simply cracks down on dissenters by expelling them, but this rigid discipline is likely behind their ongoing marginalization, Arras went on, noting that recovery can and does happen too. EKRE put forward party founder Mart Helme as presidential candidate, but lacked enough seats at the Riigikogu to register him on their own.

One further consideration is the March 2027 Riigikogu elections. Arras said the parties that backed Madise will score political points if she does get elected president, particularly the Social Democrats (SDE), who were the first to publicly endorse Madise.

"But I believe that, overall, all those who have now rallied behind Ülle Madise will benefit in any case," she added, noting that the office of president continues to carry a high degree of public trust.

With four of the six Riigikogu parties backing Madise, the presidential elections are unlikely to prove decisive come March, Arras went on. "There are still five or six months to go until the parliamentary election, which means that anything can still happen. The election results have not been decided today."

Recent opinion polls put Madise's rating with the public as high as 43 percent.

Kõlvart: Party still deciding how to act at presidential election

Kõlvart on Wednesday denied that members of the Center Party faction are prohibited from participating in the Riigikogu vote on Madise September 2-3, adding the party has not yet decided how exactly it will vote on that day.

He reiterated that there had been no debate on Land as an alternative candidate.

"We proceed based on the principle that a party should have a consistent and comprehensible policy and position. From the very outset, we have expressed the view that there should be a broader debate, and to do that you need more than one candidate. We have also expressed our support for Tiit Land. There has been no debate; we have only one candidate," Kõlvart told ERR.

This means the party still sees the situation as less than ideal, he went on. "The Riigikogu group will still decide how we express our position. But in our view, the process we are seeing now is not right, and we also do not believe it is right to take part in it."

The true issues cannot be revealed if a candidate runs unopposed, the Center chair continued. "A debate would show that. It is not possible to say on the basis of one meeting. That is why, in our view, there should have been genuine competition and a debate lasting longer than one day, so that not only the Center Party but society as a whole would have a broader understanding of what the vision of one candidate or another actually means."

The current Riigikogu composition does not reflect public support, he added, reiterating his party's support for direct presidential elections. Madise's election as head of state would remain "an appointment" and not an election, he added, noting that Madise's meeting with the Center Party did not prove sufficient to determine her suitability; a proper debate over a longer period would have been needed, he said.

Overall, the past two months has been little more than a "performance," with spectators looking on to see if Madise would run, or not.

At the last presidential election in 2021, Alar Karis ran unopposed and was voted in after the second ballot. Karis announced in mid-summer he would not be seeking re-election, even though he is eligible for a second term.

World.title: Up to 400 children without school places, says education minister
World.content:
Minister of Education Kristina Kallas (Eesti 200) believes between 300 and 400 children will be missing from the school system by mid-September as Estonia introduces compulsory education until the age of 18.

From this academic year, Estonia has raised the age of compulsory education to 18 years old, meaning all children must attend high school. However, discussions have arisen in recent weeks about the lack of school places.

When a student is marked missing from the school system, it means the state or local government cannot contact them and does not know where they are.

The minister told ETV's morning program "Terevisioon" on Tuesday that many students have not submitted high school applications. This is partly due to students returning to Ukraine for the summer, but some Estonian children have also disappeared from the system.

However, students who have submitted applications have also not received places.

Kallas said holding students back a year to repeat 9th grade is not an option in many cases, especially if they have not received sufficient support throughout their school years.

"These students need a different learning environment, teachers and approach, and preparatory studies are intended precisely for children who have such significant learning gaps or health problems that they need completely different support from what they have received at school so far," she explained.

Kallas also disagreed with teachers that preparatory studies will actually help solve the problem.

Critical situation in Tallinn

Kallas said that the situation is currently most critical in Tallinn. "A child with grades slightly below average can no longer get into any school," she said.

The number of children from outside the capital applying to study in Tallinn has also been higher than average. This has taken places away from local students, she said.

Kallas said that all Tallinn upper secondary schools are currently full, but admissions are still ongoing at almost all of them. This means that students are constantly moving from one school to another.

"Places are turned down again, places become available again. You have to constantly be on the lookout for where places become available," the minister explained. She said this is very stressful and the system should be reviewed.

Karl Erik Kirss, chairman of the board of the Estonian School Student Councils' Union, said it is important that students without a place get clarity on the situation and should be allocated a point of contact from the state or local government.

Kirss explained that many students, particularly non-Estonian-speaking students, are currently uncertain about how their studies will continue on September 1.

"On Tuesday, we instructed our state schools in Tallinn that if a student comes in who appears unlikely to cope even in vocational education because, for example, they do not speak Estonian at all, they should be officially registered as a candidate for preparatory studies," Kallas said.

She explained that this would allow the ministry to know how many additional preparatory study places the state needs to commission.

Vocational schools a viable alternative

Kallas said that new curricula have been launched in vocational education over the past two years.

Significantly more young people are entering vocational education this year than in previous years. "It has become significantly more attractive," she added.

The minister noted that over time, vocational education will become a fully viable alternative after basic school.

Kirss said that the new curricula in vocational education help change students' perception that vocational school is somehow a worse choice than upper secondary school.

"Of course, the current situation, where upper secondary school places are full and all students without a school place are being directed to vocational schools, probably reinforces the perception that vocational school is still a second choice," he added.

The minister said Tallinn College of Technology has more than 400 vacant study places. "If you are interested in the field of technology, then you should definitely contact that school in Tallinn," she added.

If it turns out that there is no suitable study path there after all, the information will be forwarded to the Education Ministry and the ministry can deal with the child individually. "If upper secondary school places are needed, then in Tallinn they are predominantly provided by the city, and in that case the Education Department should be contacted," Kallas said.

World.title: Painting conservator: Soviet‑era artists had to paint with whatever materials they could get
World.content:
Polina Richter, a painting conservator at Kumu art museum who is researching Soviet‑era oil‑painting materials for her master's thesis, says that the scarcity of supplies in that period forced artists to invent creative solutions.

Richter is studying in the master's program in heritage protection and conservation at the Estonian Academy of Arts and is currently writing her thesis. Her research focuses on the materials used in Soviet‑era oil paintings — specifically the peculiarities of material use at the time and how artists obtained what they needed.

Richter said artists working during the Soviet period mainly got their materials from the Artists' Union shop. Quantities were limited, and artists were often allocated a fixed amount of specific paints. "Many came up with quite interesting solutions because of the lack of materials," she said.

She has not heard of artists making their own pigments when supplies ran out. "But certainly someone may have gone that far," she added.

Dentist tools in the conservator's toolbox

Richter's work at Kumu centers on preparing paintings for exhibitions. Many works have already been conserved, but some were restored decades ago and need to be reassessed before being shown again.

"Unfortunately, time does its work, so they need a bit of touching up again for the exhibition," she said.

Richter compares painting conservation to treating a patient. First, the conservator must determine the artwork's history and current problems, then choose the appropriate methods to address them.

Kumu's painting department has four staff members. The museum also has departments for paper, sculpture and frames. Workload varies throughout the year — autumn and spring are busier because more exhibitions are prepared then.

Before an exhibition, conservators assess which works need preparation and whether there is enough time to restore them all. The job also involves working closely with curators, storage staff and other museum employees.

Removing old varnish not always a necessity

A conservator's toolbox includes chemicals, primers and paints. "One of the most interesting things conservators use are actually dentist tools — something you wouldn't expect, but they're great for picking and doing fine detail work," she said.

Every intervention must be carefully considered. For example, removing old varnish is a decision conservators discuss thoroughly.

"Varnish is generally part of the painting. Since varnish yellows over time and undergoes various changes, you have to look very carefully at whether it should be removed at all," Richter explained.

If the materials of a work are not well known, tests are done before starting. Samples may be examined under a microscope or sent to a lab if needed.

Unexpected situations can arise during conservation. "These are usually accidental and human. They don't happen often, but the team tries to find solutions. And since we're conservators, we have to fix them ourselves," she said.

World.title: Court rejects request by convicted traitor for early release
World.content:
Harju District Court ruled on Tuesday that it will not grant convicted traitor Deniss Metsavas's request for early release under electronic monitoring.

The Prosecutor's Office does not support Metsavas's conditional early release, and the prosecutor maintained that position during the hearing. Tallinn Prison likewise does not support allowing the inmate to continue serving his sentence under electronic monitoring supervised by a probation officer.

Metsavas's defense argued that through his conduct and efforts, he has shown that he has drawn the necessary conclusions from his crimes and that continued imprisonment is not strictly necessary to guide his behavior.

When deciding on conditional early release, the court considers the circumstances of the crime, the offender's personality and prior life, behavior during imprisonment — including participation in activities that reduce the risk of reoffending or willingness to participate in such activities during supervision — as well as living conditions and the potential consequences of early release.

The court reviewed the submitted materials, written opinions from the prosecutor and defense, and heard the prosecutor, the convict and his attorney. Based on this, the court concluded that early release would be premature and unjustified.

The court agreed with the defense that Metsavas has several positive factors supporting early release: a stable place to live, supportive family members, vocational training completed during imprisonment, work in various positions such as librarian and instructor of math and yoga groups, no unpaid claims, and savings in his release fund.

However, the court noted that these positive factors alone do not guarantee lawful behavior after release. Metsavas also had a job, home, family and supportive relatives before imprisonment, yet still committed serious crimes.

The main substantive condition for early release is a reliable forecast that the inmate will behave lawfully in the future. Despite the positive aspects, the court considers the risk of reoffending to be high.

This assessment is supported by the seriousness of Metsavas's first‑degree crime, committed over a long period. In the court's view, the risk of new offenses has not been sufficiently reduced.

The ruling has not yet entered into force.

The court convicted Metsavas of treason in 2018 and sentenced him to 15 years in prison.

World.title: Systematic thefts jump 25% in first half of year
World.content:
Compared with other crimes, systematic thefts grew the fastest in the first half of this year, Justice Ministry says. They were registered a quarter more often than during the same period last year.

A systematic theft is a petty theft committed at least three times within a short period. Most of these are shoplifting cases.

Mari‑Liis Sööt from the Ministry of Justice said this rise in systematic thefts is not unique to Estonia. The same trend is troubling Europe more broadly, where shoplifting and organized retail theft have reached their highest levels in decades.

"If we look at Finland, the UK and several other countries, theft numbers have increased there as well," Sööt said.

Mari-Liis Sööt. Source: Ministry of Justice

As for why theft has increased, she said we can only speculate. One reason may be that the cost of living has risen.

"Criminal networks have also become more professional. Interpol and Europol say this," Sööt added.

Taivo Rosi from the Tartu Police Department said repeated petty thefts have kept police busy for years. It is difficult to claim they have suddenly surged.

"In grocery stores, people pay for part of their goods and leave some items unscanned. When such reports reach the police, it becomes clear fairly quickly that this is no longer a case of customer forgetfulness but intentional behavior — a kind of invoice optimization. They pay for the cheaper goods, leave the expensive ones unscanned at self‑checkout and walk out of the store with a straight back and a proud face," Rosi said.

Politsei. Autor/allikas: Martin Dremljuga/ERR

According to him, people still steal the same things as before: expensive food and alcohol from grocery stores, and costly construction and gardening tools from hardware stores.

"We can also mention the well‑known light vehicles and bicycles, which the police have been talking about for years," Rosi added.

Ministry of Justice statistics show that a total of 14,600 crimes were registered in the first half of the year — a six‑percent increase compared with last year.

World.title: Estonian defense company to invest €200 million in Latvian plant
World.content:
Wolfram Europa will invest €200 million to build an explosives and warhead manufacturing complex near Jēkabpils, Latvia, with production set to begin in 2027, the company announced Wednesday.

The 40-hectare facility will be built on land secured under a long-term agreement with Latvia's State Forests (LVM). Construction and production are planned in three phases beginning in 2027, with around 200 skilled jobs expected once the complex is fully operational.

Wolfram Europa said the plant will produce military explosives, warheads and counter-mobility systems. At full capacity, it is expected to produce up to 300 metric tons of RDX or 100 metric tons of HMX annually, as well as assemble 100,000 anti-tank mines and 200,000 warheads per year.

Latvian Economics Minister Viktors Valainis said the investment would strengthen the country's defense industry while creating high-value jobs and increasing industrial capacity.

Wolfram Europa CEO Magnus-Valdemar Saar said the Jēkabpils facility would be the company's first major production site as it seeks to expand explosives manufacturing capacity in Europe.

The company said in its press release that Europe is producing far from enough explosives and that it aims to fill that gap. Its goal is to become Europe's largest explosives manufacturer.

"Over the past 35 years, Europe has steadily scaled back its explosives and ammunition industry, which has also brought technological development in the sector to a standstill. Europe is rearming, but investment remains focused primarily on platforms and final assembly. This is the explosives gap: weapons production is being scaled up faster than the explosives and warheads that make those weapons effective," Saar said.

World.title: US dollar exchange rate against Iraqi dinar continues to fall
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the US dollar against the Iraqi dinar continued to decline on Wednesday in both Baghdad, the capital of Iraq, and Erbil, the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq.

The US dollar exchange rate dropped in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,539.5 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,542.5 Iraqi dinars on Wednesday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,545 Iraqi dinars and 1,535 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate declined, fluctuating between 1,539.5 and 1,539 Iraqi dinars.

The Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) said in February 2023 that it has begun using the new US dollar exchange rate of 1,300 dinars to every US dollar.

The previous official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars to one US dollar, which was being exchanged in the parallel market at a rate of 1,550 dinars.

While the official exchange rate was 1,450 dinars per dollar in January 2023, the US currency was being exchanged at 1,610 dinars during the same month in the parallel market in Iraq. This variation indicated a difference of over 10 percent in the exchange rates.

World.title: Iraq’s financial revenues decline by 42% in June 2026
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s federal budget revenues plummeted to roughly 35.94 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $27.45 billion) in June 2026, down from 62 trillion Iraqi dinars (about $47.3 billion) during the same month in 2025, marking a 42 percent decline.

According to budget figures, the income generated from oil exports in June 2026 reached 28.5 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $21.76 billion), compared to 57.05 trillion Iraqi dinars (around $43.57 billion) in June 2025, representing a decline of around 28.54 trillion Iraqi dinars ($21.79 billion).

The country’s non-oil income climbed to almost 7.44 trillion Iraqi dinars (about $5.68 billion) in June 2026, up from 4.95 trillion Iraqi dinars (approximately $3.78 billion) in June 2025.

Oil’s proportion of overall revenues decreased from 92 percent in June 2025 to 80 percent in June 2026, while the contribution of non-oil revenues to the country’s budget climbed from eight percent to 20 percent.

The World Bank’s ‘Global Economic Prospects’ report, published in June 2026, highlights Iraq as a developing economy that relies significantly on commodity earnings, especially oil.

The World Bank has cautioned about the effects of commodity price volatility on the financial and economic stability of energy-exporting countries.

Commodity prices have been vulnerable to periodic shocks since the start of the current decade, the most recent being the huge disruptions caused by the Middle East conflict, which resulted in dramatic swings in global markets for oil, metals, and agricultural supplies.

Iraq’s economic output grew by 0.5 percent in 2024; however, according to estimates, it contracted by 1.5 percent in 2025 before continuing its downward trajectory in 2026. It is expected to rebound to a 12.2 percent growth rate in 2028.

The World Bank mentioned that Iraq’s economy is one of the most vulnerable to regional developments, with its growth forecast lower compared to several other Middle Eastern oil-producing countries.

World.title: Iraq’s Gulf Keystone revenue unchanged as oil prices balance output decline
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Gulf Keystone Petroleum, the operator of the Shaikan field, one of the largest developments in Iraqi Kurdistan, reported stable revenue during the first half of 2026.

The company’s revenues hit $82.8 million as higher oil prices balanced a 67 percent decline in output due to instability in the region.

The company’s shares rose by 9.6 percent following increased revenues and reduced operating costs.

The company’s revenues are nearly unchanged compared to $83.1 million in the first half of 2025.

Adjusted financial operating profitability increased by 26 percent to $51.7 million, driven by cost reduction and robust pricing.

The firm plans to increase output safely and begin a water handling project in the first quarter of 2027.

The Shaikan field is one of the largest oil fields discovered in the Kurdistan region of Iraq and serves as Gulf Keystone Petroleum’s principal asset.

The field covers around 280 square kilometers and is located about 60 kilometers northwest of Erbil, Iraqi Kurdistan’s capital.

The oilfield has an estimated 416 million barrels of proven reserves. It has been in commercial production since 2013.

World.title: President of Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council visits Iran
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The President of Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council, Faiq Zaidan, paid a high-profile, one-day official visit to Tehran on Tuesday to boost cross-border legal cooperation, develop bilateral judicial agreements, and address important security concerns.

Zaidan met with Iran’s senior executive, legislative, judicial, and security leaders, including the Iranian president, minister of justice, judiciary chief, speaker of the parliament, and secretary of the Supreme National Security Council.

The meetings focused on aligning judicial protocols and managing shared legal issues, strengthening legal relations, streamlining judicial procedures, activating cooperative security frameworks, reviewing legislative support for cross-border law enforcement, and addressing border stability and security measures.

Zaidan strongly opposed the foreign economic pressure against Iran, citing the latest US sanctions imposed under “Operation Economic Outcast.”

The Iraqi judicial chief indicated that Iraq will never forget Iran’s support during the US war against the country in 2003 and the war against ISIS terrorist groups.

Zaidan called for the full execution of existing bilateral legal and security agreements between Baghdad and Tehran.

The Iraqi official added that it is important to enhance intelligence cooperation, curb smuggling networks, streamline extradition protocols, and tackle the existence of anti-Iran groups along shared borders.

World.title: 30 Iraqi students join PetroChina Scholarship at China University of Petroleum
World.content:
Qingdao/ Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Thirty Iraqi university students are completing their preparatory semester at the China University of Petroleum (East China) in the coastal city of Qingdao, marking the inaugural cohort of the Pioneers of Excellence academic scholarship program.

The initiative represents the first time the Iraqi federal government has mobilized the state Training, Technology Transfer, and Scholarship Fund (TTSF) to sponsor undergraduate engineering scholars in China. Funded under the corporate social responsibility and capacity-building commitments of PetroChina Iraq – West Qurna 1, the program bridges bilateral energy development with engineering education.

The scholarship follows a customized “0.5 + 4” academic curriculum designed specifically by China University of Petroleum (East China):

Preparatory Foundation (6 Months): Intensive Mandarin Chinese language acquisition paired with foundation courses in advanced calculus, physics, and chemistry.

Undergraduate Degree (4 Years): Full Bachelor of Science degree tracks focusing on three core upstream disciplines: Petroleum Engineering: Reservoir management, well completion, and enhanced oil recovery (EOR). Mechanical Engineering: Industrial machinery design, refinery turbines, and pipeline hydraulics. Petroleum Geology: Geophysical seismic surveying, structural sedimentology, and basin modeling.



Selected through nationwide competitive examinations and panel interviews organized jointly by the Ministry of Oil and the Ministry of Higher Education and Scientific Research, the students represent diverse Iraqi governorates.

Bilateral Diplomatic Patronage: During the program’s official inauguration ceremony in April, the Consul General of China in Basra, Chen Peizhong, and the Scientific and Educational Counselor at the Iraqi Embassy in Beijing, Dr. Mohanad Najah Jawad Al-Shorofi, addressed the cohort, highlighting the importance of developing native technical talent to lead Iraq’s domestic energy sector.

Student Commitment: Class representative Mohammed Al-Tawous reaffirmed the students’ commitment to mastering advanced engineering curricula to support the modernization of Iraq’s oil and gas infrastructure upon graduation.

Industrial Synergy: Since assuming the role of lead contractor at the giant West Qurna 1 oil field in 2024, PetroChina has prioritized local workforce upskilling, transitioning bilateral energy ties from traditional equipment procurement to joint human capital development.

Hydrocarbons form the foundation of Iraq’s national economy. By equipping domestic engineering talent with advanced training at premier international energy institutions, the Ministry of Oil aims to build a modern technical workforce capable of operating complex extraction assets, deploying artificial lift technologies, and managing next-generation energy infrastructure across southern oil fields.

World.title: Iraq and South Korea finalize financing for air defense missile system
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — Iraqi Minister of Finance Falih Sari met on Wednesday, August 26, 2026, with the South Korean Ambassador to Iraq, Lee Jae-myung, to finalize the financing mechanisms for the contracted air defense missile system between Iraq and South Korea.

The high-level meeting was attended by the Chief of Staff of the Iraqi Army, General Staff Officer Abdul Amir Rashid Yarallah, alongside the South Korean military attaché in Baghdad, according to an official statement issued by the Ministry of Finance and reported by the Iraqi News Agency (INA).

Key Financial & Operational Discussions

Contractual Financial Framework: The talks focused on operationalizing the payment schedules, legal frameworks, and treasury mechanisms required to fulfill bilateral contractual commitments without procedural delay.

Airspace Sovereignty Mandate: Minister Sari emphasized that securing Iraq’s airspace and modernizing territorial air defense capabilities remain national priorities to protect state sovereignty and critical infrastructure against external airborne threats.

High-Level Military Coordination: The presence of General Staff Officer Yarallah underscores operational synchronization between the Ministry of Defense’s procurement timetable and the Ministry of Finance’s budgetary disbursements.

Bilateral Commitment: Ambassador Lee Jae-myung and the South Korean defense attaché reaffirmed Seoul’s commitment to expediting technical execution and delivery timelines in line with agreed bilateral protocols.

The air defense procurement contract with South Korea represents a major technological leap for the Iraqi Air Defense Command.

By securing multi-tiered surface-to-air missile interception batteries, Baghdad aims to establish full sovereign control over its national airspace, replace legacy systems, and build an integrated radar and missile shield capable of intercepting advanced airborne threats, drones, and ballistic targets.

World.title: Chief Justice Zaidan and U.S. Envoy discuss post-coalition arms control
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The President of Iraq’s Supreme Judicial Council, Judge Dr. Faiq Zaidan, received the Chargé d’Affaires of the U.S. Embassy in Baghdad, Joshua Harris, on Wednesday, August 26, 2026, to discuss judicial mechanisms and the enforcement of the rule of law following the scheduled conclusion of the International Coalition’s military mission.

According to an official statement issued by the Supreme Judicial Council and reported by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the discussions focused on legal procedures regarding entities and individuals bearing arms in violation of the Iraqi Constitution and applicable laws, as well as institutional frameworks to enforce the rule of law universally across the country.

Key Discussion Pillars

Post-Coalition Legal Framework:Reviewing judicial and legal preparations ahead of the formal conclusion of the Global Coalition against Daesh/ISIS mission in Iraq on September 30, 2026.

Prosecution of Unregulated Arms:Outlining judicial measures against groups and individuals possessing, displaying, or utilizing unauthorized weapons outside the direct chain of command of state constitutional institutions.

Universal Rule of Law:Establishing judicial coordination mechanisms to ensure that legal statutes and constitutional provisions apply equally to all entities without exception.

The meeting comes as Iraq prepares for the transition of the U.S.-led international military mission into bilateral security partnerships.Restricting weapons exclusively to state custody remains a core pillar of the Iraqi government’s institutional program.

By coordinating judicial procedures alongside executive security measures, the Supreme Judicial Council aims to reinforce national sovereignty, enhance judicial oversight over armed actors, and solidify internal stability as the international military mandate concludes.

World.title: Iraq’s GCCE and Germany’s Sutco sign major waste-to-resource deal in Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) — The General Company for Carbon Economics (GCCE Iraq) has finalized a bilateral Master Agreement with German waste treatment plant manufacturer Sutco® to construct a modern, integrated waste management and resource recovery facility in Baghdad.

The agreement, announced by GCCE Chairman Hayder Al Darraji, was signed under the joint patronage of the governments of the Republic of Iraq and the Federal Republic of Germany, marking a decisive shift toward circular economy infrastructure and sovereign carbon market integration.

The facility is engineered to process municipal solid waste at utility scale, converting daily refuse into certified agricultural inputs, renewable aviation fuel, and internationally tradeable environmental assets:

Daily Waste Intake: Processing capacity of approximately 6,000 tonnes of municipal waste per day.

Organic Fertilizer Yield: Annual output of 500,000 tonnes of high-grade organic fertilizer, produced in full compliance with German industrial quality standards to support domestic agricultural self-reliance.

Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF): Daily production of approximately 100 tonnes of SAF, providing low-carbon aviation fuel options and diversifying downstream energy products.

Industrial Recyclable Sorting: Comprehensive material recovery lines to extract plastics, metals, and inert recyclables for domestic industrial feedstocks.

Carbon Credit Generation:Estimated generation of up to 2 million tonnes of certified carbon offsets annually, positioning Iraq to enter international voluntary and compliance carbon credit markets under verified emissions reduction frameworks.

Cross-Sector Impact and Macroeconomic Value

Sector Core Contribution & Operational Outcome Environmental Protection Diverts 6,000 tonnes/day from open landfills, curbing methane emissions and groundwater contamination. Food & Agriculture Security Delivers 500,000 tonnes/year of organic fertilizer, reducing chemical fertilizer imports and restoring soil health. Clean Transportation Fuel Introduces domestic SAF production at 100 tonnes/day for cleaner aviation pathways. Climate Finance & Carbon Trade Unlocks 2M tonnes/year in carbon credits to mobilize sovereign climate capital under international standards. Industrial Circularity Reclaims secondary raw materials to feed local manufacturing and recycling clusters.

The partnership between GCCE and Sutco establishes a new benchmark for public-private environmental investment in Iraq.By coupling mechanical-biological waste treatment with advanced recycling, aviation bio-refining, and international carbon credit issuance, Baghdad is turning an acute municipal waste challenge into a high-yield green asset class.

World.title: 'Open dialogue, inclusive to all': RSS reacts to row over Mohan Bhagwat's New York event
World.content:
RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat will address the 'Universal Oneness Celebration' at Madison Square Garden on August 29.

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Interfaith forum

A major RSS outreach event is being planned in New York, with Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat scheduled to address the "Universal Oneness Celebration" at Madison Square Garden on August 29.The event is being organised by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue and is expected to bring together Hindu-American organisations and members of the Indian diaspora around the themes of shared heritage, interfaith dialogue and unity.The programme, however, has triggered a political controversy even before it takes place, with New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani publicly opposing Bhagwatâs appearance.Mamdani, New Yorkâs first Muslim and Indian-American mayor, said he did not support the planned rally, describing the RSSâs vision as exclusionary and contrasting it with his own understanding of India as a pluralistic country. At the same time, he acknowledged that the event is privately organised and said he was unsure whether the city had the legal authority to cancel it.The controversy is particularly significant because of Mamdaniâs own Indian heritage and his position as mayor of one of the world's most diverse cities.His criticism has also drawn support from groups opposed to the RSS, while critics of the mayor have questioned whether his position amounts to singling out a Hindu organisation.The RSS, meanwhile, has pushed back strongly against the criticism.RSS communications chief Sunil Ambekar said the New York gathering represents an interfaith forum where Bhagwat will engage with a âdiverse, multicultural, and multi-faith audienceâ.He said the event reflects what the RSS describes as the inclusive and welcoming nature of the Bharatiya ethos, and invited anyone interested in understanding the organisationâs philosophy to participate in open dialogue.The timing of Bhagwatâs visit is also important. The RSS is marking its centenary in 2025-26, and the New York programme forms part of a broader international outreach by Bhagwat covering the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom. The stated objective is to engage Indian-origin communities abroad and present the RSSâs views on India, Hindu society and its own philosophy.

World.title: Govt pushes to make SCADA systems in power sector Indian by 2030
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Govt wants to end imports of technology used to monitor and control Indiaâs power grid by 2030, reducing dependence on foreign companies for systems that are critical to keeping electricity flowing across the country.A committee set up by Central Electricity Authority (CEA) to draw up a roadmap for this has found that local content in these Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition (SCADA) systems is below 20%. It has warned that dependence on proprietary foreign systems can pose risks if there are disruptions in global supply chains or access to technology, upgrades and technical support is restricted.SCADA systems form the digital backbone of the country's load-dispatch network, linking power plants and substations with state, regional and national control centres. They allow grid operators to see what is happening across the network in real time and control equipment remotely.The committee found that software is the easier part of the transition: 36 of the 38 identified software modules can be developed domestically in the short term. But hardware, which accounts for about 75% of SCADA costs, will be a bigger challenge, with 16 of 25 key components expected to be ready for indigenous deployment within two years.The panel has also proposed establishing a dedicated testing platform within two years, including cyber-security validation. This would be followed by real-time pilots at load despatch centres, where indigenous systems would run in parallel with existing systems before being deployed across the grid.A senior power ministry official said the push is aimed not just at reducing imports but also at giving India greater control over the technology running its critical electricity infrastructure and reducing dependence on foreign vendors for upgrades and support.

World.title: 'Let sugar become expensive': BJP minister Vijayvargiya's odd take on price spike
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Madhya Pradesh minister and

MLA

on Wednesday said sugar should become expensive and advised people above 40 to avoid consuming it, as opposition parties stepped up criticism over rising sugar prices ahead of the festive season.

Speaking to reporters in Indore, Vijayvargiya said sugar should ideally be sold cheaply only through government fair-price shops for children, while older people should avoid it altogether.

The Chief Minister also spoke about the state government's preparations for the return of Agniveers and the establishment of a dedicated Agniveer Cell in Uttarakhand.

On the Agniveer Cell, Dhami said the initiative aims to provide employment opportunities to Agniveers returning after completing their service, while making use of the training and skills they acquire during their tenure in the armed forces.

World.title: Dasgaja from the sky: Why India and Nepal are deploying drones over no-man’s land
World.content:
Maintaining the Dasgaja buffer remains a challenge. Photo credit: ANI

What is Dasgaja?

Why India and Nepal are turning to drones to map a border where markers, rivers and land use have complicated boundary management.

An open but defined border

Cross-border occupation

What happens when a river moves but the border doesn't?

Missing boundary pillars and shifting river courses can make an already complex frontier harder to identify on the ground.

Most of the border is mapped

Why are boundary pillars a problem?

India and Nepal are using drone technology to survey parts of their open border where physical markers and changing landscapes create uncertainty.

Why use drones now?

Is this related to Kalapani and Lipulekh?

What this drone survey really means

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

India and Nepal are turning to drones to map a stretch of their border that, on paper, is supposed to remain empty.The area is known as Dasgaja, the no-man's-land or buffer zone along the India-Nepal boundary. But on the ground, parts of it have been cultivated, occupied or built upon. Rivers have changed course, while thousands of boundary pillars have gone missing or been damaged.Now, the two countries want to map that mismatch from the air.At the 13th meeting of the Survey Officials' Committee in Lucknow this month, India and Nepal agreed to use unmanned aerial vehicles to map cross-border occupation, including encroachments in Dasgaja. The joint survey is expected to begin after the monsoon, around September or October, and be completed within three years.The two sides will then jointly analyse the aerial imagery to establish how much land is being used by citizens on the other side of the recognised boundary.The move follows remarks by Nepal prime minister Balendra Shah in Parliament in May that India had encroached on Nepali land and that Nepal, too, had occupied Indian land in some places.Nepal's foreign ministry later clarified that Shah was referring to cross-border occupation and encroachment in Dasgaja, rather than making a new territorial claim against India.Dasgaja literally means "ten yards". It refers to the no-man's-land or buffer zone along the India-Nepal boundary.There is some variation in how its width is described. Indian reports generally refer to a 10-yard no-man's-land, while a study by Nepal's Institute of Foreign Affairs describes a 20-yard-wide buffer, with 10 yards extending from the boundary on either side.The principle is straightforward: the immediate area around the international boundary should remain free of occupation, making the border easier to identify, inspect and maintain.In practice, that is difficult along an open border stretching about 1,880 km. The boundary runs through farmland, settlements, forests, roads and river systems, while communities on both sides maintain deep social and economic links.Nepal's Institute of Foreign Affairs has documented people living in makeshift houses and tents within Dasgaja. Even when security forces remove such settlements, people can return.So, while Dasgaja is meant to function as a buffer on paper, parts of it have gradually become intertwined with everyday life and livelihoods along the border.India and Nepal share an open border. There is no continuous fence separating the two countries, and people routinely cross it for work, trade, family and other activities.An open border, however, does not mean an undefined border.The international boundary is established through boundary pillars, maps and geographic coordinates. Dasgaja provides an additional buffer around that line.Maintaining the physical markers has become a persistent challenge.According to Nepal's Department of Survey, 8,554 boundary pillars were installed along the border. Of these, 1,325 are missing and 1,956 are partially or completely damaged.A missing pillar does not automatically alter the international boundary. Its location can be reconstructed using survey records, coordinates and maps. But on the ground, the absence of a marker can make it far harder to establish where the boundary runs, particularly where fields, houses and roads are close to the line.The drone survey goes beyond Dasgaja. India and Nepal also want to map what officials describe as cross-border occupation.These are instances in which citizens of one country live on, cultivate or otherwise use land that falls on the other side of the legally recognised boundary.Nepal's foreign ministry said this was the issue Shah was referring to when he spoke about Nepal occupying Indian territory. It specifically linked the problem to the Fixed Boundary Principle used in riverine sections of the border.Several sections of the India-Nepal boundary run through or alongside rivers. Rivers naturally shift course through erosion, sediment deposition and the formation of new channels.That can create complicated situations when the legal boundary is tied to a position established in earlier surveys.Under the Fixed Boundary Principle, the boundary can remain fixed even when the river around it changes course.The result can be highly unusual: a farmer may continue cultivating land that a family has used for generations, only for a later survey to establish that the land now lies on the other side of the international boundary.Nepal's foreign ministry identified such riverine changes as one reason for cross-border occupation. Nepal's Kantipur has reported that decades of river-course changes have shifted thousands of hectares of land from one side of the border to the other.The new drone survey is not an attempt to redraw or rediscover the India-Nepal boundary.Technical boundary work dates back to 1981, when the Joint Technical Level Nepal-India Boundary Committee was established.After years of surveying, the committee prepared 182 strip maps covering about 98 per cent of the boundary. The maps were finalised in 2007 and excluded the unresolved areas of Kalapani and Susta.India's ministry of external affairs has also recorded that the strip maps covering 98 per cent of the boundary were authenticated in 2007.But the maps were never formally ratified by both countries as a final settlement.Nepal maintained that outstanding disputes had to be resolved, while India sought their endorsement.Even so, they remain an important technical reference.A boundary line on a map can be difficult to identify in a field without a physical marker.That is why India and Nepal maintain thousands of boundary pillars along the frontier. But many have been damaged, destroyed or lost, particularly in areas affected by rivers and erosion.The two countries have been working to restore them. At the seventh meeting of the Boundary Working Group in July 2025, India and Nepal agreed to jointly construct new pillars and repair damaged ones as part of their technical boundary work.Established in 2014, the Boundary Working Group deals with issues including the clearing of no-man's-land, construction and maintenance of boundary pillars, updating cross-border property records and other technical border matters.It does not cover the unresolved Kalapani and Susta disputes.The technical mechanism operates at three levels: the Boundary Working Group, the Survey Officials' Committee and Joint Field Survey Teams. Field teams conduct ground surveys, while the SOC and BWG examine the findings and determine the next technical steps.The immediate objective is simple: get a far more precise picture of what is happening on the ground.The UAVs will capture aerial images of areas where cross-border occupation is suspected. Indian and Nepali officials will then analyse the imagery jointly and compare it with existing maps, coordinates, boundary pillars and field records.Aerial imagery can show precisely where fields, houses, roads, rivers and other physical features sit in relation to the established boundary.But the most important element is not the drone. It is the joint verification.If both countries work from the same imagery and agree on the technical facts of a particular location, it becomes easier to determine what needs to happen next.The jointly verified record could eventually provide a basis for negotiating the removal of encroachments, restoration of land or, where necessary, compensation.The India-Nepal border has several separate disputes.Kalapani, Lipulekh and Limpiyadhura concern Nepal's territorial claims in the western sector and competing interpretations of historical maps, documents and the course of the Kali or Mahakali River.Susta is another separate dispute involving changes in the course of the Gandak or Narayani River.The current technical mechanism does not cover these unresolved areas. The 2025 BWG agreement specifically kept Susta and Kalapani-Lipulekh-Limpiyadhura outside its technical work.The Dasgaja exercise is narrower. It deals with no-man's-land, boundary infrastructure and cross-border occupation along the established boundary.At first glance, sending drones over Dasgaja may look like a relatively routine surveying exercise. It is anything but.The India-Nepal border is unusual: open to people, but fixed in law; socially intertwined, but internationally sovereign. Over decades, rivers have shifted, settlements have expanded, farms have crossed invisible lines and boundary markers have disappeared.That has created a gap between the border that exists on maps and the border experienced on the ground.The drones are an attempt to close that gap with evidence.They will not settle Kalapani. They will not redraw the map. And they will not, by themselves, resolve every dispute over land.But they could give India and Nepal something that has often been missing in sensitive border discussions: a shared, current and verifiable picture of what is actually happening on the ground.

World.title: Nepal flash floods: 95 dead, hundreds missing; India launches relief effort
World.content: The death toll in Nepal’s devastating flash floods has risen to 95, while 384 people remain missing, including 105 Indian nationals. The disaster struck Nepal’s Rasuwa district near the Tibet border after a sudden surge in the Bhotekoshi River, causing widespread destruction and triggering one of the country’s worst flood emergencies in recent years.

World.content:
Nepali police said on Wednesday (August 26, 2026) they had recovered 157 bodies after a massive flash flood in Nepal’s Bhotekoshi River swept through villages in Rasuwa in the morning, taking the overall death toll to at least 160. Rasuwa, a district bordering China’s Tibet region.

World.title: Seven missing Konaseema fishermen found safe off West Bengal coast
World.content:
The seven fishermen from Dr. B.R.Ambedkar Konaseema district in Andhra Pradesh, who went missing in the sea on August 7, were found safe near Shankarpur fishing harbour off West Bengal coast on Wednesday.

Contact with the fishermen was lost on August 7 after they went deep-sea fishing off the Andhra coast in search of tuna. They set sail into the sea on a mechanised boat from Odalrevu fish landing point.

On Wednesday afternoon, local fishermen found the boat with the missing fishermen on board near the Shankarpur fishing harbour.

Later, they gave a cellphone to the missing fishermen, who spoke to their family members in Andhra Pradesh, confirming that they were safe. The fishermen said that they were stranded at sea after the boat engine developed a technical snag.

The fishermen on board the missing boat have been identified as Kopanathi Ramakrishna, 49, of Komarigiri village; Kollati Yesudasu, 49, of Bendamuri Lanka; Palepu Santa Rao, 26, and Kollati Srinubabu, 37, of Odalarevu village; Karri Rambabu, 46, of Komarigiripatnam in Allavaram mandal. The remaining fishermen are Sangani Tatarao, 60, of Katrenikona mandal and Kataadi Satish Kumar of I. Polavaram mandal.

Dr. B.R.Ambedkar Konaseema District Collector R. Mahesh Kumar was alerted by the families of the missing fishermen.

Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu has directed the Collector to initiate measures for the safe return of the fishermen to their homes. He thanked the Indian Navy, Coast Guard and Central Marine agencies for extending timely support for the two-week search operation in the sea.

A team of Fisheries Department officials have left for West Bengal to bring the missing fishermen back home, the Collector said.

“The family members of the missing fishermen alerted the district administration that the missing fishermen had been traced to West Bengal. The boat drifted towards the West Bengal coast after the engine developed a technical glitch,” District Joint Director (Fisheries) K. Karunakar told The Hindu.

In an official release, Agriculture Minister and Dr. B.R.Ambedkar Konaseema District In-charge Minister K. Atchannaidu said, “We have confirmed the presence of the missing fishermen who were facilitated to speak to their families.”

Indian Navy and Coast Guard had been deployed for the search operation since August 17. Mr. Atchannaidu thanked the Eastern Naval Command of the Indian Navy and Coast Guard for their timely response.

‘Survived without food for three days’

The fishermen said that they survived without food for more than three days in the sea before they reached the West Bengal coast.

In a telephonic conversation with his family members on Wednesday, Karri Rambabu, 47, shared their ordeals. “We ran out of food stock three days ago. Before it, we managed with the available food stocks, with regular intervals of fasting. We survived without food for three days. The locals of Shankarpur fishing harbour found us at around 11.30 a.m. on Wednesday, Mr. Rambabu, hailing from Komaragiripatnam village said.

World.title: Non-Marathi rickshaw drivers protest, assault case registered in Kandivali
World.content:
A case of assault has been registered after a Marathi rickshaw driver was attacked in Kandivali, while non-Marathi drivers have called for a strike against the mandate on Marathi language usage.

The incident in Kandivali has brought the friction between Marathi and non-Marathi rickshaw drivers into the open. The Marathi driver stated that three to four non-Marathi drivers assaulted him and damaged his rickshaw. Following this, workers of the Maharashtra Navnirman Sena (MNS) detained one non-Marathi driver and handed him over to the police. A formal complaint has been filed at the Kandivali police station regarding the assault.

Concurrently, a section of non-Marathi rickshaw drivers has called for a three-day strike. These drivers have taken to the streets to protest the directive requiring them to speak Marathi. Some drivers have stated their position clearly: “We will speak Bhojpuri and Hindi, but we will not speak Marathi.” This protest has emerged as a direct challenge to the state’s language policy.

The drivers have cited their age and lack of formal education as primary reasons for their inability to learn Marathi quickly. A non-Marathi driver said, “We are 50-60 years old. We have not been to school. How will we speak Marathi? If we had studied, we would be sitting in offices today.” They also expressed frustration over penalties being imposed, stating that they are being fined ₹15,000 to ₹20,000, which they cannot afford. They plan to continue the strike until they receive what they consider justice.

On the other hand, Transport Minister Pratap Sarnaik has addressed the protests with a warning. He said that any “mujori” (stubbornness) would be dealt with strictly. His statement added a layer of intensity to the ongoing dispute.

The development follows a growing debate over language enforcement in Mumbai. The protest by non-Marathi drivers and the assault incident have highlighted the broader tensions in the city regarding the implementation of the Marathi language rule for public transport operators. The matter has also drawn attention from political parties, with the MNS taking a proactive role in the Kandivali assault case. The strike and the protest demand that the government reconsider its approach to language enforcement for long-term residents and workers from other States.

World.title: Karnataka High Court quashes charges against Kodagu homestay owner in U.S. national rape case
World.content:
The High Court of Karnataka has quashed criminal proceedings against the owner of a homestay in Kodagu, who was accused of failing to report to the police the alleged rape of a US national at his property in April 2026 and not maintaining registration form about the foreign national’s stay.

Justice M. Nagaprasanna passed the order while allowing the petition filed by the owner challenging the charge sheet filed against him under Section 239 of the Bharatiya Nayaya Sanhita (BNS) for intentional omission to give information, and under Sections 7 read with 14 of the Foreigners Act, 1946, for failing to register the foreign guest’s stay.

Provisions invoked

However, noticing that he was booked under the provisions of the Foreigners Act, 1946, which was repealed in its entirety on September 1, 2025, and was replaced by the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, the Court said “criminality cannot be conjured out of a statutory provision which had ceased to exist.” The alleged incident occurred on April 12, 2026, more than seven months after the repeal of the 1946 Act, the Court pointed out.

While referring to Section 33 [public to give information of certain offences] of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), which enumerates offences that the public is duty-bound to report, the Court noted that sexual offences have conspicuously been absent from this list across six successive criminal procedure codes since 1861.

The Court found that the petitioner, a private citizen, was under no statutory obligation to report the alleged sexual assault, distinguishing the case from statutes like the Protection of Children from Sexual Offices (POCSO), which expressly create such a duty on any one who has the knowledge of the commission of such offences against children.

“Morality may expect a citizen to speak; criminal law can punish his silence only when the statute commands him to speak. A moral expectation cannot, by prosecutorial alchemy, be converted into a penal obligation,” the Court said while pointing out that “the petitioner cannot be made to stand trial for failing to discharge a duty, which the law never cast upon him”.

Oral complaint

It was also pointed out to the Court that in her oral complaint, the US national had clearly stated that she had not informed the petitioner-owner or his family members about the alleged incident of rape by 45-year-old Vrijesh Kumar, a cook-cum-housekeeper of the homestay, after being given a sedated fruit juice upon reaching the homestay on April 12 afternoon.

Curiously, the complainant US national, through a videocall to the police, on May 30 made a new allegation, which she had neither made in her complaint or statement before the magistrate. In her videocall, she claimed that the driver of the taxi, which she herself had booked to reach the homestay from Bengaluru through an online app in April, had sexually assaulted her in the guise of giving her a body massage in the homestay.

She alleged that soon after reaching the homestay, the taxi driver, Thejas Kumar V, offered to give her an Ayurvedic massage. She agreed and during the massage he allegedly sexually assaulted her.

Subsequently, the cook-cum-housekeeper of the homestay also sexually assaulted her. Following the new allegations, the police arrested the taxi driver on June 2 and a chargesheet was filed against the homestay owner, cook, and taxi driver on June 7.

World.title: AI dominates ‘Five Eyes’ security talks in Australia
World.content:
The “Five Eyes” intelligence-sharing group of Britain, the United States, Australia, Canada and New Zealand held talks on Wednesday (August 26, 2026) in Sydney on using artificial intelligence to combat terrorism and organised crime.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the “massive acceleration in the capacity to cause harm through artificial intelligence” had dominated talks with U.S. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, Britain’s Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood, Canadian Minister of Public Safety Gary Anandasangaree and New Zealand Minister of Police Mark Mitchell.

The group discussed how to use AI “through all the different threat areas that we deal with... counter-terrorism, on countering drug smuggling, on dealing with scams and scam centres, on dealing with organised crime”, Mr. Burke told reporters.

The Homeland Ministers watched a display of aerial and maritime drones, Australia’s latest measure to boost surveillance of vessels along its remote and challenging northern coast.
