World.content:
At least 14 infants killed in Islamabad hospital fire

Television footage showed a gutted, blackened ward with scattered equipment and smoke still ​rising.

Police officers move past an ambulance outside an intensive care unit after a fire broke out at the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan, August 26, 2026. Reuters

World.title: Bhotekoshi flood sweeps away nine bank branches, 26 staff out of contact
World.content:
Bhotekoshi flood sweeps away nine bank branches, 26 staff out of contact

Nine commercial bank branches in Rasuwa were swept away by the flood, while communication disruptions have made it difficult to contact employees working there, the Nepal Bankers’ Association said.

World.title: What we know about the Bhotekoshi flood so far
World.content:
What we know about the Bhotekoshi flood so far

The death toll has climbed to 22, nearly 400 remain missing and 88 have been rescued. Inclement weather and disruptions in communication have hampered search-and-rescue efforts.

A similar sudden flood struck the Bhotekoshi river on July 8, 2025. The Department of Hydrology and Meteorology concluded at the time that a glacial lake outburst had caused flooding in the Lhende river near the Nepal-China border in Rasuwa. Angad Dhakal/TKP

World.title: Rasuwa floods weigh on Nepal’s stock market as hydropower, insurers slide
World.content:
Rasuwa floods weigh on Nepal’s stock market as hydropower, insurers slide

The NEPSE index fell 35.92 points, or 1.38 percent, as shares of hydropower and non-life insurance companies came under heavy selling pressure following reports of flood damage to projects in Rasuwa.

World.title: Sanctioned ICC chief urges Japan to counter U.S. campaign
World.content:
International Criminal Court (ICC) President Tomoko Akane on Wednesday urged Japan to use its diplomatic influence to counter Washington’s campaign against the tribunal and help prevent member states in the region from withdrawing from the body, calling sanctions against court officials “a crisis for the rule of law.”

Speaking remotely from a news conference in The Hague, organized by the Japan National Press Club, Akane rejected the U.S. allegation that the court had infringed upon the sovereignty of countries that have not accepted its jurisdiction.

“I can state categorically that there is absolutely no reason for me to be sanctioned,” the Japanese ICC chief said. “It is not true that the ICC abused so-called international law to deprive independent states of their sovereignty, or that I have participated in doing so.”

World.title: ‘The Full Monty’ comes to Japan to bare all and open minds
World.content:
There’s plenty of skin on display in “The Full Monty,” but for Koji Yamamoto, the riskiest part of the musical may be performing entirely in English.

Yamamoto, 49, plays unemployed steelworker Jerry Lukowski in the English-language production, which stars him and Japanese comedian Yuriyan Retriever alongside a cast of Broadway performers. The show opened Aug. 19 at the Tokyo International Forum, where it runs through Sept. 7 before moving to Osaka for a Sept. 10-14 engagement. On opening night, the cast received a standing ovation after the climactic final number.

“The Full Monty” marks the second collaboration between Yamamoto and director Trey Ellett. The pair first worked together in 2024 on “Rent,” another Japan-U.S. co-production with shows in Tokyo and Osaka, performed entirely in English with Japanese subtitles. Yamamoto had already played Mark Cohen, the musical’s lead character, in a 1998-99 Japanese production, but joining Ellett’s cast marked his first time performing it in English. He considered it a once-in-a-lifetime experience.

World.title: Japan port call by a nuclear-armed ship would help deter China: ex-official
World.content:
Tokyo should revise the principle of not permitting the entry of nuclear weapons into Japan, as a port call by a nuclear-armed ship would help deter China, former Assistant Chief Cabinet Secretary Nobukatsu Kanehara has said.

“To deter China, which keeps strengthening its nuclear forces, we have no choice but to say, ’The United States will hit back if you fire at us,’” Kanehara said in a recent interview.

The Japanese government should rewrite the principle to “not let an adversary attack (Japan with a nuclear weapon),” or abolish the principle altogether, he said. The other two of the three nonnuclear principles stipulate that Japan not possess or produce such weapons.

World.title: Japan energy plan seeks to back pipelines bypassing Hormuz
World.content:
Japan plans to support the construction of pipelines that bypass the Strait of Hormuz after the U.S.-Iran conflict laid bare the country’s vulnerability to disruptions in Middle Eastern oil supplies.

The plan is part of a new energy strategy that’s aimed at strengthening supply security, according to documents from Japan’s Cabinet Office released on Wednesday. Other measures include diversifying oil procurement sources and providing support with shipping costs, the documents show.

“The dynamics surrounding energy have fundamentally shifted, upending the assumptions underpinning government policy and corporate activity,” Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi told reporters.

Her government is seeking to finalize the strategy by year-end, she added.

Japan relied on the Middle East for more than 90% of its crude prior to the war, which started in late February, and the nation’s refiners have been forced to seek alternative supplies from countries including the U.S. Processors have also drawn on the nation’s strategic stockpiles to make up for the shortfall.

Under the proposed strategy, there are plans to enhance the risk-financing capabilities of the Japan Organization for Metals and Energy Security (JOGMEC) to encourage participation in new pipeline projects.

JOGMEC is a government-backed agency that provides money and liability guarantees to help Japanese companies buy and develop overseas stakes in resources.

Japan will also look to ensure stable oil shipments by securing necessary insurance coverage for vessels, and will seek to bolster crude reserves to cover the domestic production of naphtha.

World.title: ‘Tech-gemony’ will determine who shapes the next global order
World.content:
I first sensed a disturbance in the force in the early days of the first Trump administration. It wasn’t the president’s antics that got my Spidey senses tingling. Rather, it was a gnawing recognition of a fundamental shift in the way the world worked. Over time, the contents and contours of this new mindset became clear – to me, at least – and I called it “the new national security economy.”

While that administration’s declaration that strategic competition was the defining feature of the geopolitical moment made sense, it wasn’t clear how that concept would be applied. Unlike the Cold War, when the primary battleground was military, the U.S. and the West generally were squaring off against a real economic adversary, one that is deeply embedded in its supply chains and integral to its economic success.

The economic dimension transformed strategic – I use that word in its most elemental sense – calculations, particularly since this shifted attention to an arena, technology, where Western leadership has been taken for granted. Historically, discussions of technology in the strategic sphere zeroed in on its impact on military capabilities. Today, the civilian uses of that technology matter most. That is why David Lee and I titled our new book, which comes out today, “Tech-Gemony”: It explains how and why the future will be written by the companies and countries that lead in this field.

World.title: Deadly flash flood and mudslide cause casualties in Nepal and China
World.content:
Nepal sent helicopters to the rescue on Wednesday after a massive flash flood swept away villages in the Himalayan nation, killing eight and damaging roads, bridges and power projects in areas near Tibet, authorities said.

Across the border, Tibet reported “major casualties” with some missing in the neighboring county of Gyirong after a mudslide hit a land crossing between China and Nepal, the Xinhua official news agency said.

The waters were too high for helicopters to land in Nepal’s affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous district of Rasuwa, which has a population of about 50,000, officials said, while flagging the risk of casualties.

“There could be heavy casualties or loss of property,” said district administrator Narendra Pariyar. “But I cannot say for sure now.“

Pariyar urged those living on the banks of the Bhote Koshi river in the area to seek higher ground, pointing to reports that nearby villages and infrastructure project sites were washed away.

“It all came suddenly,” the Onlinekhabar portal quoted a witness from the area as saying. “We heard a loud sound, like a volcano erupting. People started to scream and ran away.”

Nepal’s rescue helicopters would be unable to land in the affected areas until the waters recede, however, said army spokesperson Raja Ram Basnet.

The cause of the inundation was not immediately clear, but a deadly flash flood on the same river last year was eventually traced to the draining of a glacial lake.

The mudslide on the Nepali side hit China’s Gyirong port, Xinhua added, cutting off roads, communications and power in the Shigatse region near the border with Nepal, it added without giving details.

Chinese President Xi Jinping urged “all-out” search efforts for the missing as well as stronger monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters.

Nepal’s energy ministry said 430 megawatts of electricity supplies were affected, mostly from hydroelectric projects, or more than 12% of total national hydropower capacity of 3.2 gigawatts, a calculation showed.

Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah said police and military were joining rescue and relief teams.

“Instructions have been given ... to move the people living in the lower areas to safer places,” he said. “People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert.”

From its origins in Tibet, the Bhote Koshi river empties into Nepal’s Trishuli river that eventually flows into India as the Gandak river.

Last year’s Bhote Koshi flood killed nine people, with 24 missing, as it washed away a “Friendship Bridge” linking Nepal and China to disrupt trade and transport for months.

That flood was triggered by the draining of a supraglacial lake in Tibet, a regional climate monitor said.

World.title: Deterrence can be enhanced without nonnuclear rule change, professor says
World.content:
Japan does not need to revise its nonnuclear principles as it is possible to enhance deterrence without changing the principles, according to University of Tsukuba professor Atsuko Higashino.

The issue should not be included in a planned revision of the country’s three major national security documents, Higashino said in a recent interview.

The government should convene a panel of experts on nuclear issues if it decides to amend the three principles of not possessing, not producing and not permitting the entry of nuclear weapons into the country, she said.

World.title: Japanese automakers seen facing blow from Trump’s Canada tariff hike
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump’s planned 50% tariff on Canadian automobiles and auto parts is poised to hit Japanese automakers, which have built production and supply chains spanning the United States, Canada and Mexico.

On Monday, Trump said that the United States will double the tariff rate to 50% on Jan. 1, 2027.

Japanese makers established North American production networks based on the USMCA, a free trade pact among the United States, Canada and Mexico, which exempts qualifying goods from tariffs.

But a review of the agreement, which took effect in July 2020, has dragged on, while worsening U.S.-Canada relations are another complication.

The USMCA was negotiated during Trump’s first administration. Automakers, including U.S. companies, have established vehicle plants in not only the United States but also Canada and Mexico for supply to the U.S. market.

The controversial 50% tariff is expected to apply even to vehicles and parts that meet USMCA requirements.

Toyota vehicles including some Lexus luxury brand models and the RAV4, an SUV, at its Canadian plant for export to the United States. Toyota-affiliated parts makers Denso and Aisin also export air conditioner components, door frames and other products from Canada.

Honda exports popular models including the Civic to the United States. An official at its local unit says the volume is on the scale of 300,000 units a year.

Japanese automakers are struggling even at the current U.S. tariff rate of 25% for vehicle imports from Canada. “We are in a difficult earnings environment,” an executive at one maker said.

The planned hike to 50% “would make operations at Japanese companies with bases in Canada untenable,” the executive said.

Viewing the high U.S. tariffs as more than a temporary measure, Japanese automakers plan to expand production in the United States.

The deterioration in U.S.-Canada relations could also affect the ongoing USMCA review, making it harder for companies to revamp their supply chains.

“It is clear that we need to overhaul our supply chains, but the conditions for doing this are not yet in place, leaving us little room to maneuver,” a senior official at a major automaker said.

World.title: 2 arrested in Hong Kong fight over elderly woman slapping girl
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested two women on suspicion of assault at a shopping centre in Kwun Tong, with a viral clip showing a fight breaking out after a five-year-old girl was shoved and then knocked to the ground.

The fight took place at the atrium of the APM shopping centre at around 4.45pm on Wednesday as a crowd of parents and young children gathered around a play area.

A source said one of the suspects, aged 68, was visiting the play area with her 34-year-old daughter and grandson.

A dispute reportedly erupted between the boy and a five-year-old girl over use of the installation, prompting his grandmother to get involved.

In the clip, an elderly woman can be seen forcefully shoving a girl and then slapping her, causing the child to lose her balance and fall.

At one point in the footage, the boy’s mother confronts the other mother and says: “You can’t leave.” Photo: Threads/one_mushroooom

Another woman then rushes forward to confront the first woman and strikes her.

World.title: Hong Kong lawmaker urges firms to expand into emerging markets amid US visa pause
World.content:
Hong Kong companies should accelerate their expansion into the Middle East, the Asean bloc and Central Asia to reduce their exposure to geopolitical risks, a lawmaker has said, as the US moved to disrupt immigrant-visa appointments worldwide.

Jonathan Lamport, the representative for the Hong Kong General Chamber of Commerce (HKGCC) in the Legislative Council, said the visa uncertainty reinforced the need for companies to broaden their overseas presence beyond traditional Western markets.

“The business sector cannot put all its eggs in one basket,” he told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday.

“While we will continue to maintain our relationships with traditional markets like the US and Europe, we must also accelerate our strategic expansion into emerging markets such as the Middle East, Asean and Central Asia.”

The commercial sector lawmaker said the local business community was closely monitoring whether the disruption would affect the processing and approval of business visas.

World.title: Family seeks help after Hongkonger held in Philippines despite finishing jail time
World.content:
The family of a Hong Kong man imprisoned in the Philippines for more than two decades has appealed to city authorities for help after he remained in custody despite a court in the country recently ruling he had finished serving his sentence.

Tang Lung-wai was arrested in the country in July 2000 for the possession of methamphetamine, also known as Ice, and placed on remand. He was later convicted in 2011 and sentenced to 40 years in prison.

While the court recently ruled that his sentence was now considered served after taking into consideration a good conduct time allowance, Tang’s family said he remained in prison and faced lengthy administrative procedures before he could be deported.

In a decision handed down by the Muntinlupa City Regional Trial Court on July 30, which was also seen by the South China Morning Post, Judge Abraham Joseph Alcantara ordered Tang’s release and transfer to the country’s Bureau of Immigration “for immediate deportation without further proceedings, all in accordance with the law”.

The court ruled that, as of July 5, Tang had technically served 40 years, one month and thirteen days in prison when factoring in his good conduct allowance.

“He has already served the maximum period of detention, making his immediate release warranted,” Alcantara said.

The court also said an inaccuracy in prison records previously showed that Tang had only served 39 years and four months.

World.title: Hong Kong customs seizes HK$11m of suspected sex pills, cancer drugs at warehouse
World.content:
Hong Kong customs officers have seized suspected men’s sexual health pills and cancer treatment drugs worth more than HK$11 million (US$1.4 million) in a Sheung Shui warehouse, arresting two people.

Inspector Shirley Woo Suet‑yi of the syndicate crimes investigation bureau at the Customs and Excise Department said on Wednesday that officers had noticed a rising demand for controlled pharmaceutical products in recent weeks.

Investigators launched the probe early this month and identified an industrial space in Sheung Shui believed to be linked to smuggling activities.

On Tuesday, customs officers raided the warehouse, which had been used to repackage and store the drugs.

More than 400,000 suspected controlled pharmaceutical items were seized, with an estimated street value exceeding HK$11 million.

A 56‑year‑old woman who received the goods and a 51‑year‑old man employed as a handyman were arrested at the scene. Both held two‑way permits issued by mainland China to enter Hong Kong.

Authorities believe most of the drugs originated from South Asia, although the exact source remains under investigation.

World.title: No lead poisoning cases found among children after infant formula scare
World.content:
Hong Kong health authorities have confirmed that no child has shown signs of poisoning after drinking a batch of infant formula found to contain excessive levels of lead.

The Department of Health gave an update on Wednesday, a month after Macau authorities alerted the public that a batch of Frisolac Prestige Stage 1 infant formula, manufactured by the Dutch company Royal FrieslandCampina, might contain lead levels exceeding permissible limits.

The department said its dedicated hotline and the maternal and child health centres had received 762 relevant inquiries.

Health officers provided advice on switching infant formula and referred 446 babies and young children to public hospitals for assessment and follow-up. Among them, 237 had undergone clinical assessments.

“Results indicated that their overall health is good and that none have shown signs of lead poisoning,” the department said.

The rest were either pending assessment or the parents had decided not to proceed with check-ups, it added.

World.title: Hong Kong’s first 5-year plan, policy address to be unveiled on September 16
World.content:
Hong Kong’s leader will deliver the city’s first five-year plan and his annual policy address on September 16, stressing that presenting the blueprints together will help residents better understand how they are deeply connected.

Chief Executive John Lee Ka-chiu announced the move on Wednesday after he visited residents from lower-income households and inspected community services at Un Chau Estate in Sham Shui Po district to gather public views.

Lee said unveiling the five-year plan and then his policy address shortly afterwards would help residents better grasp how they complemented each other in defining the vision for Hong Kong’s future.

“The five-year plan draws the eyes of a dragon, while the policy address draws the entire dragon … but the public may not fully understand how they work together,” he said.

“If the public can look at the two documents together, they will see how the five-year plan sets the directional requirements and guidance and how the policy address formulates policies and implements the direction of the blueprint.”

He added that the policy address would formulate measures and set out indicators for implementing the five-year plan, based on the international environment, economic forecasts and the latest developments.

World.title: Student of the Year Awards celebrates 45 years of excellence, announces new vision for nurturing Hong Kong’s future leaders
World.content:
Winfried Engelbrecht-Bresges, CEO of The Hong Kong Jockey Club, congratulated the awardees on their achievements and reaffirmed the Club’s long-standing commitment to youth development through its sponsorship of SOTY for 13 consecutive years. He highlighted the Club’s belief that success extends beyond academic achievement. “We want to inspire young people to work for the common good and for the betterment of everyone in our society - which is the purpose at The Hong Kong Jockey Club.” Noting that the HKJC has donated more than HK$16 billion to youth initiatives over the past decade, he added, “We believe in the future of every young person. I encourage you to be intellectually curious and socially engaged. Because leadership is not only about IQ, it's about EQ. It's about building trusted relationships. It's about listening. It's about understanding others to really become a leader and excel.”

Guest-of-Honour Chan Kwok-ki, Chief Secretary for Administration, described the awards as one of Hong Kong’s leading youth recognition programmes. Reflecting on this year’s theme, he said, “Leadership is not about a title, it is about the courage to step forward, the strength to take responsibility, and the determination to turn ideas into reality. That is a spirit we celebrate today, and that spirit will shape a brighter future for our city and for the world at large. The government shares this vision wholeheartedly. We are firmly committed to youth development.”

On July 11, a celebratory ceremony at the Hong Kong Convention and Exhibition Centre honoured 40 outstanding students across 10 award categories, including the prestigious Grand Prize. More than 300 guests attended, including leaders from professional associations and community organisations, distinguished academics, principals from leading secondary schools, and proud parents – all gathered to recognise the achievements of the winners, finalists and nominees.

Organised by the South China Morning Post and solely sponsored by The Hong Kong Jockey Club, with support from the Education Bureau, the annual awards programme reached another milestone this year, receiving a record-breaking 900-plus nominations from 181 schools.

Celebrating its 45th anniversary this year, the Student of the Year (SOTY) Awards unveiled a series of forward-looking initiatives while honouring a community-minded student-athlete from Ying Wa College with the Grand Prize for exemplifying this year’s theme: “Leadership in Action: Shaping the Possible.”

To mark the awards’ milestone anniversary, Tammy Tam, Publisher of the South China Morning Post, highlighted how the programme continues to evolve in tandem with national and local development priorities. She noted that under China’s 15th Five-Year Plan, Hong Kong has been designated an international education and talent hub, while the city is drafting its inaugural Five-Year Plan. “In light of this blueprint, and on behalf of our advisory board, I'm delighted to share two brand new landmark initiatives. Going forward, we will introduce a new award category on AI literacy, underscoring the importance of the responsible use of AI, starting from our students. And second, we will strategically expand the Student of the Year brand beyond Hong Kong to elevate student excellence on a broader stage,” she said.

Other distinguished guests included Lan Kwai Fong Group chairman Allan Zeman, West Kowloon Cultural District Authority chairman Bernard Chan, and Kenneth Leung, vice-president of the All-China Youth Federation and vice-chairman of the Youth Development Commission.



Student of the Year Awards 2025/26 Grand Prize winner Jayden Tang (third from the left); first runner-up Tam Ho Wang (second from the left); and second runner-up Choi Hai Tung Hazel (third from the right), receive their awards on stage from Irene Chan, Head of Public Affairs (Corporate & Charities Communications) of The Hong Kong Jockey Club (first from the left); Tammy Tam, Publisher of the South China Morning Post (second from the right); Hsu Siu-man, Executive Director of The Hong Kong Federation of Youth Groups (first from the right). A number of past SOTY winners marked this year’s anniversary by sharing how the awards had shaped their personal journeys. Dr Chan Mui Tong, Grand Prize recipient of SOTY 1984/85, recalled how his mother inspired him through her relentless pursuit of self-improvement despite long working hours and the demands of caring for a large family.

The ceremony reached its peak with the announcement of the Grand Prize winner: Jayden Tang, a Form 5 student at Ying Wa College was recognised for his outstanding contributions to the community. A committed student-athlete, he founded the platform “Health is Wealth” and led service projects supporting underprivileged groups across the city. He also captained the Hong Kong, China Men’s U16 Basketball Team.

In his acceptance speech, Tang expressed heartfelt gratitude to his school, teachers, basketball coach, and family – especially his grandmother. “She taught me to always be proactive in life and to take charge in our own life,” he said.

The Grand Prize, which includes a HK$25,000 scholarship, honours a student whose contributions demonstrate dedication and transformative impact. First and second runners-up receive scholarships of HK$8,000 and HK$4,000 respectively. The Most Nurturing Environment Award went to HKFYG Lee Shau Kee College in recognition of its commitment to fostering student growth.

To further support nominees as they plan their futures, SCMP Learn – with exclusive support from the HKJC – launched the Student of the Year Growth Network in 2025. In its inaugural year, the initiative partnered with more than 10 leading organisations across diverse sectors and organised eight exclusive events, creating a vibrant bridge between nominees and Hong Kong’s professional landscape. All nominees automatically join this network, gaining access to career development opportunities and a growing community of distinguished SOTY alumni.

One of the highlights was the opportunity to enjoy an enhanced visit to the HKJC’s Pok Fu Lam Public Riding School. Here students were able to test their riding skills on a riding simulator, join a guided tour of the stables and feed horses. In addition, one of the HKJC’s Management Trainees shared her personal journey at the HKJC, offering insights into her career development and key lessons learned from her experience, while encouraging students to embrace new opportunities, remain curious and pursue continuous growth.

The Winners

Student of the Year - Grand Prize

Jayden Tang

Ying Wa College / Form 5

Jayden emerges as a student-athlete leader shaped by service. As founder of “Health is Wealth”, he drives community outreach supporting refugees and the elderly, grounding his work in empathy. His years captaining Hong Kong, China Men’s U16 Basketball Team and winning titles for Ying Wa College sharpened his resilience under pressure and instilled a deep sense of disciplined teamwork. That same instinct for connection guides him as Student Ambassador Captain, welcoming thousands to campus, while his award-winning public speaking fuels his mission to advocate for social issues—always with humility and purpose.

Student of the Year - Community Contributor

Ng Yat San Owen

St. Paul's Co-Educational College / Form 5

Widely considered a visionary force in youth-led social impact, Owen has combined strategic thinking with contagious energy, turning ideas into meaningful change. As Founder and President of “Game On,” he transformed a simple idea into a citywide movement, rallying 500 volunteers and opening athletic opportunities for more than 5,000 disadvantaged children. His advocacy stretches far beyond the court—speaking to over 15,000 people, from the SCMP DEI Summit to interviews with NBA players, to spotlight systemic sports inequities. Partnerships with the Decathlon Foundation and YMCA further amplify his reach, while his mentorship pipeline empowers rising student leaders to build their own community initiatives.

Student of the Year - Linguist (Cantonese)

Zhao Ziyu Jaden

TWGHs Kap Yan Directors' College / Form 4

Jaden shines as a resilient, empathetic, culturally rooted student whose cross-border journey has shaped a powerful sense of mission. Earning third prize in the Biliteracy and Trilingualism Speech Competition, she channels her linguistic talent into preserving the warmth and charm of the Cantonese culture. On campus, she has spearheaded a Cantonese impromptu speech and public-speaking session, turning passion into action. Guided by her belief in the language’s social value, she is determined to support more learners and extend Cantonese’s positive influence across her community.

Student of the Year - Linguist (English)

Zaynab Kola

HKFYG Lee Shau Kee College / Form 5

Zaynab grew up in Hong Kong’s vibrant trilingual landscape with a clear purpose: using language to uplift underrepresented youth. Her grounding in debate and public speaking sharpened her own voice, but she believes its true power lies in sharing her skills. Guided by that conviction, she founded Speechless x HKIYA, the city’s first public-speaking initiative for Muslim youth, now reaching students across Hong Kong. As Head Prefect, Debate Chairperson, and Chief Editor, she treats each role as a chance to pass the microphone forward and embrace diverse perspectives.

Student of the Year - Linguist (Putonghua)

Qian Zi Zhan Clara

Diocesan Girls' School / Form 6

Clara excels as she stands at the crossroads of language, culture, and leadership, shaping stories that connect people. Her love for Putonghua and Chinese literature fuels award-winning writing and inspired her to launch a student-run literary magazine. As the CEO of a “JA Company” - a youth entrepreneur project, she introduced Hong Kong’s heritage to mainland and overseas audiences, using language as her bridge. Through speeches and study tours, she sparks teenagers’ curiosity about Chinese culture, believing that every word can illuminate differences while revealing shared ground.



Student of the Year - Performing Artist

Sin Seoyeon

Hong Kong International School / Grade 12

At the heart of Hong Kong’s performing-arts scene, Seoyeon expertly blends artistic talent and discipline with a deep sense of purpose. As a standout member of the SHIFT Pre-Professional Company, she has earned top accolades at Dance World Cup Hong Kong, World of Dance, and the International Elite Dance Competition. Leading her school’s Varsity Dance Team, she is a role model of empathy and clear communication. Through “Dance a Difference,” she guides volunteers in bringing movement to elderly and neurodivergent communities, enriching more than 80 lives and strengthening her commitment to service-driven artistry.

Student of the Year - Scientist/ Mathematician

Leung Sze Long

Diocesan Boys' School / Grade 12

Sze Long embodies his school’s motto, “To Serve and to Lead,” through science-driven action that reaches far beyond the classroom. As head of the STEAM coalition, he led award-winning research using superworms and molluscs to tackle plastic pollution, turning experimentation into real environmental impact. He devoted over 100 hours to coaching representatives from the International Junior Science Olympiad, guiding the team to its first overall championship in eight years. By expanding his school’s STEAM fair to engage 1,000 children and designing an AI course for SEN youth, he champions accessible innovation—and carries that commitment into his future in the scientific world.

Student of the Year - Sportsperson

Gilaine Ma

Diocesan Girls’ School, Form 6

As a Hong Kong, China team swimmer, Gilaine is defined not only by medals but by momentum. A record-setter at the Asian Youth Games and IS Gymnasiade champion, she leads her school team with calm resilience and disciplined drive. Missing Paris Olympics qualification reshaped her understanding of grit, fuelling her advocacy for mental wellbeing through workshops and the film Endure. Now a University of Michigan scholar-athlete, she continues her pursuit of the Olympic stage with courage, clarity, and purpose.

Student of the Year - Visual Artist

Mao Yan Su Kelly

Ho Lap College (Sponsored by Sik Sik Yuen) / Form 6

Kelly is recognised as a young artist who channels social realities and personal stories into striking, thoughtful creations. Her award-winning work – most recently the Champion and the "City Vibrance: Art and Light" Special Award at the Wharf Hong Kong Art Competition—reflects both skill and conviction. With over 150 hours of community service, she advocates for accessible creativity, inviting more people into the world of art. As chair of her school’s Art Society, she brings art to campus life, nurturing curiosity and cultural growth.

Student of the Year - Sustainability Advocate

Chiu Wing Yee Valerie

St. Mary's Canossian College / Form 4

A leader of quiet strength, Valerie demonstrates that impact is measured not by volume, but by action. At 12, she founded Teen Animals da Scientists, sparking global conversations on sustainability through fairs, workshops, exchanges, webinars, podcasts, and her magazine Healthy Planet, Healthy People. Her initiatives uplift underprivileged communities and connect youth from over 15 countries. A TEDx advocate and TIME’s Girl of the Year 2025, she shows that age and identity are not limits to one’s ability to create impact—and that building a sustainable future begins now.

World.title: Monk remanded after alleged theft of Monkey King statue from Hong Kong temple
World.content:
A mainland Chinese Buddhist monk has been remanded in custody after allegedly stealing a statue of the Monkey King, a deity famed in classic Chinese novel Journey to the West, from a Hong Kong temple.

The 57-year-old, Zha Jianxin, appeared in West Kowloon Court on Wednesday after being charged with one count of theft involving the statue belonging to Lung Mo Temple in Tsuen Wan.

The statue, valued at HK$2,000 (US$255), depicts Sun Wukong, the mythological Monkey King from the 16th century novel.

In Chinese culture, the character is often seen as a symbol of resilience, rebellion, transformation and spiritual growth.

Court documents state that Zha holds a two-way permit and lives in Shenzhen. He allegedly took the statue from the temple on August 24.

Zha did not apply for bail at the hearing but told Magistrate Amy Chan Wai-mun he wished to make a phone call to a fellow monk.

World.title: Education, health fees among key concerns
World.content:
China to legislate on preschool education

China will push for legislation on preschool education to provide a legal guarantee for the operation and management of such institutions, Vice-minister of Education Tian Xuejun said on Nov 30.

Tian made the remarks at a news conference organized by the State Council Information Office regarding a child abuse case at RYB Education New World Kindergarten in Beijing that received widespread attention in November. He said the Ministry of Education was already doing research on the legislation.

"The ministry will also complete the requirements on qualifications of teachers engaged in preschool education and is considering formulating a code of ethics for them," Tian said.

He also said a plan is on the way to step up supervision of kindergartens and solve the problem of insufficient resources for preschool education. Tian said the case exposed the conflict between public demand for preschool enrollment and insufficient development of preschool education.

"It also showed that some local authorities and kindergartens still have problems of unsound management and failure to implement or fully implement regulations," he said.

Rural health fee increase explained in detail

The National Health and Family Planning Commission recently responded to public concern of newly increased fees for a new rural cooperative medical system.

Fees charged in the new rural cooperative medical system have recently been raised from 30 yuan ($5.5) to 180 yuan.

The NHFPC explained that while fees for individuals have been raised, government financial subsidies to individuals have also been raised accordingly in recent years from the previous 20 yuan per person to 450 per person. At the same time, the government has a comprehensive medical assistance system for those unable to afford such fees. Also, the reimbursement proportion for hospitalization costs for those in the new rural cooperative medical system has also been raised from 35 percent to 75 percent.

Anti-espionage law will help national security

The State Council issued a circular on China's anti-espionage law on Wednesday with detailed rules for implementing the law.

The circular explains several terms in the law, including overseas institutions and organizations, individuals, spy organizations, spy organization agents and hostile organizations. It was made clear that national security departments under the State Council will identify unacceptable behavior.

According to the circular, providing funds, venues and materials to spy organizations and individuals will be identified as helping them.

Conducting espionage activities in the territory, accepting overseas funds to endanger national security or connect them for spying activities will also be deemed as collusion.

Staff members at national safety departments are authorized to arrest and hunt criminal suspects, and their anti-espionage activities will not be interrupted by any other illegal actions.

It said that Chinese people and organizations retain the right and privilege to secure national safety, and their contributions such as providing clues about spying activities, collaborating with national security departments and fighting espionage activities will also be rewarded.

World.title: International group praises green revival
World.content:
High-level advisory panel pitches 15-year pollution fight, but holds China up as model

A high-level international advisory body applauded China's efforts to improve the environment and suggested a 15-year strategy against pollution in a draft recommendation report on Monday.

China has made building an ecological civilization an important goal and has taken comprehensive measures to improve the environment. This has resulted in positive results, including improved air quality, Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli said when chairing the annual meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body.

Like Zhang, Erik Solheim, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, said he was impressed by China's tremendous achievements regarding its environment in recent years, in particular curbing much of the smog problem.

"China is capable of solving the environment problems themselves," said Solheim, the council's vice-chairman, adding the best practices taken by China could provide guidance to other areas facing similar issues.

His praise of China's approaches to move toward being an ecological civilization won wide support from other members of the environmental council, which includes senior officials and experts from home and abroad.

The council's draft recommendation presents highlights of the war against pollution in air, water and soil, and suggests the creation of a 15-year strategy that will be "focused on cost-effectiveness, synergies and ways to build public confidence about eventual results".

Ideally, the integrated rollout should be ready before 2020, to be in line with the 2035 pivot point, when China expects to be a "basic modern country", the draft said.

Solheim said he is confident that China can reach the 2035 goal to build a "beautiful China", considering the determined and effective efforts adopted in recent years.

Along with the longer-term strategy to curb pollution, council members suggested creating conditions for fair competition and incentives for green industries.

Based on the input from Monday's meeting, the advisers and their support teams will modify their proposal and provide a final version to the State Council through the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.
