World.title: Thirty-four Australians among hundreds missing in deadly flash floods in Nepal
World.content:
Updated WorldAsiaTragedy Thirty-four Australians among hundreds missing in deadly flash floods in Nepal Niranjan Shrestha and Sibi Arasu Updated August 27, 2026 — 4:02am ,first published 8:53pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Warning: This story contains graphic content. Thirty-four Australians are among hundreds reported missing after an avalanche of ice and rock triggered massive flash floods that swept through parts of Nepal and China on Wednesday, killing at least 160 people and causing widespread damage to villages and infrastructure. Officials in Nepal said 403 people, including 341 foreign nationals, were reported missing. Sunil Sharma, a tourism board spokesperson, said 133 were from India on pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus. Also missing were 47 from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 24 from Canada, he said. Loading At least 62 missing Nepali citizens were among hundreds of locals trekking in the Gosaikunda Lake area in Rasuwa, coinciding with the local festival of Janai Purnima on Friday, Sharma added. Nepal police spokesperson Abi Narayan Kafle told The Associated Press at least 28 police officials were missing.



Nepal police said 157 bodies had so far been recovered. Neighbouring China has reported at least three people killed and 265 missing in a border community in the country’s Tibet region. The Australian Embassy in Nepal, in a joint statement issued with the embassies of Finland, France, Norway, Switzerland and United Kingdom, said: “We are deeply saddened by the devastating flooding in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts and surrounding areas. “Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster. We express our solidarity with the people of Nepal during this difficult time. We encourage all those in affected areas to follow the guidance of local authorities and official safety advisories as the situation continues to evolve.” The Bhotekoshi River flooded around 9am on Wednesday (around 1pm AEST), destroying several villages as well as roads and hydropower projects, officials said. They issued warnings to residents of several of Nepal’s districts and asked them to stay away from the banks of Bhotekoshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers. Torrential floods swallowed roads, bridges, houses, and power projects in the border areas of Nepal, and triggered a mudslide that hit Gyirong Port, a major land crossing with neighbouring Tibet, cutting roads, communications, and power links to the area.



CCTV footage shows the moment the Chinese and Tibetan side of the Rasuwagadhi border crossing, known as Gyirong Port, is enveloped by the mudslide. Social media It is suspected that an earthquake struck the region and triggered an ice-rock avalanche on the Lhende Khola river in Nepal, causing the floods. The river runs through both Nepal and Tibet. The US Geological Survey had reported a 4.4-magnitude earthquake early Wednesday, about 100 kilometres north of Kathmandu, near the border with China’s autonomous region of Tibet. Nepal’s security personnel have rescued more than 250 people through army helicopter, while police and the military continue searching in flood-affected areas, Nepal’s Prime Minister Balendra Shah said in a Facebook post. Damaged houses stand precariously near the swollen, debris-choked banks of the Trishuli River after flash floods in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha



The Trishuli River after flash floods in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha “We have asked both India and China to help us with the rescue efforts,” said Sasmit Pokharel, a spokesperson for the Nepali government. China has deployed at least 574 rescuers to the land crossing, and India says it was coordinating closely with Kathmandu on rescue and relief efforts. People living in low-lying regions were being moved to safer places, and those along the river have been advised to remain alert, as authorities warn that a second flood may occur since a blockage is still lodged upstream. View post on X



Flood alerts have also been issued in the Indian states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, which border Nepal, since several rivers flow down the Himalayas into their plains. The worst-affected area, Rasuwa district, witnessed similar flash floods to those in August last year, when a glacial lake in neighbouring Tibet overflowed as a result of high temperatures in the mountain region. Nine people lost their lives, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting the two countries, was damaged at the time. Climate experts at the Kathmandu-based International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development say an avalanche from a glacier likely caused Wednesday’s flash flood. Rescuers use an earthmover to carry a victim of flash flooding to safety along the Trishuli River in Nepal’s Nuwakot district. AP Photo/Niranjan Shrestha A muddy river bank with debris is seen near Gyirong Port in southwestern Tibet. Anonymous/Xinhua via AP



The Lhende Khola River, a tributary of the Bhotekoshi River, witnessed maximum flooding Wednesday, they said. “The Lhende Khola has flooded twice in 14 months, this time triggered by an ice rock avalanche from a glacier on the Nepal side that blocked the river and released a sudden surge downstream,” said Saswata Sanyal, a disaster risk reduction specialist at the climate research group. “In a warming Himalaya, early warning is the first line of adaptation,” he added. The Himalayan region, which crosses Nepal and several nearby countries including India, is especially vulnerable to heavy rains, floods and landslides because the area is warming up faster than the rest of the world due to human-caused climate change. Research has shown that extreme weather events, including heat waves, heavy rains and melting glaciers, have become more frequent in the region.



Members of the Kathmandu research group found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush Himalaya region are melting at an accelerating rate, with ice loss rates doubling since 2000 primarily due to rising global temperatures and climate change. World.title: City seeks state help as bin juice issue grows to 40 Optus Stadiums
World.content:
NationalWACity of Perth City seeks state help as bin juice issue grows to 40 Optus Stadiums Indigo Lemay-Conway August 27, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The City of Perth will seek assistance from the state government for a “practical closure pathway” for Tamala Park Waste Facility after excess leachate in the landfill grew to almost 40 Optus Stadiums. The City is one of seven member councils that takes its residential waste to the facility which accepts up to a third of Perth’s household waste. Tamala Park opened in 1991. Mindarie Regional Council At its meeting on Tuesday night, the council voted to request Lord Mayor Bruce Reynolds to advocate to the state government for a “balanced regulatory response” that enables a practical closure pathway for Tamala Park. Councillors also unanimously supported their acting chief executive to monitor the Tamala Park landfill closure, leachate management, community amenity and financial implications and provide them with reports on the status.



As of October 2024, data shows there were 167 Olympic-sized swimming pools worth of leachate accumulated at the bottom of the landfill. Without any removal methods in place, that number will rise. Data in the City’s agenda report reveals that the Mindarie Regional Council – who runs the landfill – “revised its estimate of leachate stored within Stage 2 from approximately 417,000 m³ to approximately 2.07 million m³, or about 2.07 billion litres, after incorporating measurements from internal landfill-gas wells.” That equates to 828 Olympic swimming pools’ worth of leachate or 39.4 Optus Stadiums. “DWER reports potential leachate heads of approximately 30 to 40 metres above the liner at some locations, while acknowledging uncertainty as to the distribution and hydraulic connectivity of the leachate within the waste mass,” the report said.



As a result, the Department of Water and Environment Regulation issued an Environmental Protection Notice on August 3 to the Mindarie Regional Council. The notice requires the MRC to provide a detailed and accurate determination of the leachate levels as well as a leachate removal plan, with 30 days to do it. The EPN also requires the council to improve its landfill gas management, provide updated landfill closure planning, and undertake additional technical investigations. The agenda report says a 2025 assessment by the MRC identified off-site leachate treatment scenarios could cost between “tens of millions of dollars to more than $1 billion” for the amount of leachate that was in the landfill in 2024. “Given the current leachate estimate is materially higher, those historical estimates should not be directly extrapolated. It is nevertheless reasonable to conclude that a large-scale off-site program could expose MRC and its member councils to costs in the hundreds of millions of dollars,” the report said.



“The ultimate allocation of those costs between member councils is currently unknown but is likely to be based on the current ownership structure, of which the City is a 1/12 owner.” The landfill was due to reach the end of its operational life around 2028, but an excessive buildup of liquid waste is now threatening to derail the closure plans. Tamala Park is only partially lined and the MRC’s recent request to install a piggyback liner and create a leachate management area in the northern portion of the tip – closest to the nearby residential homes – was rejected by DWER at the beginning of August. A DWER spokesperson said the high leachate levels was one of the reasons behind the decision. Five of the seven councils have received exemptions to take their waste to other facilities before Tamala Park’s expected closure date, but none have anything locked in yet, leaving the site in limbo if it will ever reach its final profile height to be able to close.



The MRC is considering a Waste-to-Energy agreement at a behind-closed-doors meeting on August 27. A further report to the City of Perth council regarding the Waste-to-Energy agreements will be presented at the September ordinary council meeting. DWER was approached for comment regarding the leachate levels in the landfill.

Oakland: Meta has agreed to pay $US17 billion ($24 billion) and add child safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms to end a landmark trial over teen social media addiction and settle claims filed by 47 states in the US, state attorneys general announced on Wednesday. California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey were among 29 states that sued the tech giant in 2023, but the deal cuts short the trial, which was expected to see chief executive Mark Zuckerberg take the stand before a jury in federal court in California. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, pictured in February, was expected to give evidence. Bloomberg The agreement is worth $US353 million ($492 million) in Virginia alone and is one of the biggest in state consumer protection history, Attorney General Jay Jones said in a statement. “For years, Meta intentionally deceived the public about the addictive and harmful design features that have wreaked havoc on youth mental health,” Jones said. The settlement “will put an end to these dangerous practices and deliver meaningful relief that will protect children from online harm”.



Meta did not respond immediately to a request for comment. The $US17 billion ($24 billion) settlement is a fraction of the company’s 2025 revenue of $US201 billion ($280 billion). The lawsuit accused Meta of contributing to the youth mental health crisis by deliberately designing features that addict children to its platforms and hiding them from the public. It also argued that Meta violated federal laws by routinely collecting data on children under 13 without their parents’ consent. The trial kicked off last week in Oakland, California, with US District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers overseeing the proceedings. Adam Mosseri, the head of Instagram, began his testimony late on Tuesday and defended Meta’s record and progress on child safety and privacy. Adam Mosseri, head of Instagram, leaving the courthouse on Tuesday. Bloomberg The cases in other states had been expected to go to trial later. In addition, nine attorneys general filed lawsuits in their respective states.



Under the proposed settlement, Meta agreed to adopt a series of safety features, including a “hard cap” on daily time limits and pauses for children using Instagram and Facebook. It will eliminate push notifications during weekday school hours and bring in “robust” age assurance measures and “age-appropriate” content controls to prevent bullying and harmful material about eating disorders and self-harm. Related Article Social media ‘Meta needed kids’: Tech giant on trial in trillion-dollar lawsuit over social media addiction There will be stronger and more user-friendly parental controls and limits on social comparison features such as “like” counts. The federal lawsuit was the result of an investigation led by a bipartisan coalition of attorneys general from California, Florida, Kentucky, Massachusetts, Nebraska, New Jersey, Tennessee, and Vermont. It followed newspaper reports, first by The Wall Street Journal in 2021, that found that the company knew about the harm Instagram can cause teenagers – especially teen girls – when it comes to mental health and body image issues.



Meta has since added a host of safety features to Instagram, including separate accounts for teenagers with stronger protections around messaging and privacy, along with content restrictions. But child safety experts, along with some former Meta employees, have long contended that the features are little more than window dressing. Related Article Social media How Meta paid influencers to counter fears Instagram damages teens Arturo Béjar, a former Meta engineering director, said during his testimony last week that Meta consistently prioritised profits over safety in designing its products, focusing on how often and for how long people used them, even if it was detrimental to their mental well-being. “If you step away from the product, they are not going to make any money,” he said.



While the four states in the Oakland trial did not officially say how much they had been seeking, Meta said in a court filing that financial penalties in the case could amount to as much as $US1.4 trillion ($1.95 trillion) – a figure legal experts said was unlikely, if not impossible. World.title: Prince Harry and Meghan arrive in UK for fresh start
World.content:
London: Prince Harry and his family have arrived in Britain to begin their new lives at a private home in the English countryside, after flying from California on a charter jet.

Harry and his wife, Meghan, landed in Birmingham at around noon on Wednesday (9pm AEST) after six years in the United States, days before their two children are due to start school.

The flight believed to be carrying Prince Harry and Meghan and their children from California to the UK. FlightAware

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are expected to move to the Cotswolds, an idyllic rural district in the south-west of England, where they will live in a private residence rather than a royal estate.

While their flight had been widely expected after news broke last week of their intention to return to the UK, their arrival at Birmingham triggered more headlines about their plans and the impact of their move on the rest of the royal family.

World.title: Starship Hospital defers less urgent cases to cope with 'flood' of kids with flu symptoms
World.content:
RNZ national

Starship Children's Hospital is deferring less urgent cases to cope with a "flood" of very young children in hospital with flu symptoms.

Doctors say the free under-fives flu vaccine announced for next year cannot come soon enough and will save lives.

University of Auckland professor of paediatric population health, Cass Byrnes, works as a respiratory specialist at Starship.

The hospital treated children from around the country but was having to put a temporary stop to some of them coming, she said.

That was because, firstly, there were not enough beds for everyone and, secondly, they did not want those children to catch flu in hospital, Brynes said.

There was no treatment for the virus itself but the children in hospital often needed support for serious symptoms, she said.

"Including supporting feeding, supporting with oxygen, or on occasion needing even more intensive respiratory support," she said.

"It's... scary for the child and scary for the parents," she said.

Children in this year's outbreak were quite commonly presenting with non-respiratory symptoms like headaches, digestive problems and very high fever, she said.

Byrnes said she could not be more relieved to see the vaccine funded for under-fives.

It would save lives - but it would also prevent some children from developing breathing conditions later - sometimes long after the flu had gone, she said.

It needed to come with a publicity campaign, because parents of the small group of under-fives who were currently entitled often did not realise, she said.

"And also starting [a campaign] early enough so people get a chance to have a think about or see the campaign two or three times in a row before thinking, 'absolutely - I need to get along there and get a vaccination'," she said.

Currently children under five could get free vaccine if they had previously been hospitalised with a respiratory disease or had another serious condition.

Pharmac estimated about 260,000 more children would be able to be vaccinated for free from April next year.

World.title: Government can reverse growing number of children in poverty, retired paediatrician says
World.content:
A retired paediatrician says changes to government policy can reverse the growing number of children in poverty.

Child Poverty Action Group has released a manifesto calling for cross-party support to reduce the number of children living in material hardship.

StatsNZ figures show the number of children in material hardship rose by 47,500 between 2022 and 2025.

The manifesto's lead author, emeritus professor Innes Asher said most political parties agreed in 2018 to halve the number of children in poverty by 2028, "instead it's gone up".

"They've been pulled down into material hardship at a very time that we had a pact in 2018, the Child Poverty Reduction Act, when we all agreed that it should be halved by 2028 to six percent, and it's gone up now to 14 percent."

That meant one in seven children were living in poverty, she said, but the impact was more pronounced for some groups, with one in four tamariki Māori, one in three Pacific children, and one in four disabled children living in material hardship.

The Child Poverty Action Group said poverty persisted because of failures in the labour market, housing, health and disability, education, welfare and tax settings.

It said these were down to political choices and all parties needed to be held accountable.

One in seven children are living in poverty, the manifesto says. Supplied/ Unsplash - Providence Doucet

The group's manifesto laid out "practical" policy changes it wanted all political parties to take up, Asher said.

The policy change that would bring the fastest and greatest change would be to replace Working For Families with one simple child tax credit that reached all children in low- and middle-income families, and didn't hinge on their parents' benefit status, she said.

The Court of Appeal found in 2013 that the current In Work Tax Credit discriminated against children of parents on benefits and caused material harm to families, she said.

"Yet there's been no government that's had the courage to change it. It doesn't require courage, it requires sense to change it."

The manifesto showed child poverty was estimated to cost New Zealand between $13.5 and $18 billion a year in avoidable demands on health, education, social support, and justice.

It said there was a reduction in child proverty rates between 2019 and 2022 - after the Child Poverty Reduction Act became law.

Asher said at the time there was a families package, the best start policy, and benefits were fully indexed.

"So those are the things that helped and those things have been taken away or reduced.

"We know that government policies have driven this child poverty crisis and therefore government policy changes can turn it round," she said.

"We're wanting cross-party support for this manifesto as a pathway for a better future for our country."

World.title: No really, the economy is improving
World.content:
Things are finally looking up for the New Zealand economy, Westpac says.

It has released its latest economic overview, which says the economy is regaining momentum after a turbulent period.

Chief economist Kelly Eckhold said the country had weathered the disruption that had come with the Iran war reasonably well.

"We remain of the view that the economy can shake off the worries and deliver better outcomes ahead," he said.

How can I pay down my mortgage as fast as possible? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

"In the third quarter, where we are now, it does look like we are on a path to positive growth. Perhaps not necessarily above trend but certainly better than the second quarter. Looking forward, we would expect that to continue."

Growth was flat in the June quarter as prices rose and spending was restrained. But he said he expected economic growth of 2 percent over the full year, lifting to 3 percent next year.

Exports were a big driver of that growth, he said. Strong commodity export prices, a good tourism season and solid trading partner growth were lifting incomes and spending particularly in rural and tourism-exposed parts of the South Island.

Low short-term interest rates were also starting to help construction and household demand, he said.

Inflation at 4.1 percent reflected the 20 percent jump in petrol prices as a result of the conflict, but core inflation had been above the 2 percent midpoint of the Reserve Bank target band for five years.

Eckhold said headline inflation would stay above 3 percent until the middle of next year.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold. Supplied / LinkedIn

"The underlying pressure on prices has proven persistent and the Reserve Bank will need to manage that carefully," Eckhold said.

He said he expected the official cash rate (OCR) to increase to 4 percent through next year, to help bring inflation back to target.

Eckhold said the unemployment rate would hold at around 5.4 percent before eventually dropping to 4.9 percent.

He said it was this labour market improvement that would make the most difference to households.

"We think it's going to be at least until the end of the year and possibly well into next year before the unemployment rate will be on a firmly declining trend. When that occurs I think a lot of people will feel a lot happier about their finances, more secure about their situation."

He said while historically house prices were a significant driver of household wealth, that had not been the case over the past few years. "We can see holdings of financial assets now gradually improving and that's partially a reflection of the strong equity markets and the contributions people have through their KiwiSavers. Some of these things are playing an increasingly important role in buffering household balance sheets and helping support."

He said there were always significant risk around the forecast. "In this case the situation in the Middle East hasn't been resolved so there's plenty of risk there. We also have the election coming up with a few different kinds of policies and potential to disrupt the economy as we go through between now and Christmas but underneath that there's some decent indications of stronger times ahead."

Proposed land or capital gains taxes could reduce the attractiveness of housing to investors and could put downward pressure on house prices, he said. A centre-left government would likely shift the composition of fiscal settings towards higher spending, revenue, and perhaps greater debt issuance in the short term. Credit ratings agencies would need to remain comfortable forecast surpluses associated with any future government would materialise for New Zealand to retain its current credit rating.

World.title: Lack of consequence for MBIE boss who misled MPs sends the wrong message - expert
World.content:
An expert on public sector leadership says a top government official should be sacked for misleading Parliament about a botched multi-million dollar IT project.

Victoria University School of Business and Government associate professor Geoff Plimmer said the lack of consequences for Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) chief executive Nic Blakeley sent the wrong message to public servants about the seriousness of his actions.

The Privileges Committee - which can recommend punishments for rule-breaking at Parliament - on Wednesday found Blakeley and former Immigration NZ head Alison McDonald deliberately misled Parliament, saying their conduct was an insult to the entire public service.

During a select committee appearance in March, the pair were asked about the progress of a biometric upgrade programme and they failed to disclose that the project had already been cancelled.

The Privileges Committee did not hand down any sanctions, acknowledging Blakeley had already apologised.

MBIE chief executive Nic Blakeley (L) and the now retired head of Immigration NZ, Alison McDonald, at a select committee hearing in March 2026. Screenshot / New Zealand Parliament

In a statement, Blakeley said he accepted responsibility for the failure, and apologised again.

The Public Service Commissioner Brian Roche also confirmed Blakeley had recently offered his resignation, but that was rejected given he had only been in the role six weeks at the time.

Plimmer told RNZ the Privileges Committee should have taken a stronger stance, and requiring him to step down was a reasonable punishment for serious wrongdoing.

"A system that allows somebody to mislead a select committee and then say, 'oh well, he shouldn't have done that ... sorry, whoops', I just don't think that that's credible," he said.

"I think that the public deserves better, and I think all the public servants that act with the utmost integrity deserve better as well."

Plimmer said the lack of punishment sent a message to public servants that they could get away with lying to MPs.

"The risk is that that behaviour and other behaviours of a similar type get normalised because the boundaries of what's accepted will become grey."

However Plimmer said he believed in redemption, and that if Blakeley had lost his job, he'd have hoped he could contribute in another way "because obviously he has skills and value".

Dr Geoff Plimmer. RNZ / Rebekah Parsons-King

Worries over public sector integrity

Plimmer could not think of another instance of anyone misleading a select committee.

But there were "too many" instances of senior public sector managers being forced to step down due to integrity issues, he said, pointing to Police and the Teaching Council as examples.

"It does worry me a little bit that something has gone wrong in how we select, develop, incentivise senior managers in the public service because there have been a couple of them recently," he said.

"Maybe that's a good sign that accountability is working, and that there is transparency, people are getting caught, or maybe ... just something has gone wrong, in who we pick for the jobs."

Immigration Minister Erica Stanford said she had confidence in Blakeley "as it stands" - caveating that she was still awaiting the findings of an inquiry about the saga.

That inquiry was commissioned by the Public Service Commissioner and being carried out by Michael Heron KC.

World.title: House sales slow again
World.content:
House sales have slowed again as buyers continue to have the power in the market, Cotality says.

It has now recorded seven consecutive months in which fewer homes sold than the year before. Sales were down 6.4 percent year-on-year in July to 6935.

First-home buyers were responsible for 29 percent of those sales, a new record.

Cotality chief economist Kelvin Davidson said the drop in sales reflected buyer caution.

"They know they've got the power, they don't have to buy the house in question, they know there's probably one similar just down the road because listings are so high."

There are 27,336 properties on the market, down from 27,602 last year but higher than the five-year average of 26,314.

How can I pay down my mortgage as fast as possible? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

"But sellers aren't needing to collapse either, because most people have actually kept their job. Most people with work and with houses and mortgages have kept their job."

He said the level of turnover was higher than in 2022 or 2023 when it fell to 40-year lows of 60,000 or 65,000 a year.

"Through 2024 and 2025, it was pretty consistent growth. Last year we got back to about 90,000 sales, which is pretty close to average… It felt busier, not off the charts, but certainly busier.

"The current level of sales is not actually that bad in a long-run context. "

The recent slowdown in activity means that the 12 -month running total has eased to 89,385, from December's mini-peak of 91,411. The slowdown was sharpest in the main centres.

Davidson said the busiest segment of the market would be the cheaper end where first-home buyers were active.

"They're the active group at the moment. The lower half of the spectrum, those sorts of suburbs are trading pretty well … movers or relocating owner-occupiers are still fairly quiet.

"We're hearing anecdotally that your upper-end suburbs, your more expensive ones, where owner-occupiers tend to be more active, they're a little bit quieter.

"It's possible that someone who's trying to sell a house going to another owner-occupier, or likely to go to another owner-occupier, might just have to be a little bit more aware of subdued buyer demand and think about their price a bit more carefully."

Cotality chief economist Kelvin Davidson. SUPPLIED

He said it was hard to see a clear direction for the housing market from here.

"Farming's still doing pretty well. And we are seeing regions of the economy that are supported by farming actually going okay, in terms of property market trends … there is still a little bit of jobs growth out there.

"So it's not all doom and gloom, but then on the other side of the equation for the housing market, you've got mortgage rates sneaking higher now. You've still got an above-average unemployment rate, lots of economic uncertainty, lots of listings.

"There just seems to be a bit of a holding pattern."

House values dropped 0.3 percent in July according to the Cotality Home Value Index, and Auckland and Wellington were particularly weak. Values were down 1 percent over three months and 0.7 percent over a year. Auckland had the biggest over a year, down 2.4 percent and Wellington was next at 2.1 percent. Over three months Auckland was down 1.4 percent and Wellington 2.3 percent.

Davidson said more people were looking to insure against the risk of higher mortgage rates in future by taking longer-term fixes but that meant they faced an increase when they refixed.

World.title: Which councils could meet government's proposed rates cap?
World.content:
Few councils have been able to keep their rates rises below the proposed 4 percent a year cap in recent years, and commentators say something will have to give if they are expected to try to do so.

The government said this week it was moving ahead with plans to cap the amount councils could increase rates to a maximum of 4 percent. It would not apply to fees and charges or water services.

Only nine of just under 70 councils had proposed rates increases of less than 4 percent for the 2026/27 year. The average increase was 6.9 percent.

The largest increase was more than 20 percent for the Clutha District Council, followed by 17 percent at Waitaki District Council and 11 percent for Gore District Council.

How can I pay down my mortgage as fast as possible? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 10m

The smallest was at Wairoa District Council, up 2.8 percent, followed by Carterton at 3.2 percent.

Wairoa has had some of the largest per-capita spending in recent years, partly due to the recovery efforts from severe weather.

Simplicity economist Shamubeel Eaqub calculated Wellington had the largest rates bill across the country at almost $12,000 on average, including water entity charges, regional council and council rate, as well as other user charges and fees. Porirua was next, followed by Queenstown-Lakes.

The cheapest were in Opotiki and Invercargill.

Local government charges per dwelling. Supplied / Simplicity

Andy Asquith, a local government expert and adjunct research fellow at the University of Western Australia, said the rates cap plan was unlikely to be a success.

"They haven't done their homework and simply don't understand local government.

"I'm unaware of any example of rate capping bringing benefits to local government anywhere. It is simply a case of short term political show boating with a very blunt instrument.

"Local government, local self determination and local communities all suffer because central government isn't prepared or willing to think of a long term sustainable financial system for our councils.

"It is time for a cross party supported Royal Commission with terms of reference similar to the Inquiry chaired by David Shand almost 20 years ago."

He said council rates varied significantly across the country because each council would make the decisions it perceived to be best at any certain time for its community.

"For a long, long time now virtually all councils ignored infrastructure and depreciation. That is the reason why in the last couple of years you've had a number of councils with significant rates increase because they finally bit the bullet and realised that their predecessors have been asleep at the wheel, often knowingly.

"The driving objective of many councils has been to keep rates down irrespective of what the long-term cost is. That's a reflection of the short-termism that underscores a lot of politics in New Zealand, that's partly down to the three-year electoral cycle."

Andy Asquith, a local government expert and adjunct research fellow at the University of Western Australia. Supplied

He said there needed to be a "grown up discussion" about what local government was, what it should be, what it should be doing and how it should be funded. "The current system isn't sustainable… when you're in a situation like you have at the moment where the Crown doesn't pay rates, you've got vast parts of the state that don't pay rates as well, it's a nonsense. No one seems to be prepared to step up and address this."

Eaqub said there had been an average rates increase in the past 10 years of just under 8 percent a year.

"If you have a rates cap, you must decide what is going to cut in terms of spending. This is the gutless nature of these kinds of revenue caps. They don't say which responsibilities or expenditures of local government will be removed as a result. They're saying we'll centralise the rates bit but everything else is your problem... when you're turning off the water or whatever, it's the local council that's incompetent. It's very convenient and very cynical."

He said the conversation was pointless and there had not been a serious conversation about the purpose of local government. "Local government has a huge amount of responsibilities but it doesn't have the resources to do it."

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen said there had been generational underfunding of infrastructure that councils were now grappling with.

As that was worked through, it should mean lower rates increases in future.

But he said the fact that proposed rates caps did not cover water was important.

Infometrics principal economist Brad Olsen. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"Both operating and capital costs for water have gone up… it's hard to compare previous increases to what we might see in the future, given that water is excluded.

"If water costs have been increasing at a far faster clip than otherwise, and clearly they have, the government's current approach, which is quite right to split out water and make water pay for water, could well mean that actually those local government costs over time are larger than before or larger than anticipated purely because those water costs might well have to go up quite a bit to do all of the maintenance work, the upgrades, the renewals that New Zealand generally hasn't done for 30 years or so."

He said 4 percent seemed a simplistic number to settle on.

"There's no recognition for actual costs to local government. There's no recognition for the fact that, for example, we've seen that both central and local government, activity has grown as a stronger share of economic activity over the last decade. So it's a very simplistic policy.

"And I wouldn't be surprised if you see some pretty challenging outcomes. That means that if there's going to be rates caps, communities will have to go without on some things. And at the same time as government's more than happy to take more and more tax off us in terms of income tax … I still find it highly ironic that central government thinks that it should cap rates, but it's not willing to cap taxes."

World.title: Nikita Tszyu says Ben Mahoney 'edged' thrilling Gold Coast draw
World.content:
Nikita Tszyu and Ben Mahoney have fought themselves to a standstill in thrilling contest that was scored a split decision draw on the Gold Coast on Wednesday night.

Incredibly, Tszyu said after the fight that he felt Mahoney edged it and should have been given the win.

"I gave the fight to Ben, honestly," Tszyu said in the ring.

"Maybe one or two rounds more, but I can't be a judge. It was a close fight, but I thought he edged it."

Moments later, Tszyu walked back those comments, saying he was emotional and over-critical at himself.

"I think it was just the emotions," Tszyu said.

"I saw myself stopping him. Not being able to get it, that was just a bit emotional for me.

"I'm a huge critic inside the ring to myself."

He did note that it was the toughest fight of his career: "What do you think?" he said when asked.

The judges scored the fight wildly differently, with Phillip Holiday awarding the fight to Tszyu, 117-111 Sabrina Kerr going the other way and scoring 113-115 to Mahoney, while Carl Zappia scored it a 114-114 draw.

"I don't want to talk down on Nikita and his team, but I do believe I won that fight," Mahoney said.

Ben Mahoney took the fight to Nikita Tszyu in the contest. (Supplied: Main Event)

Mahoney was lifted into the air by his team at the conclusion of the fight, clearly believing he had done enough, and stood on the corner waving at his home crowd before the decision was read out.

The fight was desperately even, with Mahoney more active, while Tszyu delivered more power punches.

Both men were marked after the fight, with Tszyu particularly bruised at the press conference.

Regardless of the result, the number five and number seven ranked super welterweights in the IBF both delivered a terrific performance in front of a thoroughly engaged crowd.

The prize for the winner was a chance to face British fighter Josh Kelly for the IBF world title.

A draw somewhat ends those plans for the moment and, with neither fighter seemingly keen to meet in a rematch, it appears the world title ambitions of both may have to wait.

On the undercard, Cal Peters delivered another sensational result, beating Blake Wells by eighth round stoppage to move to 9-0 and win the IBF Pan Pacific middleweight title.

Peters, a 2024 Olympian and silver medallist at the 2022 Commonwealth Games,

"Those country boys, they're just built different," Peters said.

"I was hitting him with some good shots to the head and he just wouldn't go down."

Kirra Ruston beat Saundre Simmons by first round TKO to move to 10-0, much to the disgust of the Bermudan fighter and his corner.

Koen Mazoudier also kept his hopes of meeting Jermall Charlo by beating Sam Beck by majority decision in a tense contest, while heavyweights Brandon Grach and Ike Pluto started the main card off in fine fashion, with Grach winning by split decision.

Follow all the action live from the Gold Coast Convention Centre.

World.title: Giants star Toby Greene opens up on his AFL future
World.content:
Expecting to make a call on his future in the next two weeks, Greater Western Sydney captain Toby Greene has detailed his plans to meet Geelong and Essendon.

Greene, the greatest player in the Giants' 15-year history, is closely considering finishing his career in Victoria so he has more support for his young family.

Admitting it will be the toughest decision of his career, the 32-year-old denied he had already made up his mind to leave GWS.

"I felt like a lot of people in Melbourne, or friends, maybe even some people at the club, feel like I'm definitely going, which is not true," Greene told the Ausmerican Aces podcast.

"If I was definitely going, I'd say that now. I'd be up front with the Giants and make it easy for them."

Giants not sweating on Greene's future The Giants are keen to retain Toby Greene, but they are happy to wait until the 32-year-old is ready to make a call on his future.

Greene's good friend and former GWS teammate, Jeremy Cameron, looms as a natural attraction at Geelong.

Wooden spooners Essendon are desperate for senior stars to help their young talent develop.

Former Giants assistant Mark McVeigh has just been appointed Bombers coach and wants to talk with Greene.

"I'll meet with Geelong probably this weekend, I'd say," he said.

"I couldn't give a f*** about the tour, to be honest. I couldn't care about what their footy club looks like. They're a bloody good club.

"I'd do weights at Anytime Fitness, if I have to.

"'Spike' (McVeigh) has reached out as well since he got the job and asked to catch up.

"I said I'd catch up with him, but it wasn't exactly what I was thinking all year at all."

GWS missed finals for the first time since 2022, with several experienced players already making an exit.

Coleman medallist in 2024 Jesse Hogan, enigmatic forward Jake Stringer and ruckman Kieren Briggs are confirmed departures.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

"If I didn't think the Giants would finish top-four next year, I wouldn't stay," Greene said.

"One thing I want to do with them is win a flag and that's the best thing I could do ever in footy.

"I could win two or three (premierships) somewhere else [but] it wouldn't be as good as one at the Giants."

Greene has played 282 games for GWS, including the club's first AFL game in 2012.
