Tech.title: AI Slop Is Ruining Cute Animals on the Internet
Tech.content:
AI-generated videos and pictures are destroying one of the largest and most enduring sources of joy and compassion on the internet: animals. Whether the imagery features sailors rescuing a polar bear, baby cows separated from their mothers, or a lost pet that was miraculously found, many people have reached the point where they can’t take the creatures on their feeds at face value anymore. The explosion of deepfakes and AI slop over the past few years has led to widespread frustration among viewers, creators, and organizations that support animals, forcing everyone to hunt in the pixels for glitches or other telltale signs of AI.

Mibbby Butler was overjoyed one day in April when she received a text message that her lost cat, Brooklyn, had supposedly been found. Her roommate’s boyfriend had allegedly taken the cat and dumped him 30 minutes away in the Los Angeles suburbs the day prior. Butler quickly posted a missing poster on social media, and she was driving around with her roommate searching for Brooklyn when a stranger sent her a photo. In it, he is sitting on a kitchen counter while being embraced by a girl.

“My baby is OK!” Butler exclaimed to her roommate. But if she wanted to get him back, the person said, she would have to pay money up front for Brooklyn’s purported temporary care. That’s when Butler sensed she was being scammed and began looking closer at the photo.

Brooklyn was posing the same way as he had in the picture Butler used for the missing poster. In both images, a Torani syrup bottle and a microwave can be seen in the background, except in the new photo, the label text was garbled, a classic sign that it was AI-generated. A disheartened Butler didn’t pay up. “I didn’t know people scammed for lost pets,” she says, noting she also didn’t report the incident to police because she wasn’t sure a crime had occurred. Four months later, Brooklyn is still missing.

The flood of fakes has been no easier on the creators of authentic content. The nonprofit We Animals has published the work of 175 photojournalists who have documented alleged animal abuse and other harms at farms, circuses, and scientific labs. The material can be shocking, which naturally invites skepticism, says Eva von Jagow, the group’s marketing manager. For instance, drone footage We Animals shared of rows and rows of hutches allegedly used to shelter calves separated from their moms on a dairy farm in Arizona looks almost too mesmerizingly perfect to be real.

In the past, people have claimed We Animals’ work is staged or photoshopped. It’s no surprise, then, that some viewers have begun accusing the group of relying on AI, even though it bans the photographers it works with from using the technology. “How to prove it's not AI?” an Instagram user commented earlier this month on the dairy farm video.

Tech.title: Green Chef Meal Kit Review (2026): Great Ingredients, Layered Flavor
Tech.content:
At $14 a serving, Green Chef ranks among the more expensive meal kits (HelloFresh runs around $10–$12), and the 42-deep selection of meals doesn't match middle-of-the-market meal kits like HelloFresh and Marley Spoon, which each offer 100-plus. But the recipes are thoughtful, and the care taken with its ingredients—especially for those with eating restrictions—makes it one of the tastiest meal kit options I've tried, without requiring long cook times.

Here's my experience with Green Chef, and how it works.

Cost per meal $14 per serving on most plans, plus $12 shipping per week Meal plan options Three to eight meals per week; sized for two, four, or six people Lowest-cost plan at full price $96 (including shipping), for three meals for two people Size of weekly menu More than 40 options, plus salad-kit, protein, and smoothie add-ons Gluten-free meals? More than half the menu is certified gluten-free Plant-based meals? About a third of dishes are vegetarian. The vegan selection is more limited. Other dietary plans/restrictions A third of meals are dairy-free. A third are listed as low-calorie or low added sugar. Five to 10 keto offerings a week. Produce and eggs are organic unless otherwise specified. Allergens are clearly marked. Prep time 20 to 45 minutes

The Nuts and Bolts

Like many other meal delivery services, Green Chef is subscription-based. After selecting your diet preferences, whether Mediterranean or gluten-free, you'll be asked how many people you're serving and how many meals a week you'd like to receive. Cost is straightforward: It's $14 a meal, plus $12 shipping per week. Generally, for first-time customers, you'll get 50 percent off the first week.

Also, as with HelloFresh's other meal kits, you can choose which day of the week you want your meals delivered. On the appointed day, a well-organized green box will arrive with recipes and most of the ingredients you need to prepare the meals. The exceptions are basic staples like oil, butter, salt, and pepper. Each recipe comes clearly marked with allergens, whether sesame or tree nuts.

Tech.title: How Ikea Turned a Controller Thumbstick Into the Star of Its Xbox Gaming Range
Tech.content:
Ikea has taken another swing at a gaming gear collection, but this time it brought in a ringer: Xbox. The new nine-piece range, revealed at Gamescom in Cologne, Germany, came about not through whiteboard marketing brainstorms, but a meeting between the Xbox and Ikea design teams at Milan Design Week in 2024.

Hearing the Xbox team—including Carl Ledbetter, head of Xbox devices design—was in Milan at the same time, Ikea product design developer Philip Dilé wanted to show off the company's latest creations, the Brännboll gaming collection, that pleasingly stepped away from sharp edges, RGB lighting, and a black color palette.

“That was a bit of an icebreaker," Dilé tells WIRED. "We were exploring gaming, so we wanted to team up with experts who really understand how people play. We know a lot about life at home, but we wanted to specifically understand how you design for gamers.”

Tech.title: How to Watch Apple’s ‘Surprise and Shine’ Event in September
Tech.content:
Apple

Apple’s next event, which it’s calling “Surprise and shine,” is set for Sept. 9. Historically, Apple has used its September event to announce new hardware, particularly the newest models of iPhones. That means we only have a few weeks left to see if Apple will release the rumored foldable iPhone.

You can catch the Apple event on Apple’s website, Apple TV, the Apple Developer app and the company’s YouTube channel on Wednesday, Sept. 9, at 10 a.m. PT (1 p.m. ET, 6 p.m. BST). We expect to hear from Apple’s incoming CEO, John Ternus, for the first time in his role after he takes up the mantle on Sept. 1.

Here’s what Apple could announce at the event.

A foldable iPhone

Whether Apple calls it the iPhone Fold, iPhone Ultra or the iPhone Flip, the company could show off a foldable iPhone at its September event. Leaks and supply chain reports suggest the foldable iPhone will be a squat, book-style foldable, similar to the Samsung Galaxy Fold 8.

This is a mock-up of what a possible iPhone Fold might look like, according to CNET designer Jeffrey Hazelwood. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

Those same leaks also suggest the price of the iPhone foldable could be between $2,000 and $2,500, which could price many people out. According to a CNET survey, US adults are only willing to spend an average of $781 on a foldable iPhone, which is less than the price of the base model iPhone 17 ($799).

Patrick Holland, CNET’s director of content, said that foldable phones remain a niche interest among most shoppers, but that Apple is likely to price the device to reflect its expensive manufacturing costs.

New iPhone 18 Pro models

CNET’s Jeffrey Hazelwood created these custom renders of what an iPhone 18 Pro might look like. Jeffrey Hazelwood/CNET

According to Bloomberg, Apple could unveil the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max at its September event, too. Those iPhones could also see a price hike, with prices starting at $1,200, up from the iPhone 17 Pro‘s starting price of $1,100.

You might notice that entry-level iPhone 18 models are missing from that lineup. That’s because Bloomberg suspects Apple will split the iPhone launch this year. That means we could see the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max in September before Apple rolls out the iPhone 18, iPhone 18E and potentially a refreshed iPhone Air in the spring.

New Apple Watches

The (from left to right) Apple Watch Ultra 3, Apple Watch Series 11 and Apple Watch SE 3. Apple could show new Apple Watches at its event in September. Carly Marsh/CNET

Apple is also reportedly preparing to announce an Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 at its September event. According to Bloomberg, the new watches could include faster chips and new health and fitness features. However, the new watches likely won’t receive a design change.

There’s no solid information about how much these watches will cost. However, Apple has raised a lot of hardware prices this year, so while the starting price of the Apple Watch 11 is $399, the Apple Watch 12 could cost more at launch.

The AirPods 5

The AirPods 4 (pictured) are a few years old now, so Apple could show AirPods 5 at the company’s September event. Apple/CNET

Bloomberg also reports that Apple could debut the AirPods 5 at the September event, releasing an updated version of the company’s entry-level headphones. Apple released the AirPods 4 almost two years ago, in 2024. Apple isn’t expected to show the rumored camera-equipped AirPods at the September event. We could see those later this year, or in 2027.

The AirPods 4 had a starting price of $129 at launch, but given Apple’s other price increases, the AirPods 5 could also see a higher starting price.

Apple did not immediately respond to CNET’s request to comment.

For more Apple news, here’s what to know about the new M6 Mac Mini and when you might be able to preorder an iPhone 18.

Tech.title: As Apple Prepares Another Next Tech-Defining Moment, Look Back at Major Milestones From Then to Now
Tech.content:
It’s hard to imagine a world without smartphones, but when Apple launched the first iPhone in 2007, it was no guaranteed success. In fact, a smorgasbord of haters was predicting it would fail badly. Oops!

The CNET Group brands — CNET, Lifehacker, Mashable, PCMag, Popular Science and ZDNET — have been covering Apple news and product releases for combined centuries. We were there when Apple announced the MacBook switch to Intel chips in 2005 and when Tim Cook first introduced the Apple Watch as “one more thing” back in April 2015.

As Apple prepares more groundbreaking announcements for its Sept. 9 fall live event, the whole CNET Group is looking back at the most critical coverage moments for the tech giant and what its history might tell us about what comes next.

Check us out every day through the September Apple event and beyond for an “Apple a Day” highlight from the past. And if you think you know what Apple will do at that event, be sure to enter our Big Guessing Game contest for a chance to win a new Apple Watch.

Tech.title: Apple Sends Out Invites for Its Annual Fall iPhone Event
Tech.content:
Apple sent out invitations on Wednesday morning for its annual fall iPhone launch event, and this one could be headlined by the highly anticipated iPhone Fold, as well as the iPhone 18 lineup, a fresh new Apple Watch and updated AirPods.

The event takes place on Wednesday, Sept. 9 at 10 a.m. PT (1 p.m. ET, 6 p.m. BST, 3 a.m. AEST). The invite shows a glowing Apple logo on a light blue background, with the text “Surprise and shine” underneath.

The keynote will be held at Apple Park in Cupertino, California, and you’ll be able to follow every Apple announcement with CNET’s iPhone 18 event live blog that day.

Rumors suggest that Apple’s first foldable iPhone will finally be unveiled during the event. It may be called the iPhone Fold, iPhone Ultra or iPhone Flip — rumors have differed over its final name. Leaks suggest a book-style foldable, possibly in a passport size similar to the new Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8. Analysts suggest it’ll be priced between $2,000 and $2,500.

For the upcoming iPhone 18, rumors suggest the lineup of phones might come with variable-aperture cameras, a smaller Dynamic Island notification bar at the top of the display and a bigger battery. We’re expecting higher starting costs following Apple’s price hikes on Macs, iPads, HomePods and the Apple TV earlier this year. It’s also possible that Apple could split the iPhone 18 launch between fall and spring, showcasing the Pro phones in the September event and leaving the standard model for early 2027.

As for updated AirPods, Apple has been heavily rumored to include cameras in this year’s earbud offering. They would reportedly be an AI wearable, with the cameras functioning as visual sensors to give Siri AI more context about what’s happening around the wearer.

Lastly, we’re expecting the Apple Watch Series 12, which could include a ceramic model, improved screen technology, software optimizations for better battery life and more efficient processors. Rumors have pointed to there being no major design overhauls, but there could be improved blood pressure monitoring and Touch ID.

Tech.title: Flock Safety Is Losing Contracts on the Ground. Its Drones Are Already in the Air
Tech.content:
When a Flock Safety license plate reader gets covered with a trash bag or removed after a canceled contract, the camera stops seeing. When a Flock drone deploys from 300 feet at the tap of a dispatcher’s button, it’s considerably harder to stop.

The surveillance company that sparked a nationwide debate over AI-powered street-level monitoring has spent the past year building a parallel aerial capability, the result of its October 2024 acquisition of drone startup Aerodome for more than $300 million.

The Flock Alpha drone reads license plates from up to 2,000 feet, deploys autonomously within 90 seconds of a triggered alarm and covers up to 38 square miles. Privacy advocates who spent years focused on the cameras on poles are now looking up.

During an appearance on the All-In Podcast, Flock CEO and founder Garrett Langley gave the clearest indication yet of how much of a role drones will play in Flock’s future.

Describing drones as the company’s “fastest-growing business unit right now,” Langley said on the podcast that drones will account for nearly half of the company’s future revenue. He described drones as “the next big chapter in law enforcement,” with the potential to be as impactful as police body cameras.

Reading license plates from the sky

The emphasis on drones comes with the spread of “deflock” actions and grassroots opposition to license plate readers. After complaints that the LPRs can misidentify vehicles and that Flock’s network can be abused to target vulnerable populations, cities, including Los Angeles, have paused or canceled their contracts with the company.

In some communities, activists have taken down Flock cameras or physically disabled the hardware as a form of protest against surveillance. Organizations and individuals have crowdsourced the locations of local cameras, while municipalities that asked Flock to disable the cameras have put trash bags on them when their requests weren’t met.

Drones equipped with high-resolution cameras could be even more capable of identifying license plate numbers and tracking vehicle movement. And, of course, they’re harder to disable from the ground.

Instead of responding to a request for comment, the company sent CNET an automated response via email that read in part: “Our media team is currently touching grass and taking a break. Unlike our cameras, we can’t work 24/7, so we’ll get back to you when we’ve had a snack and regained the ability to form coherent sentences.”

Safety versus privacy

Flock’s website has product pages for drones that can be used as first-responder units in emergencies or by companies as automated security devices. The company told Business Insider that it plans to start manufacturing its own drones in Georgia and has about 200 of them deployed as first-responder devices.

During the All-In Podcast interview, Langley acknowledged that Flock sits dead center in the debate over personal privacy versus community safety. “What kind of society do we want to live in? I want to live in one where we’re safer. I want to keep my privacy while I do it, but it’s hard,” he said. “We’ve gotta find a common ground.”

Langley said that, unlike some of Flock’s competitors, the company does not use its cameras (presumably including those on drones) for facial recognition or for looking inside cars.

However, a recent investigation from Wired found that the company already has code that would expand its product’s capabilities to identify drivers and vehicles based on their movement patterns alone. While Flock Safety maintains that the software remains in a testing phase, privacy critics argue that the tool — called OS Investigate — integrates vehicle scan data with police incident reports and arrest records, transforming Flock’s camera network into a powerful system for generating suspect lists.

The expanded capabilities of drones used for surveillance have been met with criticism from the American Civil Liberties Union, which issued a report in March about the privacy dangers they present.

“If there is a drone in the sky above us, we should have a way to know whether that drone belongs to Amazon, the police, ICE, a real estate agent, or an ordinary citizen,” the ACLU report said. “We should also be able to see what the purpose of its flight is, what equipment it is carrying, and what its privacy practices are.”

Tech.title: AI Detectors Are Being Used to Discipline Students. I Tested Whether They Should Be
Tech.content:
Academic integrity offices across the country are making disciplinary decisions based on AI detection scores. Students are appealing grades and fighting academic misconduct charges on the strength of what those scores say. And the tools producing those scores, like Turnitin, GPTZero and the others, are operating with a confidence that my testing didn’t find them to have earned.

I submitted both AI-generated text and human-written text to every major detector I could access, documented the results, and reached a conclusion that anyone using this technology to evaluate student work should probably read before they do it again.

Detectors, homework helpers, essay writers, AI math wizards and even sneaky backdoor test assistants have entered the student-focused chats on cheating in a big way. Here’s a roundup of all the biggest tools and how they’re being used to get around old-school schooling.

Have AI write, and then rewrite it again

The big names like ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini and NotebookLM (now Gemini Notebook) still appear to be the gold standard for getting away with skipping out on writing in school. I spent an afternoon slinging assignments in PDF format into all these tools and each generated polished, accurate responses in the form of persuasive and well-researched essays.

Most students and educators already know about these use cases, but what is surprising is the closed loop created by AI and plagiarism-detection tools. In essence, the cops are helping the culprits get away with the heist. These companies are having their cake, eating it, throwing it up and selling it again as a muffin-of-the-month subscription.

I tried a number of AI text humanizers and tested them against AI detector tools, and after being “humanized,” every single blurb passed with flying colors.

There’s a lot of talk in and out of academic circles about whether AI-detection tools are accurate or useful. From my research for this piece, I can confidently say they are worthless. Unless you’re a student who used AI to write your work and want to prove you didn’t use AI to write your work.

Do your homework, but don’t

The idea that students are at least absorbing some part of the materials in assignments or school work when they use AI, because they have to copy and paste things and put together a cohesively structured output that illustrates learning outcomes they can review, has reached One Wish Willow levels of delusion.

I threw a PDF of an assignment that’s supposed to be AI-proof into Claude — one of those “make something out of your work” assignments that educators like to point to as a better outcome, even if AI is involved.

The only instruction I gave the tool was: “Do this assignment. Complete all the required elements, including the visual elements, and put them into a standardized, cohesive format for submission. pdf please.”

The tool produced a couple of slick infographics that looked good enough to be made by someone using a Canva template and not slick enough to raise any alarm bells on the part of an educator.

Created by Rachel Kane using Claude

This is just the right level of mediocre that passes classes, and at no time did I ever read the assignment or review the generated work. These types of deliverables from assignments were actually the most difficult to pin down as AI within the confines of my research. I used several AI image detectors, and the results were mixed.

In one case, a tool called Winstonai flagged my AI created infographic as 100% AI, but it also flagged a graphic I created long before generative AI was available to the masses as 100% AI.

Another AI image detector, AI or Not, determined my entirely AI infographic was just 1% AI.

AIorNot/Screenshot by CNET

So it’s not a foolproof method, and a student looking to get away with passing this work off as their own just has to point to conflicting detectors to shut down an argument.

Hard problems call for easy solutions

There were exactly zero AI apps, tools and services used in the research for this piece that claimed to be “cheating apps.” Instead, words like “study guide,” “homework helper,” and even the bold promise to provide an “A+ result” were used to advertise each tool’s capabilities.

That didn’t mean any of them balked at being asked for outright solutions to complete problems. or stop them from highlighting features like the Advanced Assignment Solver right next to Homework Helper. I wonder which appeals to a student using these tools.

Services like Gauth AI, a paid study helper, and Studocu, a free study helper with a paid tier that starts at $7 a month, either explicitly offered to do student work wholesale, or put up zero resistance to solving multipage, complex assignments when simply prompted with “do this assignment.”

I used Studocu to generate answers to a complex, five-page astronomy assignment (PDF) from the University of Northern Iowa that included explicit instructions to use a dataset unique to each student based on their student IDs.

Studocu/Screenshot by CNET

In a matter of seconds, the tool used the unique data given and the five-page assignment to generate customized answers to every problem. Gauth AI was also more than up to the task, for a price ($12 a month, or $100 for a year).

Gauth/Screenshot by CNET

Not bad, considering you could probably pass the class without ever having to look at an HR diagram, or even learn what one is.

Test taking when you didn’t study

Testing is supposed to be the time-honored, proven ground for measuring competency, but in the age of AI tools, it’s just another hurdle to limbo under.

Some universities are now doing testing differently, using randomization of questions from large pools and more in-person testing.

For those schools still testing with lockdown browsers and through timed digital, students can get around protections with a variety of easily available tools that utilize “stealth” or discreet windows and integrate AI software, like ChatGPT, to provide on-demand answers.

Tools like Hiding AI even use data on how test scores improved using their subscription-based software that claims to provide an undetectable experience ($192/year).

Hiding AI/Screenshot by CNET

Another covert AI tool that advertises itself as an exam helper, Pluely (starting at $15/month and up to $120 for a lifetime subscription), is particularly adept at call-and-response. All a student needs to do is read out the questions to the exam they’re taking, and Pluely will provide the answers in a discreet, undetectable window. All the student has to do is click.

The bottom line

For every AI app, service or tool designed to build and generate all the different mediums and modes educators are asking students to demonstrate competency, there is an equal and opposite AI app, service or tool designed to help them argue that the work was done by a human.

It’s a marketplace of double dips where the primary customer — the thousands of people keeping investors interested in a growing consumer base — is the student, not the educator.

No matter what it says in the marketing materials, these tools aren’t made to help teachers teach or students learn. They’re made to serve the core customer who most likely just wants to get it over with.

Correction, July 31: A previous version attributed tools and functionality to Turnitin that do not exist on that website.

Tech.title: Meta to Pay Up to $18 Billion to Settle With US States on Teen Social Media Addiction
Tech.content:
Instagram and Facebook’s parent company, Meta, has struck a deal with the US states currently suing the tech giant for intentionally designing its social media platforms to be addictive and harmful to children and teens. If approved by the court, CEO Mark Zuckerberg and the company will avoid a high-stakes trial, whose consequences could have significantly affected how the tech industry operates. Meta says it will pay approximately $18 billion.

Reuters first reported the settlement on Wednesday. According to court filings, Meta could pay up to $16.68 billion to states and territories in the agreement. In a blog post, Meta said it will initially pay over $12 billion to participating states, in annual payments over a 10-year period, to fund child safety initiatives. If Snap, TikTok and YouTube join the agreement, Meta will pay an additional $5.3 billion, bringing the company’s total up to $18 billion. Meta said it expects to pay $10 billion in legal expenses in the third quarter.

“Today, we have secured a settlement with Meta that will make social media less dangerous for our kids and make a world of difference for children and their families,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who helped lead the case, said in a statement Wednesday. The proposed agreement brings 47 states, the District of Columbia and US territories into the deal, not just the attorneys general who were party to the original lawsuit.

The settlement is ultimately less than 10% of Meta’s 2025 annual revenue ($201 billion), and it’s significantly less than the potential $200 billion penalty the states said would be likely during the early stages of the trial. It’s the proposed platform changes that will likely have the biggest impact on Meta.

Under the new rules, Meta will enforce default daily usage limits, including blocks during school hours and at nighttime. Stronger parental controls, more rigorous age-verification tech and limiting access to “extreme” beauty filters are also part of the deal. Teens won’t be able to see the total number of likes on their posts, either. They will also be able to turn off autoplay on videos, like Instagram Reels, and opt into a nonalgorithmic feed. All of these features are popular recommendations that have been made for years by psychologists, tech experts and child-safety advocates. Some are already part of Instagram’s teen accounts, which were rolled out in 2024.

“This is a historic settlement that will have a lasting impact, but we cannot truly protect all children and teens until these protections are required on every platform and are permanent – that’s something only Congress can do,” Sacha Haworth, executive director of The Tech Oversight Project, said in a statement.

In a blog post, Meta calls on TikTok and YouTube to join its efforts. “While this is an important step, the fact is that teens move fluidly between dozens of apps a day. All platforms should empower parents and support teens by putting the same measures in place, because we know that when teens are restricted on one app, they simply move to another,” the company wrote. Meta did not immediately respond to a request for additional comment.

Not every state is party to the agreement, notably Florida. James Uthmeier, Florida’s attorney general, told CNET: “The payouts to the states are peanuts compared to the profound harms Meta’s profit-driven addictive features have inflicted on our children. This agreement is nothing more than a slap on the wrist for a trillion-dollar corporation that has already paid more to its lawyers than it will pay the states. We’ll see them at trial.”

We rejected Meta’s weak payoff attempt.



Meta knows about the damage they caused, and we will hold them accountable in Florida. pic.twitter.com/40htzE0vHQ — Attorney General James Uthmeier (@AGJamesUthmeier) August 26, 2026

New Mexico is also not part of the deal, nor is Texas. However, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton announced on Wednesday that Meta will pay over $1 billion to remediate child safety concerns. Texas is taking TikTok to court later this year for similar reasons.

“We had hoped a nationwide settlement might echo the full strength of the protections New Mexico secured in court — including a direct ban on romantic and sexualized AI chatbot interactions with minors and stronger safeguards against adults targeting kids in private messages,” New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez said in a statement. “But this settlement still represents real progress and adds momentum to finish the job of protecting kids online.”

Social media giants like Meta and Google-owned YouTube have been under intense scrutiny in recent years for how well (or poorly) they protect their youngest users. In two separate landmark cases preceding this one, Meta was ordered to pay $375 million to the state of New Mexico after a jury ruled the company enabled child exploitation online. Soon after, a Los Angeles court ordered Meta and Google to pay a combined $3 million in damages for similar claims.

Tech.title: Ring Gave Itself a Security Makeover Called TAKE. Here’s What’s Actually Changing
Tech.content:
Starting this September, Amazon’s Ring security brand is clarifying how it encrypts customer data on cameras, including security video data used for AI analysis, like turning it into video descriptions on your phone. This begins with a unique Ring standard called Throw Away the Key Encryption.

Previously, Ring’s cloud practices were a bit of a black box. We knew the sort of encryption used, but not how easily or frequently Ring could access videos for analysis. Privacy concerns quickly followed, especially as Ring has come under scrutiny — and lawsuits — for features like its AI familiar face technology.

Now Ring has redefined the process and outlined several encryption practices made to give customers more protection or at least more information. Here’s how TAKE works.

A tale of two keys

Ring’s cloud storage is typically necessary to save videos and use intelligence features. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

TAKE is a new approach and a significant jump in transparency for Ring. When TAKE is used and a Ring camera records a video, that video is encrypted with rotating encryption keys, which means the keys are periodically updated with new versions.

One copy of the key is held in the cloud by Ring, in what Ring describes as a “secure enclave,” which requires specific permissions and situations to access. If you have any Ring artificial intelligence features enabled for your Ring device, like video descriptions and summaries, familiar face detection, advanced object recognition and so on, then Ring takes the key out of its vault and uses it — once — to analyze your video footage.

After Ring uses its copy of the key to analyze your video and use the data gathered, it deletes the key and can no longer access that video for any purpose. The company says, “Ring can only receive access to power the intelligent features that you have active on your account.” Ring also told me the company, “Only trains on video recordings that have been made publicly available, or on recordings from users who have given Ring explicit permission to use them for this purpose. Users can revoke permission at any time.” This indicates Ring won’t automatically be using its one-time key for other internal analysis purposes.

Meanwhile, you keep the master key for your Ring video, so you can access your cloud storage clips whenever and how often you want, until the cloud storage limit runs out. (Ring’s storage starts at 180 days.) If you have Shared Users on your Ring account who you’ve enabled to access videos, they’ll have this master key, too.

Jamie Siminoff, founder and chief inventor at Ring, told CNET, “We wanted to provide E2EE-like security while allowing customers to continue using all the features they expect from their Ring devices.”

What about end-to-end encryption?

Ring has excellent cameras, but you may want to turn off certain features. Tyler Lacoma/CNET

In the past, Ring has offered an end-to-end encryption mode for users to enable with a password. The video is automatically encrypted and can only be viewed by those who have the password. This option will remain with TAKE, offering the highest level of privacy for Ring security videos — but at a cost.

With the end-to-end encryption mode on, most of Ring’s cloud-based features won’t work. That includes all its AI features. However, you’ll still be able to use live view, access videos in cloud storage and share videos as long as you have your password. It’s a give and take that benefits anyone worried about Ring’s AI or analysis and wants to skip that part of the cameras altogether.

What if I don’t have a Ring subscription at all?

You can get local storage on Ring devices, but it will disable a lot of features. Julie Snyder/CNET

Without a Ring subscription, you can’t store videos in the cloud, so none of this really applies. There are ways to get local storage with Ring, notably using a Ring security hub, that can act as a local storage device if you add a microSD card. But much like end-to-end encryption, you won’t get any of Ring’s extra cloud features.

Getting Ring’s TAKE standard

The new TAKE approach is free for users, although you’ll have to pay a Ring subscription in the first place to access any of this cloud storage. Ring subscriptions start around $5 for a single camera, but you’ll need a $20 subscription to start accessing more advanced AI features and 24/7 professional monitoring.

Ring told me the TAKE standard will start rolling out in September, but the company didn’t give me any indication of how long it would take to update for all users. When it comes to your camera, TAKE will be turned on by default. I’ll keep an eye on my Ring app and let you know if I notice significant differences, although most of this update is behind the scenes.

Tech.title: The Google Pixel 11 Pro Still Has the Best Display for Gaming, but Other Troubles Emerge
Tech.content:
In 2025, I lauded the Google Pixel 10 Pro for its bright, vibrant display that was great to game on. Now, its successor has arrived, and although it looks identical — with some slight hardware changes — the luster has worn off. The Google Pixel 11 Pro feels underpowered when it comes to gaming, and odd glitches that emerged while playing make it harder to recommend for gaming on the go.

The Google Pixel 11 Pro is unquestionably the best phone Google has ever released, with its AI-powering Tensor G6 chip, a trio of great cameras with refined photo software and an expansive list of generative AI features. With all these advantages, the 11 Pro is one of the best phones out there for taking pictures. But its hardware and software edge doesn’t extend as much to gaming as other phones do, such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 and its Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 chip.

In practice, the Pixel 11 Pro struggles with higher graphics settings within games and will pop up warnings about overheating and battery drain when I pump it up above the lowest resolution, frame rate and detailing. It’s a bit surprising given the phone’s premium price.

That price has gone up, though in a roundabout way. Google got rid of the 128GB entry option for its entire lineup, so the $1,099 starting price for the Pixel 11 Pro with 256GB of storage is the same price as last year at that storage level — you just can’t pick up a lower-storage configuration for under $1,000 anymore. That’s especially limiting for mobile gamers, since installing multiple titles can quickly eat through the available storage. The action RPG Genshin Impact alone takes up 55GB.

When reached for comment, Google confirmed that the raised storage and price reflect the impact of the RAM shortage, driven by AI, which has made components more expensive across consumer tech. But it bites the Pixel 11 Pro phones in another way: That new entry model comes with only 12GB of RAM. You’ll still get 16GB with the 512GB and 1TB storage options ($1,219 and $1,499 respectively, $50 higher than last year’s prices), but it’s a bummer after last year’s 10 Pro series all shipped with 16GB.

Google says that this reduction in RAM doesn’t matter as much, since its 11 Pro phones are faster and smoother than last year’s, thanks to optimizations in silicon and software. I wasn’t able to test this claim, as the Pixel 11 Pro review unit Google sent me had 512GB of storage and 16GB of RAM, but it’s worth keeping in mind.

With those considerations, the Pixel 11 Pro starts off with compromises, which progressed as I spent more time gaming on the phone.

The Pixel 11 Pro’s svelte design made it easy to handle while gaming, though not everyone may be comfortable with the sizable camera block on the back side. David Lumb/CNET

What it’s like to play games on the Pixel 11 Pro

As with last year’s Pixel 10 Pro, the new Pixel 11 Pro stands out among other phones with its 6.3-inch OLED display. Details are crisp with its 2,856×1,280-pixel resolution, and colors are vivid with HDR10 Plus support.

Once again, the 3,600-nit maximum brightness sets the Pixel 11 Pro’s screen apart from competitors, allowing me to play in direct sunlight and brightening up dark rooms. Other phones are catching up, with screens on this year’s Samsung Galaxy S26 at 2,600 nits and the iPhone 17 Pro Max at 3,000 nits. But the Pixel 11 Pro maintains its lead, delivering a stunning array of colors and details in games across all genres.

The phone itself is comfortable enough to hold and play. While it’s physically identical to the Pixel 10 Pro from last year, the metal frame ringing the sides feels slightly more polished, leading my fingers to slip on it while gaming — perhaps the tiniest nitpick I’ve ever had with a phone. The wide camera bump on the back of the Pixel 11 Pro rises up enough to make for a decent finger hold, though unavoidably touching the bump’s metal rim and glass becomes a problem when the handset heats up during high-graphics gaming (more on that later).

The dual speakers at the top and bottom of the device pump out admirable sound. Like a lot of phones, the speaker on the bottom edge of the phone can be easily covered by a finger when holding the handset sideways to play games, which cuts off half the audio — unfortunate, but not uncommon.

What is extremely rare in gaming are the sound issues I ran into while playing the action RPG Diablo Immortal, in which the audio occasionally switched into an echoing, garbled mess. I’d never experienced this before.

Most games have touchscreen controls in the form of parts of the screen converted to digital buttons, which are suitable, if clunky, necessities when playing on an all-glass display. The Pixel 11 Pro had suitably responsive touch controls, and the only trouble was with my own fat thumbs incorrectly pressing one part of the display instead of another. A physical wrap-around controller is a big upgrade for most games, and I relished using my Backbone One to play Dead Cells and others that rely on fast responses with a range of options to dodge or attack.

Unlike some other premium Android phones, the Pixel 11 Pro has magnets embedded in its rear cover (playfully called Pixelsnap) that make it compatible with a lot of accessories, including wireless chargers. I was able to snap on an official Apple MagSafe charger and play while juicing it back up, which was convenient — and helpful. The phone’s 4,850-mAh battery lasted awhile through gaming, but its wired charging maxes out at 30 watts, which is slower than other phones, but I worry about the heat buildup if it were any faster. Its Qi2.2-supporting wireless charging tops out at 25 watts. Being able to top up in the middle of a play session was nice, even if it doesn’t match the faster 45-watt ability of a phone such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 Plus or even the 60-watt charging of the Galaxy S26 Ultra.

The Pixel 11 Pro is truly plug-and-play with the Backbone One after the Backbone app is installed — slide it in, pull it out and the game continues either way. David Lumb/CNET

The Pixel 11 Pro’s gaming problems are in the present Tensor

While the Pixel series’ Tensor chips power superior AI features such as Magic Eraser and live translation, they’ve been underpowered compared to other silicon in benchmark testing, with Pixel phones routinely coming in lower than devices running Snapdragon chips such as the Samsung Galaxy S26 series. Silicon makes a huge difference in graphically intensive tasks, like gaming.

It stands to reason that the Pixel 11 Pro’s Tensor G6 chip is what keeps it from mustering the higher-tier graphics capabilities that other premium phones achieve. When I loaded up Diablo Immortal, the game defaulted to the lowest graphical setting possible, and even just ratcheting that up to medium with a faster framerate, a pop-up warned me that I was risking overheating and battery drain.

Typical play, even with higher graphics settings, got the phone warm but not toasty, only reaching dangerous levels of heat when I had it plugged in to recharge and was downloading more game content. The camera block on the back of the phone became uncomfortable to touch with its metal rim and glass atop the cameras. Most games didn’t do this, and it was only in specific circumstances that the heat hit concerning levels, but it still leads me to conclude that the phone’s heat management isn’t quite as good as other premium phones during graphically heavy tasks.

It’s worth mentioning that, with heat management concerns, I removed Google’s official case from the phone to ensure heat could escape from the back and sides. This made the warm metal on the sides of the phone less comfortable to hold, but hopefully would keep it from cooking within the case.

Supposedly, this is Genshin Impact. Things still happened on-screen, but I couldn’t see what was going on. David Lumb/CNET

Then there’s the field of pink. I loaded up Genshin Impact, an older HoYoverse game that’s presumably more optimized than more recently released titles such as Wuthering Waves. Yet when I booted up Genshin (after downloading the 55GB of content), I loaded into the game’s world to find it awash in pink, a layer of obfuscating color that made it impossible to tell what was going on. Clearly, it was a graphical glitch, but one I reproduced over and over.

I’ve never had a major mobile game become unplayable just as I was dropping in, but a statement from Google confirmed that this particular issue is expected to be fixed soon: “We are currently working with our partner HoYoverse to address this optimization issue on the Pixel 11. A fix is expected to be implemented in Genshin Impact’s upcoming update.”

Combined with the odd audio issues on Diablo Immortal (again, something that hasn’t happened when loading the game on other phones), I’m unsure whether this is just post-launch glitching that’ll be fixed in immediate patches or a deeper issue with the phone’s hardware. It’s bothersome for sure, though these were the only bizarre issues I ran into across the half-dozen games I played.

Overall, the Pixel 11 Pro remains a good gaming phone for its fantastic display, which also shines when you’re taking photos and watching films and TV shows. Other concerns keep it from being a top recommendation for gaming, but if it’s a secondary or tertiary priority over photography and AI, the Pixel 11 Pro would serve you well — and hopefully those glitches won’t affect the games you want to play.
